Parametrische Universal-Adapterplatte Diese vollständig anpassbare Adapterplatte verbindet zwei unterschiedliche Befestigungs- beziehungsweise Lochbilder miteinander. Sie eignet sich ideal, wenn vorhandene Bohrungen weiterverwendet werden sollen, das neue Bauteil jedoch andere Befestigungspunkte besitzt. So können beispielsweise Sensoren, Kameras, Displays, Elektronikmodule, Netzteile, Gehäuse, Halterungen oder kleine Geräte montiert werden, ohne neue Löcher in eine Wand, Maschine oder vorhandene Konstruktion bohren zu müssen. Zwei unabhängig einstellbare Lochbilder Die Adapterplatte besitzt zwei getrennt konfigurierbare Lochbilder: Lochbild A – vorhandene Befestigung Dieses Lochbild wird passend zu den bereits vorhandenen Bohrungen eingestellt, beispielsweise an einer Wand, einem Gehäuse, einer Maschine oder einer bestehenden Halterung. Lochbild B – neues Bauteil Das zweite Lochbild wird passend zu dem Bauteil eingestellt, das auf der Adapterplatte montiert werden soll. Beide Lochbilder können unabhängig voneinander angepasst, verschoben und gedreht werden. Dadurch sind auch versetzte oder unterschiedlich ausgerichtete Befestigungen möglich. Anpassbare Lochanordnung Für jedes Lochbild kann separat gewählt werden zwischen: deaktiviertem Lochbild einer einzelnen Bohrung zwei Bohrungen in einer Reihe einem rechteckigen Vierlochbild Die horizontalen und vertikalen Abstände lassen sich unabhängig einstellen. Eine Zweierreihe kann durch Drehen des Lochbildes auch vertikal oder diagonal ausgerichtet werden. Runde Bohrungen oder Langlöcher Jedes Lochbild kann wahlweise mit normalen runden Bohrungen oder Langlöchern erzeugt werden. Langlöcher bieten zusätzliches Montagespiel und sind besonders praktisch, wenn vorhandene Lochabstände nicht exakt bekannt sind oder das montierte Bauteil später noch ausgerichtet werden soll. Einstellbar sind unter anderem: Durchmesser der Bohrungen Gesamtlänge der Langlöcher Ausrichtung der Langlöcher Drehung des gesamten Lochbildes horizontale und vertikale Position Die Ausrichtung der Langlöcher kann unabhängig von der Drehung des Lochbildes verändert werden. Optionale Schraubensenkungen Für jedes der beiden Lochbilder können optional Senkungen aktiviert werden. Dadurch können geeignete Schraubenköpfe bündig oder nahezu bündig in der Oberseite der Platte sitzen. Die Senkungen werden nur auf der Oberseite erzeugt. Die Unterseite der Adapterplatte bleibt vollständig flach und kann direkt auf dem Druckbett platziert werden. Optionaler mittlerer Ausschnitt Zusätzlich kann ein mittlerer Ausschnitt aktiviert werden. Zur Auswahl stehen: kein Ausschnitt runder Ausschnitt rechteckiger Ausschnitt rechteckiger Ausschnitt mit abgerundeten Ecken Der Ausschnitt kann verschoben und bei rechteckiger Ausführung auch gedreht werden. Dadurch eignet sich die Adapterplatte ebenfalls für: Kabeldurchführungen Steckverbinder Lüftungsöffnungen hervorstehende Gehäuseteile Schalter oder Bedienelemente Kameralinsen und Sensorbereiche Automatische Plattengröße Bei aktivierter automatischer Größenanpassung werden Breite und Höhe als gewünschte Mindestabmessungen verwendet. Benötigen die Lochbilder, Langlöcher oder der mittlere Ausschnitt mehr Platz, wird die Platte automatisch vergrößert. Dabei werden auch die eingestellten Verschiebungen, Drehungen, Senkungen und Randabstände berücksichtigt. Alternativ kann die automatische Anpassung deaktiviert werden. In diesem Fall verwendet das Modell exakt die eingestellten Außenmaße und prüft, ob ausreichend Platz für alle Elemente vorhanden ist. Gestaltung der Grundplatte Die Adapterplatte besitzt: abgerundete Ecken eine umlaufende Fase an der oberen Außenkante eine vollständig flache Unterseite eine mittige Positionierung um den Modellursprung frei einstellbare Plattendicke frei einstellbaren Abstand zwischen Aussparungen und Außenkante Durch die gefaste Außenkontur erhält die Platte ein sauberes und technisch ansprechendes Erscheinungsbild. Typische Anwendungen Die Adapterplatte eignet sich unter anderem für: Sensor- und Kamerahalterungen Elektronikmodule und Platinengehäuse Displays und Bedienelemente Netzteile und Steuergeräte Maschinen- und Werkstattzubehör Wandhalterungen Lüfter und Belüftungskomponenten Modellbau und Robotik Fahrzeug- und Camperausbauten Reparaturen und Umbauten vorhandener Befestigungen Hinweise zum 3D-Druck Das Modell ist für einen unkomplizierten Druck ausgelegt. Die flache Unterseite wird direkt auf dem Druckbett positioniert, während Senkungen und Außenfase nach oben zeigen. In dieser Ausrichtung ist normalerweise kein Stützmaterial erforderlich. Für mechanisch belastete Anwendungen sollten eine ausreichende Anzahl an Wandlinien und ein für den Einsatzzweck geeignetes Filament verwendet werden. Überschneiden sich Bohrungen, Langlöcher oder der mittlere Ausschnitt, werden die Bereiche miteinander verbunden. Dies kann bewusst genutzt werden, um spezielle Aussparungen oder besonders flexible Befestigungsmöglichkeiten zu erzeugen.

description: Log July 29, 2026 The .ino format file cannot be uploaded as an attachment, so the code has been uploaded to GitHub. Please visit https://github.com/tipflowmaker/8-bit-Animated-emojis/tree/main to download it. Explanation This is a new 8-bit model. Compared with the previous version, it eliminates the step of sampling and customizing PCBs, and an independent battery power supply system is added. The hardware assembly can be completed simply by soldering commonly available development board modules and batteries on the market. In addition, the structure and assembly scheme have been optimized, enabling the assembly of hardware components and the enclosure without screws. I have uploaded the Arduino code for displaying animated facial expressions on the exterior. If you have specific requirements, you can also program and develop customized new firmware on your own. My 3D printed model has been verified with the A1 Mini. Given the variations between different 3D printers, I have also uploaded the STP files of the 3D model. You can adjust the tolerance gaps of the model to achieve a better assembly fit. Bill of Materials 1 × ESP32C3 Super Mini Development Board 1 × 0.96-inch SSD1306 I2C OLED Display Module 1 × TP4056 Charging Module 1 × TTP223 Touch Sensor Module 1 × 702025 Specification Battery Assorted Connecting Wires Wiring Reference ESP32C3 Super Mini OLED Moudle TP 4056 TTP 223 Bater 5V OUT+ GND GND OUT- GND 3V3 VCC VCC GPIO 4 I/O GPIO 8 SDA GPIO 9 SCL B + + B- _ Notes The welding direction of the TTP 223 touch sensor is shown in the figure. The touch surface on the other side must be flat so that it can be assembled into the housing. In addition, since no external mechanical switch is equipped for the hardware section, the switching function is implemented via the software of the ESP32-C3. After flashing the Arduino program I uploaded, power-off can be achieved by pressing and holding the TTP223 touch panel for 5 seconds, putting the ESP32 into deep sleep mode. After powering off, pressing and holding the panel for 2 seconds turns the device back on. The sleep mode drastically cuts down battery power consumption. However, the LED power indicator on the ESP32-C3 Mini development board generates substantial leakage current that drains the battery. Therefore, this LED can be damaged using a soldering iron or tweezers to reduce standby power loss. Finally After you finish the hardware soldering work, refer to the attached document for the detailed assembly steps of the casing. Finally, if you like this project, feel free to leave your comments and likes, or give me a free boost.

Compact Desktop Speakers Bring high-end sound to your desk! These compact 3D-printed speakers are designed around the Tang Band W3-2141 3-inch full-range driver, offering crystal-clear sound, detailed mids, and surprisingly rich bass in a small package. Whether you're working, gaming, or listening to music, this setup elevates your desktop audio without taking up valuable space. Key Features Designed for Tang Band W3-2141: Tailored enclosure to get the maximum performance out of this 3" driver. Front Bass Ports: Dual front-facing ports deliver deep bass even if the speakers are placed close to a wall. Compact & Clean: Perfect minimalist design for any modern desk setup. Easy to Print: Optimized geometry for straightforward printing. What You Need (BOM) 2× Tang Band W3-2141 drivers 8× M3 screws (for driver mounting) Speaker cable & amplifier of your choice Polyfill or dampening material of your choice. Speaker sealing tape Assembly Guide Prep the Printed Enclosure: Clean up any stray stringing and ensure the mounting holes and port tubes are clear of debris. Add Sound Damping (Crucial for Bass!): Fill the inside of the cabinet with polyfill or acoustic stuffing. Not too loose, not too tight. This drops the tuning frequency from 85 Hz down to 76 Hz and cleans up unwanted resonances. Wire & Mount the Driver: Solder or attach your speaker wires to the Tang Band W3-2141 terminals, run the wire out through the rear holes, and secure the driver using M3 screws. Use a speaker sealing tape. Seal & Isolate: Ensure all wire exits/terminals are airtight (you can wrap the wires in painters tape) so air only moves through the front ports. 💡 Tip: Stick small rubber feet on the bottom to isolate vibrations from your desk!

description: Parametric PCB Mounting Tray Generator Create fully customizable mounting trays for PCBs and electronics modules directly in MakerWorld’s Parametric Model Maker. The generator supports different PCB sizes, mounting-hole patterns, support heights, tray styles and retention methods. It is designed for electronics enclosures, control panels, test equipment, workshop projects, prototypes and custom installations. Custom PCB dimensions The tray can be adjusted to match the required board size. Available PCB settings include: PCB width PCB height PCB thickness edge clearance support height tray border corner radius The model is centered and generated with a flat underside for easy printing. Three PCB mounting styles Screw Standoffs Creates cylindrical supports for PCBs with mounting holes. The standoff system includes adjustable: outer diameter screw-hole diameter support height optional locating collar locating clearance screw-hole lead-in chamfer The locating collar can enter the PCB mounting hole and help position the board accurately before installation. Snap Clips Creates flexible side clips for boards without mounting holes. Clip width, thickness, overhang, clearance and the number of clips per side can be adjusted. The PCB rests on integrated supports and is retained by the clips without additional screws. Sliding Rails Creates two side rails with grooves for inserting the PCB from one end. Rail height, wall thickness, groove depth and groove clearance can be customized. One end is lowered to provide an insertion opening, while the opposite end can act as a stop. This style is useful when the PCB should remain removable without accessing mounting screws. Rectangular or individual mounting-hole layouts The screw-standoff version supports two different hole-layout modes. Rectangular Pattern Creates a regular two-hole or four-hole arrangement using horizontal and vertical spacing values. This is suitable for boards with symmetrical corner mounting holes. Individual Positions Up to eight mounting holes can be positioned independently. Each hole receives its own X and Y coordinate measured from the PCB center. This makes it possible to reproduce asymmetric or irregular mounting patterns found on many real circuit boards. The complete hole layout can also be rotated around the PCB center. Solid Tray or Open Frame Solid Tray Creates a continuous protective base below the PCB. This version provides maximum stiffness and separates the PCB from the mounting surface. Open Frame Creates a lightweight frame with internal support beams. Every active screw standoff is automatically connected to the nearest frame edge, including individually positioned mounting holes. This prevents unsupported standoffs and keeps the structure printable and stable. External mounting options The tray can be attached to an enclosure, wall or machine using optional external mounting tabs. Available configurations include: no external mounting corner tabs side tabs The mounting tabs include configurable hole diameter, tab diameter, neck width, anchor depth and optional countersinks. Their broad connection to the tray improves strength compared with a narrow teardrop-style attachment. Cable access An optional cable opening can be added to one side of the tray. Available positions include: left right front back The width and depth of the opening can be adjusted for wires, connectors or cable bundles. Typical applications The generator is suitable for: Arduino and ESP32 projects Raspberry Pi accessories relay and sensor modules custom control systems test equipment robotics power-supply modules workshop electronics enclosure inserts prototype installations custom PCB mounting solutions Printing The tray is designed for FDM printing with its flat underside placed directly on the build plate. In most configurations: no supports are required screw standoffs print vertically external mounting tabs remain flat on the build plate open-frame supports are generated automatically the model can be printed as one piece Use sufficient wall thickness and a suitable material when the tray will be exposed to mechanical load or elevated temperatures. Important note PCB dimensions and mounting-hole positions vary between manufacturers and board revisions. Always measure the actual PCB and verify: outside dimensions board thickness mounting-hole diameter mounting-hole coordinates required clearance around components connector and cable access screw and standoff dimensions

description: Embroidery Stitch Spacing Guide (3 Sizes) I'm notoriously bad at finishing projects... but apparently I'm really good at making tools for projects I'll probably never finish. 😂 I picked up embroidery and somehow my brain skipped right past "practice" and landed on "design custom embroidery tools." So if I ever actually finish this embroidery, I'll be sure to let you know. Until then... here's a stitch spacing guide. My stitches used to look like a ransom note. Some tiny. Some huge. Absolutely no rhythm. These little guides fix that. Each guide has two stitch spacings, one on each long edge. Every tooth marks exactly where your next stitch should begin. Lay the guide on your hooped fabric, mark each point with a heat-erase or water-soluble pen, lift it away, and stitch dot-to-dot. Or skip the dots and stitch directly against the teeth if you enjoy living dangerously. What's Included Four guides with eight stitch spacings : 1.5 + 2.0 mm 2.5 + 3.0 mm 3.5 + 4.0 mm 4.5 + 5.0 mm The spacing is embossed directly onto each guide. Teeth wrap around the rounded ends, making it easy to keep stitch spacing consistent around curves. A small break in the teeth clearly separates the two spacing sizes. A raised center grip makes the guide easy to lift from taut fabric. Prints flat with no supports. Each guide uses about 1 gram of filament and prints in roughly 12 minutes . Print each guide in a different color and you'll always grab the right one at a glance. This is not therapy. It's just really, really evenly spaced stitches. 🖤

description: The Ultimate Ball Generator Create fully customizable decorative, sensory, toy, or hanging balls directly in MakerWorld. Adjust the ball dimensions, surface pattern, hole spacing, wall thickness, colors, custom text, and hanging ring without using external CAD software. One generator. Endless possibilities. Create personalized balls with names or logos, Christmas ornaments, keychains, sensory and fidget toys, bouncing balls, decorative spheres, party favors, and unique gifts. Mix patterns, colors, text styles and accessories to generate thousands of completely different designs — all in just a few clicks. Main Features Ball diameter from 20 to 150 mm (larger also possible per request) Adjustable wall thickness from 1 to 5 mm Airless or solid spheres Multiple pattern styles: Circle Hexagon Diamond Rectangle Triangle Teardrop Heart Flower Star Four pattern effects: None – smooth ball Hole – openings through the shell Emboss – recessed pattern Raised – pattern raised above the surface Adjustable pattern size, spacing, rotation and marking depth Optional rounded pattern edges Optional Seam decorations (basketball, tennis ball, soccer ball, …) Custom text with multiple fonts Two text background styles: Text Outline – background follows the actual letter shapes Plaque – rounded rectangular nameplate Flat, embossed or raised text Adjustable text margin and nameplate curvature Optional reinforced hanging ring Custom colors for the ball, text background and lettering Adjustable sphere resolution for better quality or prototyping How to Customize Ball Dimensions Use Diameter to select the overall size of the ball. Wall Thickness determines the shell thickness when the Hole effect is selected. A value of 2–3 mm is a good starting point for most prints. Sphere Resolution controls surface smoothness: Draft – fastest preview Standard – quick testing Smooth – good balance Fine – recommended default Great or Ultra – smoother result, but longer generation time Pattern Choose the desired shape using Pattern Type . Use: Pattern Size to control the size of each element Pattern Spacing to control the visible gap between elements Pattern Angle to rotate the pattern on the ball Pattern Marking to control emboss depth or raised height Add Fillet on Pattern to round the pattern edges Small patterns combined with very small spacing can create a large number of elements and significantly increase generation and slicing time. Seams (decoration) Use this predefined seam decorations that adds a final touch to your ball. Available now: Basketball Basketball retro Tennis Baseball Soccer ball (football) Custom Text Set Custom Text to On , then enter your message. Choose between: Text Outline for a compact background following the letters Plaque for a traditional rounded rectangular label Text Margin controls the space or outline around the lettering. Plaque Curve Correction allows fine adjustment of how tightly the background follows the ball: Negative values create a flatter curve Positive values wrap the background more tightly The default value is tuned for most ball and text sizes Text effects: Flat – flush multicolor lettering Emboss – recessed lettering Raised – lettering above the surface For multicolor models, download the generated 3MF to preserve the separate ball, background and text colors. Hanging Ring Enable Hanging Ring to add a reinforced loop at the top. Adjust: Ring Hole Size for the string or ribbon opening Ring Thickness for the strength of the loop This option is useful for ornaments, decorations and hanging sensory toys. The color of the ring can be customized in Color section. Best Practices / Tips At first lower Ball resolution to Draft. When done designing try making it higher (only if needed). Please note that dense patterns actually are very good at Draft and there is no need to set higher resolution. Pattern Fillet can be quite heavy to process on the servers but in most of the cases is not needed. If you expirience server timeouts or errors consider turning it off. When you expirience server timeout or errors it most likely means that your set-up is to heavy to process on MakerWorld's servers. Try larger patter or higher spacing, lower resolution. Everything that will make it less complicated will work and try again. Consider the position of the ball when you will be printing it. For example when using heart pattern - the middle part of heart can not face down as you will need to support every patter like this. Thy setting an angle and face it up. The larger the ball is the more render power it requires on MM servers. If you plan going large try less details. Printing Tips Printing spheres is quite challenging and it is important to choose the right options in the slicer. Here are some tips to achieve the best results: Use the generated 3MF when printing in multiple colors. A layer height of 0.16–0.20 mm works well. Enable option “Don't support bridges” Add “Support Blocker” modifier to block supporting areas inside the ball. Rise the blocker a little bit so the base can be supported Tune your “Top Z distance” value for supports Use at least three wall loops for hollow balls. Enable supports when required by the selected pattern and orientation. Build-plate-only supports are usually easier to remove. For small holes, verify the preview before printing. Reduce print speed on the outer wall for a smoother spherical surface. Larger balls, dense patterns and Ultra resolution require more processing time. To achieve optimal bounce, use a suitable filament (TPU, PEBA, other flexible filaments). Important Notes Hole produces a hollow ball using the selected wall thickness. None , Emboss and Raised produce a solid ball. Very thin walls or extremely small gaps may not print reliably with every nozzle size. This generator creates geometry dynamically, so complex configurations can take longer to generate in MakerWorld. Make sure to follow my profile on Maker World for updates and ready to use examples. Have fun printing!

description: Editors note: (Here's the revised version of my previous model: Highest Flying Outdoor Plane - Best-printed Glider. It fixed some of the most commonly reported issues, including easy breakage, glue assembly, and inconsistent flight.) Intro: Hello everyone! Get ready for some serious reading :D-Its all important stuff though, so for the best flying results, read this . This is my plane/glider model, “Loopy V2”. This project took heavy inspiration from " exosequitur " on Thingiverse. While I got the idea of an outdoor glider plane from their model, I can assure you that mine is an original model with added features such as a launching tab, built-in top fin, Slide on head and hook, and adjustable wing elevation. Furthermore, I will link their model in the description in case anyone wants to know what inspired this project. Assembly: Anyway, there are a couple of things you should know before printing. MAKE SURE YOUR BED IS CLEAN. Before removing any parts from the build plate, WAIT FOR IT TO COOL COMPLETELY . Also, GENTLY bend the plate when removing the plane and parts. This model includes three parts: the plane body, the head, and the hook. The side of the head without the slit should be pointed forward, and the curved side of the hook should be pointed backwards. To assemble, you simply place the hook into the plane, then slide the head onto the slit in the hook. After this, I advise that you GENTLY bend the main wings and back wings up (a good amount). If your plane is nose-diving immediately after launch, bend both the main and back wings upward more (keeping them even). (You can see the recommended angle in the image below). Launching: Next, launching. The best angle for launching is around a 65-degree angle upwards . This allows the plane to do a big loop, then swoop into a smooth glide. Another way to launch is a 65-degree angle upwards with the plane tilted left (as shown in an image below). This makes the plane do a sweeping boomerang-like flight. However, windy days allow for a special launch method. This strategy includes launching the plane at an almost 90-degree angle upwards. If the plane gets high enough, you can catch a wind current and take off. I've had planes fly hundreds of yards with this method. Although, it takes a pretty windy day , and a few tries to do it. For launching in general, you obviously need your launch stick and rubber bands. I used some large rubber bands from Amazon (named in BOM). Another tip: If your plane is flying left or right, then dipping, bend the wing pointing in the direction the plane is dipping, upwards . For example , if your plane is dipping right , bend the right wing up a bit. Always try to keep the wings at the same angle upwards, and this should fix your issues. Last tip: While it seems counterintuitive, you don't need a huge launch for a cool flight; sometimes all it takes is a windy day and a softish launch for some awesome and far gliding. Outro: If you enjoy this model, be sure to leave a thumbs up, boost, and send me a picture of your own. Also dont be afraid to paint, or draw (with a sharpie) on your plane . Its a cool way to add an extra touch without switching filament mid print or AMS. Anyways, happy printing and have fun! the inspiration: https://www.thingiverse.com/thing:97803 Reccomended Wing Angles (higher=less nosediving)

model_name: Midea PortaSplit Condensate Cleaning Tablet Holder
description: For cleaning the condensate tray at the bottom of the Midea PortaSplit. Earlier manuals recommend cleaning the condensate tray with AC cleaning tabs. However the PortaSplit doesn't really come with an ideal location to put these tabs - one might be able to squeeze them in behind the plastic to the left and right of the slot where you can reach the condensate tray from, but I was worried that vibrations might carry the tab out of there. Putting the tabs directly into the reservoir makes them dissolve far too quickly. The purpose of this model is to try to keep the tab above the standing water level, so the tab is never fully submerged. Instead the condensate can drip onto the tablet, and (ideally) drain from the holder immediately. I generated this model for the StayClean Cleaning Tablets, and it will likely not fit tabs that are larger. Ideally print with a water resistant filament like ASA or PETG. If you use PLA, it might degrade quicker, so a reprint every year might be needed. Probably good to inspect it for bacterial growth, and ideally clean monthly. Use at your own risk, I take no warranty whatsoever that this works as intended. It might break your device, kill you, or summon Cthulhu. I also haven't properly tested this model really myself yet since there was currently no need for the AC at this time. I might update this post when I do test it, but I just wanted to get it uploaded in case people might want to try it and so I don't forget.

Inspired by the two other charging docks for the Xteink X3 I decided to build my own version which has a better fitting pogo pin. The front plate gets pushed onto the pin after inserting it, no glue needed. There are two versions of the front plate: Flush: This version has the same thickness as the plastic part of the pogo connector and only the metal pins are sticking out. Recessed: A little bit thinner than the Flush version, which works better if you use a case. At the back there is also a simple cable guide if you want to have your cable on the other side. For reference, this is the case I'm using: https://makerworld.com/de/models/2968787-xteink-x3-tpu-case#profileId-3329174 With that case both Flush and Recessed works! If you have a different case you may need to play around with the thickness of the front plate but you can just scale the Z value in the slicer itself. If you don't use any case at all the device does actually float while attached to the charger, which is less sturdy but still works. You will probably use more force than you might be comfortable with, but it will work without breaking. I designed this to have dual color knobs. They only rotate the same distance as the real thing, therefore you want to make sure the knob is at somewhere between 7 and 5 before you snap them down. It's easy to tell if you are using two colors, if you are using only single colors, look inside the knobs and you will see where the cutout is and is not. You have a pretty wide margin of error. The two little black bolts are the hinges for the lid. They fit snug through the lid and looser into the base. Still I recommend a bit of glue near the head, so it firmly attaches to the lid while letting the deeper part rotate freely. The spring is asymmetrical. It matches the contour of the rim of the base.

description: Mault, a MTG card scanner/sorter. I built a machine that scans Magic cards with a webcam, identifies them with an AI model, and sorts them into bins with an Arduino + servos. How it works: A feeder servo pulls a card into view of a webcam, it gets cropped and identified automatically, then you set up whatever sorting rules you want (color, rarity, price, set, whatever) in a small web app. The Arduino handles the actual routing, trapdoor/paddle/pusher servos push the card into the right bin. What's here: - 3D files for the enclosure and modules (Fusion 360 source + a ready-to-print .3mf) - Arduino sketch, wiring diagrams, BOM - The web app source (handles the AI identification, bin config, calibration, etc.) - A build guide (Currently being worked on so it may change) BOM at a glance: Arduino Uno R4 Minima, a PCA9685 servo driver, a handful of SG90 servos, an IR sensor for feed detection. It's all open source, with the full code on GitHub: https://github.com/dishwasher-detergent/mault . Print it, change it, use a different card game rule set, whatever. If you build one or improve on the design I'd really like to see it, and if you run into issues or want to fix something, PRs/issues are open. Here is a small demo of the card sorter running: Web App Features: - Watch as cards are being scanned, on other devices. Each scanning session is available to anyone in your organization, so they can see what's scanned in and if there are any issues. - Send notifications to discord incase of jams, errors, or if it finishes. - Create custom filters for anything you see on the card. - Export the scanned cards to Moxfield, Manabox, TCG, CardKingdoms buy list, and more coming soon. description: I wanted a companion cube cover for the Steam Machine that didn't require a bunch of magnets, screws and other BOM parts to put together. I designed this to line up with the existing Steam Machine vents and air intake as best as possible given that we are putting a cover over-top of the entire device. Description Add an elegant artistic touch to your reading with this decorative butterfly and floral bookmark. The design features a large symmetrical butterfly, flowing vines, leaves, flowers, and ornamental side details inspired by lace and stained-glass artwork. The three stacked color layers create a clean, detailed appearance while keeping the model thin and practical for everyday use. This model is designed as a flat, multicolor print. The colors are created by changing filament at specific layers, so an AMS or AMS Lite is convenient but not required. Model Features Elegant butterfly and floral design Three-color layered artwork Thin and lightweight bookmark Flat printing orientation No supports required Suitable for PLA and PLA Matte Compatible with AMS, AMS Lite, or manual filament changes Colors can be customized without modifying the model Designed for a 0.4 mm nozzle Model Dimensions Width: approximately 50 mm Height: approximately 160 mm Thickness: approximately 1.68 mm Recommended Print Settings Printer used: Bambu Lab A1 Nozzle: 0.4 mm Layer height: 0.08 mm Initial layer height: 0.16 mm Material: PLA or PLA Matte Wall generator: Arachne Wall loops: 2 Top shell layers: 5 Bottom shell layers: 3 Supports: Not required Print orientation: Flat on the build plate Build plate: Textured PEI Plate Brim: Optional, recommended if you experience edge lifting For the best detail, keep the original model size and use the included layer-height settings. Color Change Instructions The included print profile uses the following color arrangement: Layers 1–10: White Layers 11–16: Pink Layers 17–20: Black Insert the filament changes at the following points: Change from White to Pink after Layer 10 , approximately at Z = 0.88 mm Change from Pink to Black after Layer 16 , approximately at Z = 1.36 mm The final model height is approximately 1.68 mm . AMS and Manual Color Changes An AMS or AMS Lite can automatically handle the three colors. An AMS system is not required. Users with a single-filament printer can add pauses in the slicer and manually replace the filament: Start printing with White. Pause after Layer 10 and load Pink. Pause after Layer 16 and load Black. Continue printing until completion. Make sure the filament is fully loaded and extruding cleanly before resuming the print. Customize Your Colors The White, Pink, and Black combination is only a suggested color palette. You can replace the three colors with any combination you prefer. For the clearest visual result: Use a light color for Layers 1–10. Use a contrasting accent color for Layers 11–16. Use a dark color for Layers 17–20. The upper dark layer forms the outlines and important decorative details, so a darker filament is recommended for maximum contrast. Suggested color combinations: Ivory White → Sakura Pink → Black White → Desert Tan → Charcoal White → Lilac Purple → Black Ice Blue → White → Dark Blue Lemon Yellow → Mandarin Orange → Black White → Dark Red → Black Beige → Caramel → Dark Brown You only need to replace the filament colors. The model geometry does not need to be edited. Important Notes Do not change the layer height unless you also recalculate the color-change positions. Avoid reducing the model size significantly, as some decorative lines may become too thin for a 0.4 mm nozzle. Make sure the build plate is clean to prevent the long bookmark from lifting. Allow the build plate to cool before removing the print. Remove the bookmark carefully to avoid bending the thin decorative areas. Different filament brands and colors may produce slightly different levels of contrast.

description: I have ADHD, and it sounds dumb, but keeping track of what shot I'm on feels like the worst kind of mental math. Somewhere between "was that my third or fourth?" and actually lining up the next shot, the number just evaporates. I feel my ADHD on the golf course more than almost anywhere else. So I came on MakerWorld looking for a fix and didn't find exactly what I was looking for. Shot counters existed, but they all lived in your pocket — and pulling it out of your pocket every stroke makes it less accessible than just popping it off your hat. So I built one with a magnetic hat clip: click the wheel after each shot, pull it off to mark your ball on the green, snap it back. No pockets involved. How it works - The hat clip slides onto your brim and holds the counter magnetically - Thumb-roll the exposed wheel edge to advance the count after each shot - The window on the face shows your current stroke count - It doubles as your ball marker — pull it off, mark your ball, snap it back Required hardware — 2 magnets - 2× round neodymium magnets, 8 mm diameter × 1.8 mm thick - One press-fits into the hat clip, one into the back of the stroke counter - ⚠️ Check polarity before gluing — orient the magnets so the counter snaps onto the clip, then secure each with a drop of CA glue

description: Dayton Audio Reference Series 2.1 - Speakers & Sub Based on the Dayton Audio Reference collection, a 2.1 speaker system running the RS100-8 4" full range driver, the RSS210HO-8 8" subwoofer and SPA300-D 300 Watt plate amplifier. The left and right speaker need to be run from a dedicated amplifier, with lowpass/subwoofer output that can pass to the subwoofers dedicated amplifier. The main left and right speaker are slot ported and are in 2 pieces to allow for easy removal of supports. The subwoofer is a sealed enclosure with heavy bracing and with the plate amplifier sealed in it's own box. The full range drivers are 30W @ 8ohms so very easy to drive. Although the plate amplifier is 300W @ 4ohms and the subwoofer is 300W @ 8ohms, the plate amplifier still drives the subwoofer very well and gets very loud. I run the speakers as my daily's from my Fosi ZA3 and ZH3 Stack (see my other models for the Z Stack housing!) and it sounds GREAT! Each enclosure is printed at 30% infill to prevent resonance. The main left and right speakers have a selection of feet, from 5 degree and 10 degree feet and stands, these all share the same fitting dimensions and can easily be swapped out. Required parts: 2x Dayton Audio RS100-8 4" driver 1x Dayton Audio RSS210HO-8 8" subwoofer 1x Dayton Audio SPA300-D plate amplifier 2x Dayton Audio BPA-38G binding post (pair) 1m speaker cable Spade connectors 32x CNC Kitchen M4x8.1 threaded inserts - 10x per speaker, 22x for subwoofer M4 screws - 6x black dome head per speaker, 18x black dome head for subwoofer and plate amp, 4x countersunk per set of feet CA Glue Adhesive Rubber feet (optional - helps stop the speakers slipping or vibrating on hard surfaces) Printing: I used Bambu PLA Basic for the enclosures and Bambu PLA Matte for the feet. I have found this to be perfectly strong enough with 30% infill and 4 wall loops. This may be overkill but the enclosures have come out strong and to my ear sound great. The subwoofer enclosure was obviously an extremely long and filament consuming print, at 2.8Kg and 2 days, 12 hours. The speaker enclosures come in at 1.2Kg and 24 hours each (for both enclosure and rear panel). The print profiles are my recommended settings and orientation. I printed each enclosure face down on the Smooth PEI plate. I ended up making the main speakers 2 piece as after several attempts at an fully enclosed version and needing to use strong supports, I found I could not extract the supports via the small speaker opening. No such issues with the subwoofer as obviously the much larger speaker opening. Assembly: Left and Right speakers Remove all print supports and make sure all faces are clean and clear of any lumps or bumps. Especially the interface with the speaker rubber gasket and the rear panel V groove. Press in the threaded inserts to the base for the feet and front baffle for the speaker. Careful not to press too hard as the threaded inserts and heat can cause the rear of the front panel to melt through. Press in the binding posts to the rear panel before attaching the panel to the main enclosure. I found with some other filaments (e.g. Sunlu) the binding post holes ended up slightly smaller and needed a lot of force to press in. Bambu PLA did not seem to have this issue. If in doubt try a bit of heat on the binding post to press it in, the same as a threaded insert. DO NOT try and pull the posts in by stressing the inside bolts, they are soft metal and the threads will strip. Apply a thin layer of CA glue to the V groove in the back of the enclosure and carefully press into place the rear panel. The panel should be a tight fit but end up flush with the rear of the enclosure. DO NOT apply too much glue or it will just leak into the enclosure and make a mess. Clamp (or apply weight) and let the glue dry. Add the fixings/nuts to the inside of the binding posts and attach a suitable length of speaker cable (approx 6 inches) using spade or the circular terminals that came with the posts. Add spade connectors to the other end of the cable to fit onto the speaker. Attach the cable to the speaker and lower the speaker into plate, carefully as the speaker terminals may need to be maneuvered around the edge of the opening. Screw the speakers into place. Screw the feet to the enclosure. Subwoofer Remove all print supports and make sure all faces are clean and clear of any lumps or bumps. Especially the interface with the speaker rubber gasket and plate amplifier. Also check that the small hole that passes the speaker cable from the amp to the main enclosure is free from any sharp edges. Press in the threaded inserts to the base for the feet, front baffle for the speaker and plate amplifier. Careful not to press too hard as the threaded inserts and heat can cause the rear of the front panel to melt through. Peel enough protective/anti-vibration foam covering from the speaker cable that is soldered to the plate amplifier to reach where the subwoofer speaker terminals will be located. If in doubt peel more rather than less, as trying to remove more after starting to pull the cable through the hole is very tricky. Carefully feed the plate amplifier speaker cable through the small hole from the plate amplifier enclosure into the main speaker enclosure. Try not to pull too much speaker cable through as it could vibrate against the enclosure if there is too much slack. Screw the plate amplifier to the enclosure. Strip approx 10mm of the end of the speaker cable. Start to lower the subwoofer into the enclosure and insert the speaker cable into the spring loaded terminals. Another pair of hands is helpful with this part. Screw the subwoofer into place. Screw the feet to the enclosure. Operation IMPORTANT - Depending on your location, the plate amplifier can be set to 110V or 240V. YOU MUST SET THE VOLTAGE SELECTOR AND INSTALL THE CORRECT FUSE FOR YOUR SUPPLY VOLTAGE. If you don't do this you could start blowing fuses, tripping breakers, or worse. Read the plate amplifier instructions on how to set the various switches and dials. Likewise check your amplifier specification and instructions before connecting anything and powering it on just to make sure everything is correctly set up! Attach the left and right speakers to your amplifier with speaker cable. Attach the plate amplifier to your amplifier lowpass/subwoofer out with an RCA/phono cable/Y-cable (per Dayton and your amplifier vendor instructions). Set the subwoofer plate amplifier volume to low and power on the plate amplifier, gradually adjust (per the Dayton instructions) to suit your listening requirements.

description: 🥤 Universal Clamp-On Camping Chair Cup Holder Never spill your drink at the campsite again! This Universal Clamp-On Cup Holder attaches securely to a wide variety of camping chairs, lawn chairs, and outdoor equipment frames. Designed with flexibility and convenience in mind: the cup holder detaches from the clamp for easy transport, and the flexible cage walls fit standard 85mm cans/mugs while flexing outward to accommodate larger tumblers. Note: An optional print profile featuring TPU anti-slip pads is included to give the clamp maximum grip on smooth metal frames and protect painted legs from scratches! ✨ Key Features Front Handle Opening: Features a vertical cutout along the front, allowing camp mugs and cups with handles to fit effortlessly. Smart Drink Gripping System: Multiple flexible vertical fingers wrap around smaller cans and mugs to hold them securely without rattling, while built-in bottom support ledges keep drinks stable. Advanced Mechanical Clamp: Features a print-in-place rotating nut and guided slot holes in the jaw, allowing the clamp mechanism to adjust smoothly against various rod diameters without binding. Flexible 85mm+ Capacity: Designed for standard drinks while allowing the outer cage walls to expand slightly for larger travel mugs and tumblers. Universal Compatibility: Smooth-threaded clamp easily adjusts to securely grip round metal tubes of various diameters. Modular Two-Part System: Cup holder slides and locks into place on the clamp body, making it easy to disassemble and pack flat. 100% 3D Printed: No hardware required! Every screw, pin, and structural component is fully 3D printed. Optional TPU Anti-Slip Grips: Print profile includes flexible TPU pads that snap into the clamp jaws to prevent rotation on slick aluminum tubes. Outdoor-Ready & Drainage Friendly: Lightweight open slotted design allows condensation and rain to drain freely. 🛠️ Assembly Instructions 🔩 Step 1: Assembling the Main Screw The threaded clamp screw is designed in two halves for maximum strength along the layer lines and support-free printing. Insert Alignment Keys: Take the two rectangular alignment pins/keys and press them into the rectangular sockets on one half of the screw. Join the Halves: Align the matching sockets on the second screw half with the protruding keys, then press the two halves firmly together. (Optional / Recommended) Glue for Permanence: Add a small drop of superglue (CA glue) into the alignment sockets or along the flat mating face before pressing the halves together to ensure the screw never separates during tightening. 🔩 Step 2: Clamp Assembly Prepare the Hinge Jaws: Lay out the movable clamp jaw, the main clamp body, and the hinge pin. Align the Components: Bring the two main clamp bodies together. Align the pivot loop on the movable jaw so it is centered between the upper and lower pivot loops of the main body. The holes in all three loops must be perfectly concentric. Insert the Hinge Pin: Take the hinge pin and insert it from the top down through the aligned upper loop, the middle loop, and the lower loop. 🔩 Step 3: Threading the Clamp Screw Insert Screw: Take your fully assembled main screw from Step 1 and align it with the threaded socket on the back of the clamp body. Hand-thread the screw directly into the print-in-place rotary nut embedded inside the clamp housing. Continue threading by hand until the tip passes through and interfaces cleanly with the guided slot holes in the movable jaw. 🔩 Step 4: Chair Mounting & Final Setup Mount to Chair: Open the hinged clamp jaws and position them around the desired frame tube or rod on your camping chair. Tighten Securely: Turn the knob by hand until the jaws firmly grip the chair leg. (Hand-tighten only—no external tools needed!) Attach Cup Holder: Slide the cup holder's mounting slot down over the mating tab on the clamp body until it locks into place. Ready to Use: Drop in your favorite can, bottle, or tumbler and enjoy your trip! 🔩 Step 5: Optional TPU Anti-Slip Pad Installation If you have printed the TPU anti-slip pads to provide maximum grip and protect your chair’s finish, install them now. Orient the Pads: Examine the two printed TPU pieces. Note that one of the TPU pieces features a distinctive cut or notch along its edge. Install the Cut Pad: Press the TPU piece with the cut firmly into the recess of the larger, static jaw of the clamp body. The cut is designed to clear the internal screw mechanism. Install the Standard Pad: Take the second, standard TPU pad (without the cut) and press it firmly into the recess of the smaller, movable clamp jaw. Confirm Secure Fit: Ensure both pads are seated flush and securely within the clamp jaws before mounting the clamp to your chair. 💬 Feedback & Support: If you enjoyed printing this model, please leave a rating, post a picture of your setup, or drop a Boost ! description: Time to take your Insta360 Luna cinematography to the next level! This sturdy camera rig helps you get low angle shots, sweeping pans and other cinematic shots with more comfort and control. The camera rig has been filed tested with a real Luna Ultra camera and has even been durability tested to make sure it keeps your camera safe. The print is separated into these parts: 1. The screen connects to this mount point in the same way that it connects to the Luna gimbal body. To disconnect the screen, simply use the same red side buttons that you would normally use to detach the screen from the Luna gimbal body. This is the recommended mounting option for keeping the camera secure while also enabling you to easily detach the Luna from the rig. You can insert the Luna body directly into the slot at the end of the Gimbal Mount Arm then use (2) velcro straps (pictured as red straps in the product renderings) through the holes and around the Luna body to provide 2 layers of support to keep the Luna in place. You can optionally use a combination of options (a) & (b) to provide added stability for action heavy shots by mounting the Luna on the threaded handle with camera screw through bottom and also attaching the (2) velcro straps around the Luna body. 3. description: Active Spring-Damped Isolation Rig A Mechanical Z-Axis Stabilization Platform for Insta360 The Active Spring-Damped Isolation Rig is a compact, scientifically designed mechanical stabilization system developed specifically around the Insta360 Luna Ultra . It reduces vertical impacts, vibration, and sudden motion before those disturbances reach the camera’s gimbal and imaging system. Unlike rigid mounts, which transfer nearly all movement directly into the camera, this design places the Luna Ultra on a suspended carriage supported by an adjustable spring and oil-damped shock absorber. The mechanical suspension manages larger physical disturbances, while the Luna Ultra’s internal gimbal and electronic stabilization correct the remaining fine motion. The rig is designed primarily around the Luna Ultra’s geometry, controls, gimbal clearance, and remote-operation capabilities. Its modular mounting interface can also be adapted for other compatible Insta360 cameras. Design Objective The project was developed to create a practical, 3D-printable Z-axis isolation system that could be used across multiple filming environments without restricting the operation of the Luna Ultra. The main design requirements were: Reduce vertically transmitted shock and vibration Preserve unrestricted gimbal movement Maintain access to controls, ports, screen, microphones, and cooling areas Support handheld, tripod, bicycle, pole, suction-cup, and vehicle-mounted use Use readily available hardware Remain easy to print, assemble, maintain, and customise Avoid specialised machining The result is a lightweight mechanical isolation platform that works with the Luna Ultra rather than replacing its existing stabilization system. How the System Works? The Luna Ultra is mounted on a vertically suspended carriage rather than being rigidly connected to the lower mounting structure. The carriage is guided by a bearing-supported linkage and controlled by an adjustable spring and hydraulic oil damper. When the lower mount experiences a vertical disturbance, such as a footstep, road impact, bicycle vibration, or sudden vehicle movement, the lower structure moves first. The suspended camera carriage is allowed to move relative to the frame, reducing the acceleration transmitted directly to the camera. The suspension behaves approximately as a spring–mass–damper system: where: m is the suspended mass of the Luna Ultra and camera carriage k is the effective spring stiffness c is the hydraulic damping coefficient F(t) is the disturbance entering through the handle or mount x is the relative displacement of the suspended carriage The coil spring supports the camera mass and absorbs impact energy during compression. The oil damper controls the velocity of the motion and dissipates energy during compression and rebound. This prevents the repeated bouncing commonly associated with spring-only stabilizers. The mechanical suspension therefore removes a portion of the larger vertical disturbance before it reaches the Luna Ultra. The camera’s gimbal and electronic stabilization then correct the lower-amplitude residual motion. Testing & Validation A preliminary performance assessment was conducted using the Insta360 Luna Ultra payload, approximately 233–235 g, together with the adjustable piggyback oil-damped suspension used in the design. The assessment compares the expected vibration transmitted through a conventional rigid mount with the Active Spring-Damped Isolation Rig during walking, running, cycling, vehicle mounting, and rough-terrain use. The values below are simulated engineering estimates intended to represent realistic prototype performance rather than instrumented physical test results. The suspension was tuned to keep the camera near the centre of its available travel, preserving compression and rebound capacity while reducing vertical shock transmission. The bearing-guided linkage and hydraulic damping provide the greatest improvement during higher-frequency vibration, such as gravel cycling and vehicle use, while still reducing the repetitive vertical motion associated with walking and running. The design also maintains clearance around the Luna Ultra’s gimbal, ports, controls, detachable display, and camera body throughout the simulated motion range. * Future physical validation should compare the rig against a rigid mount using accelerometers, suspension-displacement tracking, high-speed video, and frame-by-frame footage analysis. Testing should also verify fastener retention, bearing wear, structural fatigue, gimbal clearance, and material performance. The current prototype uses PLA with TPU grip components, while PETG or ABS is recommended for functional real-world testing and repeated dynamic use. Test Scenario Rigid Mount RMS Acceleration Active Isolation Rig Estimated Improvement Walking 0.42g 0.27g 36% Running 0.91g 0.54g 41% Ashpalt biking 0.68g 0.29g 57% Gravel Biking 1.18g 0.43g 64% Vehicle Mount 0.82g 0.27g 67% Rough Terrain 1.46g 0.42g 71% Suspension System The central suspension component is an adjustable piggyback oil shock absorber paired with a coil spring. The shock absorber provides three primary functions: Supporting the suspended camera mass Controlling compression under impact Controlling rebound as the carriage returns to its neutral position The threaded adjustment collar allows the spring preload to be changed according to the installed camera mass and the desired suspension response. A softer setup can improve sensitivity to walking and smaller vibrations, while a firmer setup may be more appropriate for bicycle, off-road, or vehicle-mounted use. The suspension should be adjusted so the Luna Ultra carriage rests near the middle of its available travel. This provides sufficient movement in both compression and rebound and reduces the risk of bottoming out or reaching full extension. The shock absorber is connected to the printed suspension structure using two M2 × 16 mm screws , one at each mounting point. Hybrid Manufacturing Approach The rig employs a hybrid manufacturing approach , combining custom 3D-printed structural components with commercially available precision mechanical hardware. Rather than attempting to manufacture every component through additive manufacturing, each element is produced using the process best suited to its mechanical function. The primary structural components, including the main frame, suspension carriage, linkage arms, camera interface, bearing housings, and universal mounting platform, are 3D printed. Precision motion and high-load interfaces are achieved using commercially available metal hardware, including an adjustable oil-damped shock absorber, sealed ball bearings, steel fasteners, and standard mechanical hardware. This combination provides the flexibility of additive manufacturing while maintaining the durability, precision, and reliability of conventional mechanical components. For the prototype presented in this project, the majority of the structural components are printed in PLA , while the handle grip and contact surfaces are printed in TPU to improve ergonomics, provide a more secure grip, and reduce high-frequency vibrations transmitted to the user. For long-term functional use, however, PETG, ABS, or ASA are strongly recommended for the structural components due to their superior impact resistance, fatigue performance, temperature stability, and outdoor durability. These materials are better suited for repeated dynamic loading and demanding environments such as automotive, cycling, and outdoor filming. TPU should continue to be used for the grip sections where flexibility, comfort, and vibration damping are beneficial. This hybrid approach offers several engineering advantages: Lightweight yet rigid printed structure Precision, low-friction motion through sealed ball bearings Proven hydraulic damping using an adjustable oil-filled shock absorber Readily available off-the-shelf hardware Easy maintenance and replacement of wear components Modular construction for future upgrades and customization Compared with a fully printed mechanism, this approach significantly improves durability, dimensional accuracy, wear resistance, and long-term reliability at the moving joints. At the same time, it preserves the affordability, accessibility, and rapid iteration made possible by desktop 3D printing, resulting in a practical, serviceable, and high-performance stabilization platform. Attribution: I was inspired by this model to make this design - Action Camera Anti-Vibration Arm Dual Camera Mounting Options As shown in Figure below , the rig supports two interchangeable camera mounting options that attach to the suspension assembly using the same pair of mounting screws, allowing the interface to be swapped without modifying the rest of the mechanism. The left mount is a standard ¼″-20 UNC threaded interface , where the camera is secured using a ¼″ × ½″ hex-head screw. This option provides broad compatibility with cameras and accessories that use the industry-standard tripod thread, making it well suited for general handheld filming, vlogging, and everyday operation. The right mount is a dedicated slide-lock mounting interface that engages directly with the Luna Ultra camera cover. Once inserted, the camera is mechanically retained within the mount, providing a significantly more secure connection than a threaded attachment alone. This configuration is recommended for high-dynamic applications such as running, mountain biking, vehicle mounting, and other environments with sustained vibration or repeated impacts, where it virtually eliminates the possibility of the camera loosening or separating from the rig during operation. Assembly Instructions (All hardware used is listed in BOM) Step1: Press-fit the bearings into their designated pockets on both side mounting brackets. Ensure each bearing is fully seated and rotates freely without excessive force or deformation of the printed part. Use superglue and mallet if required. Step2: Insert the ¼″-20 UNC × ½″ hex-head screw into the hand grip and secure it in its dedicated recess. Verify that the screw is properly aligned and firmly retained before continuing. Step3: Heat-press four M3 × 4 mm threaded inserts into the screw cover plate using a soldering iron or heat-set insert tool. Ensure all inserts sit flush with the surface and remain perpendicular to the mounting face. Step4: Position the cover plate over the handle assembly and fasten it using four M3 × 8 mm socket head screws . Tighten each screw evenly in a cross pattern to obtain uniform clamping without overtightening. Step5: Assemble the left and right suspension beams onto the common center mount using the M4 pivot hardware . Confirm that both beams rotate smoothly with minimal play while maintaining free movement through the installed bearings. Step6: Mount the piggyback spring-damper between the upper and lower mounting points using two M2 × 16 mm screws and nuts . Verify that the shock articulates freely throughout the suspension travel without binding or interference. Step7: Repeat the bearing installation procedure for the camera-side mounting bracket, then install the selected camera mounting interface (threaded or slide-lock) using the appropriate ¼″-20 UNC screw . Ensure the mount pivots freely while remaining securely fastened. Step8: Apply a thin, even layer of cyanoacrylate (super glue) to the mating surfaces and bond the TPU grip to the handle. And the TPU pad to the surface shown here. Maintain uniform pressure until the adhesive has fully cured before placing the rig into service. Some More Pics……. 😊😊😊 VOILÀ! Fully printed system to make plaster moulds. This produces a 3-part mould (2 sides and a small insert for the base) to cast round tumblers/mugs with a smooth sided design. You need to cast plaster in the larger mould two times for the sides, for every one cast of the small insert. This gives a complete plaster mould. This print has been scaled to 112% to account for clay shrinkage, with most casting slips this should give a final tumbler size of 9cm diameter and 9.5cm height, or a capacity of around 400ml. With any fully 3D printed mould, you’ll benefit from using a release agent on the base plate surface. I use a generic mouldmaker’s soap, but any product designed for plaster release should be fine. It needs around 1350ml of plaster for the side pieces and around 180ml for the base insert, and you can calculate the weight of water and plaster needed with this tool: Plaster Calculator You can get a much better cast surface, even if your plaster mix is full of air bubbles, by using a paintbrush to dislodge any trapped air from the surface. I would suggest that you pour plaster until the ornament surface is covered but it isn’t completely full, then get a relatively small paintbrush and move it around in the plaster so that you’re brushing all of the details on the base plate surface. This will dislodge air bubbles, and once dislodged they’ll float upwards. Once you’ve finished this, pour in the rest of the plaster. If you manage to avoid adding more air as you do it (just brush gently), you’ll eventually remove all the bubbles from the surface and get a perfect cast.

It was designed to be the heaviest fully enclosed armoured fighting vehicle ever built, weighing about 188 tonnes. The tank had extremely thick armour and was armed with a powerful 128 mm main gun paired with a 75 mm secondary gun. Although its protection and firepower were impressive, the Maus was very slow, difficult to transport, and required enormous amounts of fuel, making it impractical for battlefield use. Only two Maus prototypes were built before the war ended, and neither saw combat. The project was cancelled because Germany faced shortages of resources and changing military priorities. description: Fully printed system to make plaster moulds. This produces a 3-part mould (2 sides and a small insert for the base) to cast round tumblers/mugs with a design based on the future MP for Clacton. You need to cast plaster in the larger mould two times for the sides, for every one cast of the small insert. This gives a complete plaster mould. This print has been scaled to 112% to account for clay shrinkage, with most casting slips this should give a final tumbler size of 9cm diameter and 9.5cm height, or a capacity of around 400ml. With any fully 3D printed mould, you’ll benefit from using a release agent on the base plate surface. I use a generic mouldmaker’s soap, but any product designed for plaster release should be fine. It needs around 1350ml of plaster for the side pieces and around 180ml for the base insert, and you can calculate the weight of water and plaster needed with this tool: Plaster Calculator You can get a much better cast surface, even if your plaster mix is full of air bubbles, by using a paintbrush to dislodge any trapped air from the surface. I would suggest that you pour plaster until the ornament surface is covered but it isn’t completely full, then get a relatively small paintbrush and move it around in the plaster so that you’re brushing all of the details on the base plate surface. This will dislodge air bubbles, and once dislodged they’ll float upwards. Once you’ve finished this, pour in the rest of the plaster. If you manage to avoid adding more air as you do it (just brush gently), you’ll eventually remove all the bubbles from the surface and get a perfect cast. VOTE BINFACE!

Fully printed system to make plaster moulds. This produces a 3-part mould (2 sides and a small insert for the base) to cast round tumblers/mugs with a Twist design. You need to cast plaster in the larger mould two times for the sides, for every one cast of the small insert. This gives a complete plaster mould. This print has been scaled to 112% to account for clay shrinkage, with most casting slips this should give a final tumbler size of 9cm diameter and 9.5cm height, or a capacity of around 400ml. With any fully 3D printed mould, you’ll benefit from using a release agent on the base plate surface. I use a generic mouldmaker’s soap, but any product designed for plaster release should be fine. It needs around 1350ml of plaster for the side pieces and around 180ml for the base insert, and you can calculate the weight of water and plaster needed with this tool: Plaster Calculator You can get a much better cast surface, even if your plaster mix is full of air bubbles, by using a paintbrush to dislodge any trapped air from the surface. I would suggest that you pour plaster until the ornament surface is covered but it isn’t completely full, then get a relatively small paintbrush and move it around in the plaster so that you’re brushing all of the details on the base plate surface. This will dislodge air bubbles, and once dislodged they’ll float upwards. Once you’ve finished this, pour in the rest of the plaster. If you manage to avoid adding more air as you do it (just brush gently), you’ll eventually remove all the bubbles from the surface and get a perfect cast.

description: Update: Added a reinforcement on Level C to allow an for intermediate tension on the 40m element. I've been using flavors of this design for about 6 months and have been very happy with its performance. The SWR on 40, 30, 20, 17, 15 and 12m are between 1.02 and 1.9 across the band. 10m tunes under 2.0 for a portion of the band. V4 of the antenna incorporates a number of changes (V3 not released on MakerWorld): Plates B, C, D and E were reinforced to address creep over time due to tension A new style guy rope attachment was added that is circular and has a small rotating ring (it won't hit wires like the original) Holes for filament ("Bird Defender") were removed because they weren't really working NOTE: If printed in PETG, this design will warp within weeks under high temperature. This is the first version I have printed in ASA. I like building antennas. This is an ongoing project and there have been 3 major version, with V1, V2 and now V4 uploaded to MakerWorld. It makes use of a 12m Spider Pole. There may be more changes to come based on how it works since I post the designs as I implement them. If you want a “sure-thing” and support - I'd recommend a DX Commander. V2 seems to have addressed the deformation of the base, so far. However, over time the upper plates that had tension on them started to deform (B, C, D and E). This release addresses that. It also adds a new style of guy rope connector. The plate style had extensions that can hit the driven elements. It is still in the file, but a 3 piece rotating collar has been added. The hub is in two parts. The collar should be placed on the lower hub (thicker base) and glue applied to the groves on the inside diameter, then insert the upper hub (with "fingers"). The base is designed to use ¼" by 1" stainless steel bolts. You'll also need washers, lock washers and nuts (11) ¼" x 1" stainless bolts (11) ¼" stainless lock washers (22) ¼" stainless washers (11) ¼" stainless wing nuts This uses a 12m Heavy Duty Spider Pole with the top two sections removed. You will need the “stay up” kit. You will also need stainless/marine grade ¼" ring terminals for wiring the driven elements, driven element linking, base ground element linking and radials. (See photo for wiring.) A panel mount SO-239 is used. Note: when wiring it, have the wire make a complete loop (feed the driven elements in both directions). When installing the plates, they can be above or below the “stay-up” clamps. (I found slight tolerance differences in fit on my Spider Poles.) If the plate fits snuggly against the lower section, place the stay-up clamp above it. If it fits loose, place the stay-up clamp below it, and you can put electrical tape on the inside collar of the plate, if needed, for a tighter fit. The Spider Pole mounts on a pipe in the ground. For guy ropes, Kevlar line is recommended. The lines don't need to be tight, they are just there to provide support in the wind. To hold tension on the driven elements, marine-grade shock cord is recommended. For tuning, start with 40 meters. Disconnect the driven elements for all other bands while leaving them installed. Once 40m is tune, go higher in frequency band by band. NOTE: I initially couldn't get 10m to tune. The issue is that with harmonics/parasitic coupling interactions its hard to tell which low is for the 10m element and which is just a harmonic. With all other elements tuned, disconnect the 10m element and use your NanoVNA to do a sweep from 1 MHz to 30 MHz using NanoVNASaver. Save that sweep as a reference. Connect the 10m element and do another sweep. The new now it identifies is the one you would use for tuning 10m. (The 10m element only covers a section of the 10m band due to it's large size.) The putter head is designed to incorporate removable weights, allowing the player to change the balance of the putter to their liking. These removable weights also increase the mass and MOI of the putter head, providing for a much more forgiving and comfortable feel. One of the key features of this design is its modular construction. The shaft insert is a separate component that bolts into the main putter head, allowing different putter head designs to be swapped without needing to remove or reinstall the shaft. Simply remove a few screws, install a new head, and you're ready to go. The shaft insert has a lie angle of 74 degrees and a static loft angle of 3 degrees to match the feel of many center-shafted putters. The design of the head of the putter has been carefully made to ensure that the center of mass is aligned with the center of the face. Therefore, the design of this putter naturally eliminates the majority of the torque that can open or close the face while putting. This can make it significantly easier to keep the face square at impact. To improve feel, the striking face is printed from TPU, providing a soft but responsive impact that closely resembles the insert faces found on many premium putters. Including the printed parts, added weights, screws, and epoxy, the total mass of the head of the putter is right around 350g. The order in which some of these steps are taken is very important! Print all required components in your favorite colors. Be sure to print each component in its recommended material. Support removal. This step can be rather difficult due to the way the model must be printed, so my recommendation is to work from the outside inwards. I've used normal supports for the flat-bottomed sections to allow for each of the gaps for the weights to be cleared in a singular piece. Press the TPU face into the putter body. Secure it by using super glue or epoxy. Install the weights. All weights should sit flat within the head of the putter when installed correctly. A total of 30 individual 0.25oz weights are to be inserted, with 4 stacked near the face and 2 stacked in all other locations. While removing the film on the weights (making them stick) is recommended, it is not required for the putter to work great. Doing so may reduce noises heard when making contact with the ball slightly but will make it more difficult to remove the weights if interchanging putter heads. Prior to installing the bottom plate, it can be helpful to lay a layer of tape over the bottom plate and cut to size. This will reduce some noise made when putting. Install the bottom plate to the putter head at the 5 holes around the perimeter. Ensure that the side which features cutouts matching the position of the weights is facing the inserted weights. Use 5x M3 x 3/8" wood screws (link provided below for the ones used). Screws should only be hand tight, and do not over-tighten them! Cut down the putter shaft to your desired length (I cut mine down to 36in for my height). For a great step-by-step process to complete this, check out this YouTube video: How to Shorten a Putter with a Steel Shaft . Install the grip to your putter shaft. I recommend completing this step before installing the shaft adapter and putter head as there is less time to work and straighten out the grip in comparison. For a great guide to doing this, check out this other YouTube tutorial: How to Install a Putter Grip (jump to 3:00 in the video). Bolt the shaft adapter/insert into the putter head after sliding the shaft adapter into place from the top. Using 3x M3 x 3/8" wood screws, secure the bottom plate, main body, and adapter together through the bottom in the three central holes. Then, complete the installation by using one more screw in the hole near the top of the putter towards the back. Screws should only be hand tight, and do not over-tighten them! Epoxy the shaft into the adapter by applying epoxy to the shaft and sliding it in from the top. The epoxy which is suggested has a long working time which allows you to rotate the putter shaft so the the grip precisely lines up with its correct orientation. My recommendation for alignment of the grip is as follows: look down the shaft and line up the flat part of the grip with the line on top of the putter which is parallel to the direction of your stroke. Once aligned properly, wipe away any excess epoxy from the top of the putter. Let the putter sit overnight so that the epoxy can fully cure. Next step, rolling putts! Shaft: 0.370in Tip Diameter Straight Stepless Putter Shaft ( Amazon Link ) - $29.95 Grip: Any putter grip should do, but the one seen in all images here is a SuperStroke Zenergy Tour 3.0 ( Amazon Link ) - $34.39 Weights: Important to uses these weights due to their exact size and 1/4oz weight ( Amazon Link ) - $6.99 Screws: M3 x 3/8" Wood Screws ( Amazon Link ) - $6.79 Required Tools/Adhesives: Links are provided in case you may need to get these. If you don't already have some of these, they are also great to have in general for a variety of projects. Epoxy: Simple JB Weld 2-Part Epoxy ( Amazon Link ) - $5.93 Steel Tube Cutter: I used a copper pipe cutter (although it worked, not recommended), but using a proper steel pipe cutter is advised if possible ( Amazon Link ) - $13.99 Total (For Required Components and Printed Parts): ~$80 USD Future Plans This modular platform was designed with expansion in mind. I plan to release additional interchangeable putter head designs that will all use the same shaft adapter, allowing you to experiment with different shapes and weight distributions without building an entirely new putter. If you build one, I'd love to see your make! Feel free to leave feedback or suggestions for future head designs. Happy printing, and good luck on the greens!

description: The Jagdpanzer IV was a German tank destroyer used during World War II. It entered service in 1944 and was built on the chassis of the Panzer IV tank. Instead of having a rotating turret, it had a fixed, low-profile armoured structure with a powerful gun mounted at the front. This design made it harder for enemy tanks to spot and hit, while also giving it strong firepower against Allied armour. The Jagdpanzer IV was used on both the Eastern and Western Fronts, where it was effective in defensive battles and ambushes. Its sloped armour provided good protection, but the lack of a rotating turret meant the entire vehicle had to turn to aim at targets outside its limited firing arc. Although it was a capable tank destroyer, Germany produced it in smaller numbers than some other armoured vehicles, and it could not change the outcome of the war. description: I have created a “simple” Lockable Fly Rod storage/travel box. I made this in response to finding other similar boxes not being big enough for my 7 weight bass rods. These boxes fit my 2, 4, 5, and 7 weight rods with room to spare. Within the main housing itself you can buy foam to cut out an impression of your reel(s) to make the fit more secure. I have not done that yet myself, but, will be doing so soon! The main housing and cap are made to take in a 2 inch PVC pipe; the fit is very snug . There is no need for adhesive because of this, but, as you see in the pictures, I put some electrical tape arounf the cap just for ease of mind. I would highly suggest to lightly tap the cap on with a rubber mallet or similar. The main housing can be a bit of a pain to get on there but you can wiggle it on there with some forceful finesse. For the latch; I used a 10mm bolt x 130mm in length. With a matching nut and a lock washer. This does not need to be super tight. The locking side can be used with whatever you deem fit. I used a few extra mater locks since I had some extras laying around. The PVC pipe; it will fit a 2 inch PVC pipe. Any length you desire. In the pictures I have a 4.5 foot, 2 inch PVC pipe. I did 4.5 feet so i could break my rods down in half and they would easily fit in my truck bed. But, if you have a bigger bed than I do, you could get a 6 foot long PVC, etc.. This profile seems to be just fine for simple protection. If you'd like it to be “stronger” add more wall loops/infill as you deem fit. Thank you!

Se incluye un codigo simple de prueba hecho en arduino. #include // Pines para TB6612FNG const int PWMA = 8; // Motor Derecho const int AIN2 = 7; const int AIN1 = 6; const int STBY = 5; // Pin de Standby (Obligatorio en HIGH) const int BIN1 = 4; // Motor Izquierdo const int BIN2 = 3; const int PWMB = 2; const int botonInicio = 12; const int pinIR = 11; QTRSensors qtr; const uint8_t sensorCount = 8; uint16_t sensorValues[sensorCount]; // Variables de Control bool enCarrera = false; int lastError = 0; // --- AJUSTES DE CONTROL --- float Kp = 0.35; float Kd = 2.5; int velocidadBase = 100; // -------------------------- void setup() { pinMode(botonInicio, INPUT_PULLUP); pinMode(pinIR, OUTPUT); digitalWrite(pinIR, HIGH); // Encender emisores QTR // Configuración de pines del TB6612 pinMode(PWMA, OUTPUT); pinMode(AIN1, OUTPUT); pinMode(AIN2, OUTPUT); pinMode(PWMB, OUTPUT); pinMode(BIN1, OUTPUT); pinMode(BIN2, OUTPUT); pinMode(STBY, OUTPUT); digitalWrite(STBY, HIGH); // Activar el driver pinMode(13, OUTPUT); qtr.setTypeAnalog(); qtr.setSensorPins((const uint8_t[]){A0, A1, A2, A3, A4, A5, A6, A7}, sensorCount); // Calibración digitalWrite(13, HIGH); for (uint16_t i = 0; i < 400; i++) { qtr.calibrate(); } digitalWrite(13, LOW); } void loop() { if (!enCarrera && digitalRead(botonInicio) == LOW) { for(int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { digitalWrite(13, HIGH); delay(500); digitalWrite(13, LOW); delay(500); } enCarrera = true; } if (enCarrera) { seguirLinea(); if (digitalRead(botonInicio) == LOW) { enCarrera = false; detenerMotores(); delay(500); } } else { detenerMotores(); } } void seguirLinea() { uint16_t position = qtr.readLineBlack(sensorValues); int error = position - 3500; int ajuste = (Kp * error) + (Kd * (error - lastError)); lastError = error; int velIzq = velocidadBase + ajuste; int velDer = velocidadBase - ajuste; mover(velIzq, velDer); } void mover(int vI, int vD) { // MOTOR IZQUIERDO (B) if (vI >= 0) { digitalWrite(BIN1, HIGH); digitalWrite(BIN2, LOW); analogWrite(PWMB, constrain(vI, 0, 255)); } else { digitalWrite(BIN1, LOW); digitalWrite(BIN2, HIGH); analogWrite(PWMB, constrain(abs(vI), 0, 255)); } // MOTOR DERECHO (A) if (vD >= 0) { digitalWrite(AIN1, HIGH); digitalWrite(AIN2, LOW); analogWrite(PWMA, constrain(vD, 0, 255)); } else { digitalWrite(AIN1, LOW); digitalWrite(AIN2, HIGH); analogWrite(PWMA, constrain(abs(vD), 0, 255)); } } void detenerMotores() { analogWrite(PWMA, 0); analogWrite(PWMB, 0); // Opcional: poner AIN/BIN en LOW para freno pasivo digitalWrite(AIN1, LOW); digitalWrite(AIN2, LOW); digitalWrite(BIN1, LOW); digitalWrite(BIN2, LOW); }
