晨昏线与南极圈相切，南极圈内极昼，北极圈内极夜。 6.3 春分、秋分无极昼极夜 公转至春分或秋分刻度，太阳直射赤道，晨昏线过两极，全球昼夜等长，无极昼极夜。 6.4 极昼极夜范围渐变演示 缓慢连续转动公转主臂，观察极昼/极夜范围从极点逐步扩大至极圈，再逐步缩小的动态过程，完整还原全年变化。 7. 月相、日食、月食完整演示（结合黄白交角） 7.1 月相周期演示 开启光源，手动转动 月球公转轴 ，月球沿白道面公转。观察月球被照亮部分的形状变化： 新月（朔）→娥眉月→上弦月→盈凸月→满月（望）→亏凸月→下弦月→残月→新月。 （因潮汐锁定，月球同一面始终朝向地球，但被照亮区域随公转位置变化。） 7.2 日食演示（朔日限定） 将月球转至 日—地之间（朔点） ，并微调月球公转角度以抵消黄白交角偏差，使日、月、地三者近似共线。此时月球影子落在地球上，可演示日全食/日偏食效果。 解释 ：因黄白交角存在，多数朔日不共线，故日食罕见。 7.3 月食演示（望日限定） 将月球转至 日—地延长线（望点） ，微调角度使日、地、月共线，地球阴影覆盖月球，演示月食。同理，并非每望日都发生。 8. 标准操作注意事项 四轴结构精密，转动需轻柔匀速，禁止暴力操作。 常规演示中地轴岁差旋进轴应保持锁定 ，仅当演示岁差或初始校准时方可调节。 演示晨昏线、极昼极夜、日月食时，建议在暗光环境下进行。 可根据需要自主适配光源亮度与供电方式。 设备为精密模型，禁止摔落、撞击、浸泡；儿童操作需成人陪同。 禁止私自拆卸轴体，以免四轴联动精度失效。 9. 常见故障与原理答疑 Q1：为什么月球不会自转？是否为缺陷？ A：不是缺陷。真实月球为潮汐锁定，自转与公转周期相同，永远同一面朝地。本设备科学还原该特性。 Q2：为什么演示四季时不需要转动地轴岁差旋进旋钮？ A：真实地球公转中，地轴在空间中的指向保持恒定（指向北极星附近）。四季更替完全由公转位置改变太阳直射点而产生。若在公转中手动旋转地轴，将得到错误原理。本设备的地轴岁差旋进轴仅用于初始校准或演示岁差。 Q3：为什么太阳模型比地球小？ A：这是为了桌面教学的可行性而进行的工程缩放。真实比例无法在桌面模型中实现，本设备牺牲尺寸比例但保留了所有角度、光照几何和相对运动关系，不影响任何天文现象的教学。 Q4：黄白交角5°09′是如何实现的？月球没有自转轴会影响吗？ A：黄白交角是月球公转轨道面（白道面）与地球公转轨道面（黄道面）的夹角，通过倾斜的月球公转副臂机械实现，与月球是否自转无关。本设备正确保留该夹角，用于演示日月食发生条件。 Q5：为什么无法每次朔望日都演示日月食？ A：设备精准还原了5°09′黄白交角，多数朔望日三者不共线，与现实一致，非故障。 Q6：极昼极夜、晨昏线演示效果不明显怎么办？ A：检查公转位置是否准确对应节气刻度，并确认地轴指向已锁定且倾角无误（未误触岁差旋钮）。重新按第4章归位即可。 Q7：晨昏线为什么不会和经线完全重合？ A：仅春分、秋分两天太阳直射赤道，晨昏线与经线重合；其余时间因地轴倾角，晨昏线与经线存在夹角，本设备可完整呈现该变化。

Kinetic Galton Board A kinetic Galton board that demonstrates the Maxwell–Boltzmann speed distribution instead of the usual Gaussian you get from a classic bead-and-peg Galton board. It went semi-viral on Instagram (4M+ views), so I'm publishing the files here for anyone who wants to build one. Watch it run: https://www.instagram.com/p/DZauWk2SiXA/ How it works There are two chambers, left and right. The left chamber holds about 400 balls resting on a slider above a fast-spinning cylinder fitted with two fins. The fins agitate the balls and inject energy into the system. The balls collide with each other and with the chamber walls, behaving like gas particles in a box. At the top-right corner of the left chamber there is a small hole, roughly one ball wide. A ball only escapes (effuses) through this hole when it arrives with the right velocity. On the right side there are about 14 bins. The bin dividers are slightly shorter than the height of the escape hole, so a ball that effuses has to fall a small distance before reaching the tops of the bins. The physics is the interesting part: Because the hole is about the size of a single ball, a ball leaving it has essentially no vertical velocity at the moment of escape. So the time it takes to fall the small gap to the bins is the same for every ball . With d = v·t and t constant, the horizontal distance a ball travels (and therefore the bin it lands in) is proportional to its speed at the moment of effusion . Read the bin, and you've effectively measured how fast that ball was moving when it escaped. Do this for all ~400 balls, which have been colliding and exchanging energy like gas molecules, and the bins fill in to trace out the signature Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution . Printing There are two versions depending on what motor you have. Version for CIM (FRC) I built mine around an FRC CIM motor , just because I had some lying around. They're big and frankly overkill for this, but a lot of FRC people have them on hand. If that's you, open the Version for CIM folder and print the STL files there. Version for 775 For everyone else, the most common suitable motor is a 775 . They're cheap and easy to get almost anywhere. Open the Version for 775 folder and print the parts there. Both folders also include the raw STEP files if you want to modify anything. Cover The cover on mine is laser-cut acrylic . If you don't have a laser cutter, there's an STL so you can print it instead out of a transparent material, it just won't be as clear as acrylic. If you want to chase clarity, look up guides on printing crystal-clear PETG, though I didn't have much luck with it myself. Balls You need about 400–600 balls . They are 4 mm diameter , so do not substitute airsoft BBs, those don't work. To save you from duplicating a ball 400 times in your slicer, there's a 20×20 grid of them included. A few notes: Add a brim when printing the grid, otherwise the balls pop off the build plate. The sliced result should look like this: After printing you'll have a sheet with all the balls attached to it. Don't try to pull them off by hand , you'll tear the sheet and it becomes a miserable job getting the sheet off the balls. Instead, use pliers and twist each ball off the sheet. It's tedious, but it works. 400 balls took me about 20 minutes. Assembly and operation You will need 1x 775 motor, 2x M4x8 bolts, 4x M3x8 bolts Assembly is straightforward Place the balls into the device. Insert the slider. Shake the balls into the left chamber. Important: Use the slider to drop the balls onto the agitator while it is already spinning . If the balls surround a stationary agitator and you try to spin it up, it will stall the motor and the whole thing jams. That's it, spin it up and watch the distribution build.

model_name: SMARS rover remake for use with ESP32-WROVER-CAM
description: I've printed the SMARS tracked rover to see if I can adapt to use an ESP32-WROVER-CAM Dev.B microcontroller which has a built-in 2Mpx camera so I can turn it into a tracked mobile, WiFi controlled webcam. Although the ESP32-WROVER-CAM has enough GPIOs to use with the L298N dual motor driver, when the webcam is turned on in the sketch along with the WiFi, there are only 4 usable GPIOs remaining. Luckily, I found that it should be possible to use just the 4 GPIOs to control the two motors, but it also requires that the L298N EN-A and EN-B pins be raised to +5V. If you discarded the two jumpers that usually come with the L298N, then use two DuPont wires to connect the two enable pins on the driver to +5V. The print profile available for the BambuLab A1 Mini worked perfectly although I cannot use the IR sensor mount since the chassis is fully occupied by the L298N and the 2S1P 18650 pack with switch and voltmeter, but more importantly, there are no more GPIOs left to use the IR sensor. As you can see from the photo I took of the result is not very good looking but it does move quite nicely. I have two 100rpm DC motors which give it a decent scurry speed. The code I can share upon request if anyone wants to give it a go. Ping me and I can share the sketch and describe the wiring since it took a bit of experimenting to get the ESP32 to eventually be able to control the two motors as desired.

Meet one of the largest and most impressive predators to live before the dinosaurs. Inostrancevia alexandri was a huge carnivorous gorgonopsid that lived in what is now northern European Russia during the Late Permian, shortly before the greatest mass extinction in Earth’s history. With its long skull, powerful jaws and enormous sabre-like canine teeth, it was one of the dominant predators of its ecosystem. Although it is sometimes described as a “mammal-like reptile”, Inostrancevia was actually a non-mammalian synapsid . This means it belonged to the evolutionary branch that later produced mammals and was more closely related to mammals than it was to dinosaurs, crocodiles or lizards. The printed skull measures approximately 250 mm long . Adult Inostrancevia alexandri skulls are generally reconstructed at around 500–510 mm long , making this model approximately half-scale . A full-sized skull would therefore be roughly twice the length of this print, while the complete animal may have measured around 3 metres from nose to tail . How is it related to other gorgonopsids? Gorgonopsids were a diverse group of sabre-toothed predatory therapsids rather than a single type of animal. They ranged from relatively small hunters to enormous apex predators such as Inostrancevia and Rubidgea . Inostrancevia belonged to the inostranceviine branch of the gorgonopsid family tree and was part of a group containing several primarily Russian genera, including Pravoslavlevia , Sauroctonus and Suchogorgon . Its closest relatives were other species of Inostrancevia , with Pravoslavlevia generally regarded as one of its nearest related genera. The similarly massive South African Rubidgea was still a gorgonopsid cousin, but it belonged to the separate rubidgeine branch . They filled similar apex-predator roles, but were not simply different species of the same animal. This model makes an imposing addition to any collection of Permian animals, prehistoric predators, fossil replicas or unusual skulls. The Basics: This print is a Ranque-Hilsch Vortex Tube (RHVT) cooler or Maxwell Demon's tube, a remarkably simple device that mysteriously separates compressed air into hot and cold streams without any moving parts or electricity. The physics of this phenomena have been a long-running subject of scientific investigation and remain unsettled to this day. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vortex_tube Default Print Setup: 0.2mm nozzle preferred for flow dynamics and accurate threads All tolerances are setup for Bambu Labs PETG Basic The Minutia: The design being shared is modular to allow interchanging of internal components for optimal nozzle, vortex and tube diameter geometries. Various vortex generator nozzles and hot pipe divergers with part numbers are included for the user to experiment with. Recommended starting configuration is: Vortex Generator: RF1006-00D-0909 Hot Tube Diverger: RF10-15D Hot Tube Throttle Valve: Close fully and unscrew ~ 3.5x turns Once assembled per the diagram below, simply inject compressed air via the ¼" NPT inlet and appreciate the almost instantaneous separation of hot and cold air from the ends of the device. Feel free to experiment with the included generators, divergers and throttle valve settings to optimise cold vs. hot air fraction for a given inlet air pressure. Notes: Vortex Generators and Hot Tube Divergers are denoted with LF and RF to indicate “low flow” and “regular flow” and are intended to be paired together. RHVT's are capable of generating extremely hot and cold temperatures (-50 ° C to 200 ° C) far beyond the capability of regularly used materials so brittle and melting failures are quite possible depending on how you configure the device and the duration of use. Due to the many factors affecting print strength, it is left to the end user to assess what air pressure can be safely used without compromising the device. I have routinely used pressures up to 60psi on PETG Basic without any failure.

description: 這是我自己設計的一款 彩虹套圈圈疊疊樂 ！在設計上，我特別採用了「錐形中心柱」 搭配 「不同外徑與內徑」的套圈，讓這個簡單的玩具有了更聰明的玩法與教育意義。 💡 我的設計理念與玩法特點： 防呆排序設計，建立順序概念 ： 因為中心柱是錐形的，圈圈如果放錯順序，就「完全放不到底」。這個直覺的物理限制，能讓孩子在動手過程中，自己發現問題並建立「由大到小」的順序與空間邏輯概念。 訓練大、小肌肉發展 ： 孩子在抓取圈圈、並精準對準中心柱套下去的過程中，能很好地鍛鍊手臂的大肌肉動作，以及手指抓握與精細操作的小肌肉發展。 顏色與大小順序的視覺鏈結 ： 透過繽紛的色彩對比，孩子可以在視覺上觀察不同的顏色，將「顏色」與「圈圈的大小順序」產生記憶鏈結，一邊玩一邊刺激大腦發展。 🛠️ 打印建議： 為了讓小朋友玩得更安全，建議在打印完成後，稍微檢查並打磨邊緣，確保表面光滑無毛刺。 [English Description] This is a Rainbow Stacking Rings Toy of my own design! I specially engineered the "tapered center post" to work with "rings of varying inner and outer diameters," giving this classic toy a smarter gameplay and great educational value. 💡 My Design Philosophy & Features: Error-Proof Sequence Design : Because the center post is tapered, the rings "will not slide all the way to the bottom" if stacked in the wrong order. This intuitive physical feedback allows children to self-correct and naturally grasp the concept of size sequencing and spatial logic. Gross and Fine Motor Skills Development : The action of picking up the rings and aligning them to stack onto the post exercises both gross motor skills (arm movement) and fine motor skills (finger grip and precision control). Visual Link Between Color & Size : With vibrant contrasting colors, children can visually observe and link specific "colors" to their corresponding "size order," strengthening visual association and memory during play. 🛠️ Printing Tips: For child safety, please check and lightly sand the edges after printing to ensure a smooth, burr-free surface.

INFO These are magnetic separation racks for 0.2mL PCR sized tubes. Works for SPRI, ConA, or any magnetic beads. My lab is a big fan of the epicypher racks but they cost $500 dollars so we were always fighting over the one, and even then when you have more than 8 or 16 samples it is inconvenient to always switch out tubes while doing high through put experiments. I wanted more racks so I designed these with a similar style and functionality to the epicypher racks with some added improvements. 1.Racks come in 8-tube and 12-tube sizes so you can make full use of the multichannel and scale up easier 2.Magnets are removable, so you can simply slide the magnet out rather than removing the tubes from the rack 3.The magnet can be turned around to work better for either small or large volumes. 4. Less than 1% of the price of Epicypher magnet racks (even with the cost of magnets) BEFORE YOU PRINT While smooth, semi-textured, and textured plates all work, I find that printing on a textured plate results in a tighter fit of the magnet holders inside the rack. I prefer the slightly looser fit I get when printing on my BIQU cool plate. If you use my print profile then you don't need any supports, however, these are kind of tall prints so I recommend making sure you have a clean bed and dried filament to avoid any adhesion errors. If you are having adhesion problems then you can take it a step farther and use a cool plate and/or a brim. ASSEMBLY You will need 10x5x3mm magnets. One 8 tube rack takes 16 magnets and one 12 tube rack takes 24 magnets. After printing, glue the two halves of the magnet holder together with the magnet holes in the same orientation. Then, insert the magnets. While they have a snug press fit, I find that they stay in better if the magnets on either side of the holder have opposite poles facing each other (the orientation where they stick together). A dab of super glue doesn't hurt either.

A simple gear set I created for a maker day event at the library. I would have preferred to just use something that was already out there, but as is typical for me, I began to want certain features / tweaks, so I just made my own. These were modeled in TinkerCAD using the gear generator shape. I wanted: something small and simple and lite for kids a grid / board that supports a large number of combinations of gear connections a way to drive the gears without turning them by hand an indicator for direction they were turning Ended up with: 5mm spaced grid board Works with 10T, 12T, 18T, 20T, 21T, 24T, 30T, 31T, 40T gears (most perfectly, some combinations have a tiny spacing error) Small hole direction indicator Handle / driver PDF activity for kids (8+) I initially didn't want to use pegs and fully open pegboard holes because I wanted the gears to be standard with hole in the center and no attached peg. So I initially started with a true board of pegs for gears to slip onto, but then realized I would be very limited with gear placement without some deep hubs on the gears to clear the peg heights. So then I moved onto a design with gears that slotted onto removeable pegs with separate c-clips to keep them on (like @osamutake models). The pegs screwed into slots on the board and then c-clips locked the gears onto them. This worked, but then I realized it wasn't so simple for kids, and the print resolution would have to be very fine to ensure threads were clean and c-clips were strong enough for kids to not break them. Kids screwing pegs in and out of the board and snapping c-clips into place, especially if the prints weren't perfectly clean, was going to be a problem.. So finally I reluctantly accepted a pluggable gears design into a holed pegboard as posted (similar to design by @Ioannis Tsar). The grid spacing evolved from 10mm to 5mm to support more gears. Also evolved from a hexagonal shape to conserve space and keep diagonal distances equilateral, but then the 5mm hypotenuses worked even with small spacing errors, so kept the grid shape for simplicity. The handle didn't work great and could be redesigned. This was my 3rd design, but still not driving the gears as well as hoped. Could definitely benefit from redesign. I had to print about 100 pieces of everything (sans 40T gears), so needed fast prints. Profile defaults to Random seam so seam is less of a hurdle. A grid bound at 0% sparse infill, draft 0.24mm layer print worked fine for me for my event. Gears were printed with 10% infill. A few posts snapped if kids were rough, so consider higher infill for longer lasting model. Sanding posts definitely helps but is time consuming. I would only recommend if you wanted to keep the kit around for a long time. If it's a one-off event, the gears work fine once snapped in and turned a bit.

!!!!! Hinweis bitte vor dem Drucken die kompette Beschreibeung lesen !!!!! Dieses Getriebe ist Teil eines Projektes aus der Vorlesung Konstruktionslehre IV aus unserem Studium. Ich habe das Getriebe zusammen mit @dontbanme , @Scheppa , @silas_irgendwas und zwei anderen Kollegen entwickelt. Wir haben dies zusätzlich zu der Ausarbeitung abgegeben und sind mächtig stolz darauf. Es ist ein wunderbares Anschauungsmodell, welches weiter optimiert wurde als die ursprüngliche abgegebene Version. Hier die wichtigsten Infos zum Getriebe: - das Planetengetriebe ist Teil eines Antriebstranges einer Presse. Um das Getriebe herum befindet sich noch ein deutlich größeres Schwungrad, sowie eine Kupplung. - ich habe das Getriebe komplett aus PLA gedruckt, wie es sich mit anderen Materialien verhält weiß ich nicht - ich habe einen P1S von Bambulab und sehr feine Einstellungen gewählt. Ob das notwendig ist, weiß ich nicht. Das Ergebnis lässt sich aber auf jeden Fall sehen - ich würde das Getriebe nicht skalieren, da sich sonst Abstände zwischen Lager und Welle proportional erhöhen, diese jedoch aufeinander abgestimmt sind - Für ein komplettes Getriebe muss man die Platten 1-3 und 4 oder 5 drucken. Die Platte 4 enthält einen Ständer mit Fläche für ein Schild (Siehe in der pdf), die Platte 5 ein Ständer ohne Fläche für ein Schild. - nach meiner Farbkodierung ist: weiß die Antriebswelle, schwarz der Abtrieb von Planetenträger, grau das Gehäuse, rot die Zahnräder, grün die Lager und gelb der Stopfen bzw. die Schrauben - ich habe folgendes geklebt: die Stifte in das Gehäuse, den Stopfen in das Gehäuse, die inneren Lager, direkt am Gehäuse - die Deckel können auf das Gehäuse geklebt werden, dann kann das Getriebe jedoch nicht mehr auseinandergenommen werden. Damit das Getriebe trotzdem zusammenhält ist die Klammer da. Diese kann von unten auf das komplette Gehäuse geschoben werden - die Kleinen Lager gehen lassen sich nur sehr schwer in die Zahnräder pressen. Dafür diese vorsichtig mit etwas diese in die Zahnräder schlagen, bis die Lager deutlich unter der Kante des Zahnrades sind - der Deckel vom Planetenträger hat extra eine Aussparung, sodass man ein Zahnrad sieht. Die „Schrauben“, welche Wirklichkeit nur Stifte sind, gingen bei mir sehr schwer. Wenn ihr das Getriebe wieder gut aufmachen können wollt, diese am besten ein wenig kleiner Skalieren und evtl. an den Deckel vom Planetenträger kleben - das angehängte pdf enthält die Beschriftung (52mmx22mm), ich habe dies auf Papier (DIN A4) ausgedruckt, welches man als Aufkleber verwenden kann. Es lässt sich aber auch mit normalem Papier ausdrucken und aufkleben - das ganze Getriebe mit Gestell braucht ca. 130g Filament - ich habe für die Stützen unter dem Gehäuse ein paar Schichten Support for PLA verwendet. Wenn kein Support for PLA Filament vorhanden ist dies einfach zu PETG ändern. Das funktioniert genauso. (Wenn das Getriebe aus PETG gedruckt wird dann zu PLA wechseln) Daher kommen auch ein paar wenige Filamentwechsel. Wer dies möchte einfach das Profil normale Stützen drucken. Ich habe insgesamt 5 Modelle gedruckt bis das Getriebe die finale Version hattte. Viel Spaß damit! english version: This gearbox is part of a project from the “Design Engineering IV” course in our degree program. I developed the gear together with @dontbanme , @Scheppa , @silas_irgendwas and two other colleagues. We submitted this in addition to our term paper and are incredibly proud of it. It’s a wonderful demonstration model that has been further optimized beyond the original version we submitted. Here’s the key information about the gearbox: - The planetary gearbox is part of a press’s drive train. Surrounding the gearbox is a significantly larger flywheel, as well as a clutch. - I printed the gearbox entirely out of PLA; I don’t know how it would behave with other materials. - I used a Bambulab P1S and selected very fine settings. I’m not sure if that was necessary. In any case, the result is definitely impressive. - I wouldn’t scale the gearbox, as doing so would proportionally increase the distances between the bearings and the shaft, which are designed to be precisely matched. - To build a complete gearbox, you need to print plates 1–3 and either 4 or 5. Plate 4 includes a support with space for a label (see the PDF); plate 5 includes a support without space for a label. - According to my color coding: white is the drive shaft, black is the output shaft of the planetary carrier, gray is the housing, red is the gears, green is the bearings, and yellow is the plugs or screws - I glued the following parts in place: the pins into the housing, the plug into the housing, and the inner bearings directly to the housing - The covers can be glued to the housing, but then the gearbox can no longer be taken apart. The clip is there to keep the gearbox together anyway. It can be slid onto the entire housing from below - The small bearings are very difficult to press into the gears. To do this, gently tap them into the gears with a small tool until the bearings are clearly below the edge of the gear. - The cover of the planetary carrier has a special cutout so you can see a gear. The “screws”—which are actually just pins—were very difficult for me to insert. If you want to be able to open the gearbox easily again, it’s best to scale these down slightly and possibly glue them to the cover of the planetary carrier - The attached PDF contains the label (52mm x 22mm); I printed this on paper (DIN A4), which can be used as a sticker. However, you can also print them on regular paper and stick them on. - The entire gearbox with the frame requires about 130g of filament. - I used the Super Cool Track Pro plate for the housing and the Textured PEI Plate for the rest. That’s how it’s set up. If you use different plates, be sure to take this into account! - I used a few layers of “Support for PLA” for the supports under the housing. If you don't have “Support for PLA” filament, simply switch to PETG. It works just the same. (If the gearbox is printed in PETG, switch to PLA.) That's why there are a few filament changes. If you don't want those, just change the support settings in the slicer back to normal supports. I printed a total of 5 models before the gearbox reached its final version. Have fun with it!

I wanted to electroplate my models and investigated online for suiting models. Found none that I was happy with. So I decided to design and build my own. The design consists of three main parts: 1) the motor assembly 2) the controlbox 3) the arc bridge assembly The motor assembly is designed so it can easily be fitted on different sized arc bridges, because not all containers have the same width/height requirements. I will share the dimensions of the current container i used, orderable off amazon. If you have another container, I will share the SCAD file as well, so you can easily adapt the width to your needs. Keep in mind that the min dia is always the width of the motormount plate and standoffs to the side of the container. The motor assembly itself houses the stepper (28BYJ-48) and the ULN2003 motor driver board. The controlbox has a couple of easy to acquire and solder components: an ESP32 board (i used a SEED XIAO ESP32-C6, very small board), a LM2596 buck converter, a rotary encoder (KY-040) to control the speed, a battery and an on/off switch. I will share the scheme here as well. The ESP firmware will also be shared (rename the main.c.txt to main.c) IMPORTANT NOTE; make sure to trim your buck convertor to 5v before connecting anything to it, otherwise it may be set too high and you will fry your electronics The arc bridge is pretty straightforward; it clamps on to the side of the container (dont overdo it, just keeps it from moving around) and comes with a nut to secure the motor assembly in place. I also designed a model hook that allows a straight copper wire down into the bath, by easily sticking the wire in from below, where it exits on the side and you can loop it around the rough thread of the hook. this is a 10/10 connection to your model. Moreover; this allows you to prep and test your hookup before you connect it to the hook of the rotary and allows for multiple models to be prepared in parallel. In functional terms; the device is powered either through usb or through a 9v block in the compartment of the control box, it's wired to prefer the USB power when available. The movement is started by pushing in the rotary encoder button, that controls start/stop movement. then turning the knob controls the speed of movement. The movement is designed as an oscillator; it turns 1,25 times and then reverses that movement. This is to make sure your connecting wire (to the negative lead) doesnt get looped (ruining your electrical connection). I added the whole setup in one .3mf on two plates. enjoy and let me know if you have questions or are happy with your build !

description: The STEM MicroLaunch Rocket is a hands‑on chemistry experiment disguised as an awesome mini rocket. Designed for classrooms, STEM clubs, home learning, and curious kids everywhere, this project demonstrates how a simple chemical reaction can generate real thrust. This 3‑part printable kit includes: A micro rocket with internal reaction chamber A dual‑measure scoop (large side for vinegar, small side for baking soda) A snap‑fit launch base Kids measure, mix, assemble, and launch — learning about pressure, gas expansion, and propulsion in a safe, engaging way. Using everyday household ingredients (baking soda + vinegar), the rocket builds up carbon dioxide inside the chamber. When the pressure becomes high enough, the rocket pops off the base and launches upward. It’s a perfect introduction to chemical reactions, Newton’s laws, and basic rocketry. This project is designed for easy printing, simple assembly, and repeatable demonstrations anywhere — in the classroom, at home, or outdoors. The included instructions guide users step‑by‑step through measuring, loading, launching, and cleaning the rocket after use. Instructions 1. Using the smaller scoop, add 1 full small scoop of baking soda into the rocket base. 2. Using the large scoop, add 1 full large scoop of vinegar into the rocket. 3. Quickly push the base onto the rocket firmly . 4. Set the rocket down in an open space, then stand clear for launch. Do not lean over the top of the rocket !!! Base Fit & Launch Technique The launch base is tapered slightly — thinner at the top and wider at the bottom. This design helps accommodate small tolerance differences between printers and makes it easier to place the rocket onto the base smoothly. When securing the rocket onto the base, start with light pressure . If the rocket doesn’t build enough pressure to launch, increase the pressure slightly until you find the “sweet spot” where the rocket seals well, builds CO₂ pressure, and launches cleanly. Placing the rocket down too firmly can cause it to get stuck and not launch. If this happens, please seek help from an adult. The adult should hold the rocket upside down , then gently press the base from each side. This will cause the base to pop off with the same force the rocket would have launched — so make sure it is pointed away from people, pets, or objects . For best results, try to place the rocket as evenly as possible onto the base so all sides have equal pressure. It may take a little practice, but once you get the feel for it, the STEM MicroLaunch Rocket launches beautifully and travels a surprisingly good distance for such a small rocket. How It Works The chemical reaction between baking soda and vinegar creates a rapid build‑up of carbon dioxide gas. As pressure increases inside the rocket, the gas escapes through the base, creating thrust and launching the rocket upward. Warnings & Safety Read and follow all instructions Securely install the base before launching Only launch outdoors in a safe open space Powerful thrust — never lean over the rocket Eye protection recommended Move away from the rocket when launching Tips & Maintenance Clean the rocket thoroughly after use so the vinegar doesn’t corrode the parts The fuel will splash — wear clothes you don’t mind getting wet

This is my Astronomy Without Borders Onesky 130F5 upper tube assembly. I found two major deficiencies with the original upper tube assembly. The sloppy threads in the helical focuser, that does not have adequate rigidity The finicky secondary mirror collimation The sloppy threads in the original helical focuser is well known with kludgy fixes like wrapping the threads in Teflon tape or using grease on the threads… But the bigger problem was the thin plastic cantilevered design. If you tried using any moderately heavy eyepieces the weight was cause it to sag and vibrate intolerably at higher magnifications, making planetary observing incredibly frustrating. And for some reason that I can not imagine, people making these entry level telescopes put the spring between the secondary mirror and the hub thingy. When you loosen the locking screw the whole thing just goes wherever it wants and makes collimation a total pain. Also, having the whole assembly on the one round rod made one more axis it could rotate on and need adjusting. Very annoying. In this upper tube assembly, the whole things is printed thick and solid, allowing for the mounting of a full size Crayford focuser. This upper assembly is very solid and has very little deflection. It uses a four vane spider, and I relocated the spring to the top side of the hub so it's in a push/pull orientation. Now when you loosen the center screw a turn or two, the spring holds the mirror mount against the three screws so you can actually see what effect your adjustments have on your collimation. As an added benefit, the holes for the strut rods are much deeper, which leaves a lot less unsupported rod length further increasing stiffness. And finally, I rotated the focuser around a bit for easier seated observing. IMO, the stock orientation seemed better for standing and hunching over the telescope. Now the focuser is at a 45° angle which I think offers better ergonomics. There are a couple of compromises though. First, it makes the telescope very top heavy. I had to slide the dovetail all the way as far as it can go, and it's still not 100% perfectly balanced but it's good enough. And second, the large Crayford sticks out axially further than the original focuser, requiring the use of 22mm spacers limiting how far the telescope extends to achieve focus. This is the focuser: https://agenaastro.com/gso-crayford-focuser-reflector-telescope-dual-speed-eaf-1-25.html Use the 176mm base curvature option. The design also utilizes this dovetail mounting shoe https://a.co/d/0iBxRjiH It is designed for m6 screws but I wanted to only use M4 on this design so I made this insert that allows the use of two M4 x 16mm countersunk head screws.` The designed it to use 4mm heat set inserts. https://a.co/d/0dv4AGsl Finally, I purchased this red dot finder scope https://a.co/d/04XIdzyd My only criticism is that even on the dimmest setting it's still pretty bright. I printed all the parts in ABS at 0.16mm layers, 6 wall loops, 20-25% gyroid infill with 3 fill lines. PETG or either ABS or PETG CF would also be nice, but I didn't have that and the normal ABS seems plenty stiff enough. This print requires minimum supports. I would not print in PLA, as it will warp if left in a hot car. I flocked the inside of the telescope tube and shroud, and painted the inside of the upper tube and spider in Musou black paint. https://a.co/d/06kpUJR0 https://a.co/d/05EYCLqY When assembling the strut rods into the upper tube assembly, it's a snug press fit and might require some persuasion with a plastic tipped hammer. The ends of the tubes must be flush with the bottom of the counter-bores. A keen eye will notice the end screws are missing on my telescope. I lost one somewhere along the way but I made the counter-bores a little too tight and makes installing the screw difficult. I fixed this on the uploaded model. I contacted Celestron and Skywatcher for replacement screws but neither were any help, so I'm on my own to find a suitable substitute but it seems like an odd thread. The tube extension fits into a groove and is fixed in place with CA glue. The shroud snaps in firmly, glue is optional. I used a soldering iron set to 280-290C to set the threaded inserts. All finished I could not be happier with the performance of the 'scope. It focuses fast and easy, especially with the Bahtinov mask. The 10:1 micro adjust is a dream. Collimation is easy and holds solidly. Vibrations are minimal and settle quickly.

Pinza Multiuso Gommata (Scala 1:4) | Meccanismo Articolato Porta la vera ingegneria sulla tua scrivania! Questo non è un semplice giocattolo, ma la riproduzione in scala 1:4 di una vera " Pinza Multiuso Gommata " industriale, basata su un efficiente meccanismo a ginocchiera. La Storia del Progetto 🎓 Ho progettato questo cinematismo per un progetto di Laboratorio di Progettazione Meccanica in Università. La versione reale (in scala 1:1) è stata rigorosamente dimensionata e verificata dal punto di vista strutturale per sollevare in totale sicurezza carichi fino a 10 kN (circa 1 tonnellata). Ho deciso di scalarla in formato 1:4 per permettere a tutta la community di testare con mano la cinematica e la fisica dietro questo tipo di macchinari: più l'oggetto da sollevare è pesante, più la forza di serraggio orizzontale delle ganasce aumenta! (Per i più curiosi e gli appassionati di meccanica, ho allegato tra i file anche la mia relazione di calcolo originale completa di verifiche e dimensionamenti in lingua italiana). Dettagli di Stampa Ho caricato il profilo .3mf completo e già ottimizzato per BambuStudio. Il progetto è completamente stampabile in 3D , inclusi tutti i perni di articolazione (non avrete bisogno di viti o ferramenta esterna). Materiali: PLA o PETG per la struttura principale. Stampa Multimateriale SENZA AMS (Il trucco per le ganasce): Nel piatto dedicato alle ganasce ( Jaws ), ho impostato una pausa strategica prima degli ultimi layer. Questo vi permetterà di cambiare manualmente la bobina anche se non avete un AMS. Potete usare del filamento nero per un semplice contrasto estetico, oppure caricare del TPU . Usare il TPU per i primi strati simulerà il vero cuscinetto in gomma industriale, garantendo il giusto attrito per afferrare e sollevare davvero gli oggetti sulla vostra scrivania! Guida al Montaggio 🔧 (Screenshot) Le Chele Principali: Iniziate unendo le due chele centrali tramite il perno di articolazione mediano. I Bracci Superiori: Collegate le bielle alla parte superiore della struttura, posizionando l'anello di sollevamento (cruna) al centro ed i relativi perni. Le Ganasce: Agganciate le due ganasce inferiori (quelle con la presa gommata) ai bracci esterni e collegatele con i rispettivi perni. Nota sui perni: Inserite tutti i perni stampati in 3D nei rispettivi occhielli per chiudere il cinematismo (I perni più lunghi colleganmo gli elementi portanti della pinza, mentre quelli più corti collegano le chedle della pinza con le risepttive ganasce gommate). Buona stampa e buon sollevamento!

This radius gauge is specific made for Mitutoyo vernier calipers. There are many simular devices on Makerword but ALL of them have a 45 degree angle. That means you must multiply the mesurement by some weird value. My radius gauge has an angle of 60 degrees. This means that if you mesure a round object then you get exact radius on your caliper. You don't have to calculate anything anymore. Just mesure and you have the exact radius on your caliper display. Disclaimer: This still is a printed pard and can bend while mesuring. If you bend the arms too much your mesurement will deviate. Usage: Puss your Mitutoyo calipers end (for depth mesurement) in the hole of the gauge with the display facing the round indent of the gauge all the way in. Close the caliper to zero. Place your round object against the 2 arms of the radius gauge. Hold the round object and push only the part of the caliper with the display towards the round object untill the pin tuches the round object. Now read the radius of the round object from the screen. This should be half of the outer diameter of the round object. It could be off a little bit because of your printers settings and temperature but my mesurements are realy close. I hope you like my model Leave a comment if you have any sugestions.

description: DESCRIPTION ----------- A three-stage rubber band motor that stores and releases energy through a sequence of rack-and-pinion stages. When the first rubber band contracts, it pulls its rack and turns the gears. Once that stage is fully contracted, a lever trigger releases the second stage, and the same hand-off then fires the third. The complete run lasts about five seconds and is satisfying to watch in motion. This design explores a way to store more energy in rubber bands by chaining stages instead of relying on a single band. The lever-trigger approach works well here, though other methods (for example bevel or worm gears) could also be used. In theory the same idea can be extended to any number of stages, which makes the model a useful base for anyone who wants to understand the mechanism and improve on it. ASSEMBLY NOTES -------------- Assembly needs care so that every trigger and lever engages correctly. A practical approach is: 1. Get the first stage to reliably trigger the second. 2. Glue that hinge in its exact best position once it works. 3. Then set up and tune the third stage the same way. 4. The axle is made of several parts that fit together inside the middle of the pinion gears. Photos of the fully assembled machine are included to show how the finished model should look.

description: 36:1 Dual-Stage Planetary Gearbox for NEMA 17 This is a functional 36:1 dual-stage planetary gearbox designed for a NEMA 17 stepper motor. It was developed as a joint reducer for my base-actuated robotic arm, but it may also be useful for other low-speed rotary mechanisms, positioning systems, and experimental robotics projects. This design is the result of a long process of printing, measuring, disassembling, redesigning, and testing. It was not created using nominal CAD dimensions alone. The final geometry was repeatedly adjusted according to the actual behavior of FDM-printed mechanical parts, including: Bore shrinkage Extrusion and outer-wall spread Temperature-dependent dimensional changes Bearing and shaft press fits Deformation caused by assembly pressure Gear-tooth contact Wear during initial running-in One of the most important features is the lower hub of the central sun gear. It was designed as the primary alignment reference between the motor shaft and both planetary stages. Even accurately modeled gears can develop noise, vibration, uneven wear, and backlash when the sun gear is loose, tilted, or eccentric. For this reason, the shaft interface, bearing support, gear clearances, output structure, and six-point fastening system were developed together as one complete mechanical assembly. The gearbox may feel slightly tight immediately after assembly. During controlled low-speed running-in, microscopic high points on the printed tooth surfaces gradually wear away, allowing the gearbox to reach a smoother and more stable final operating clearance. Running-in should only remove minor surface irregularities. Severe binding, tooth skipping, concentrated heating, or large plastic fragments indicate a printing, dimensional, or assembly problem. Demonstration Video https://youtube.com/shorts/FVjSa3sgb2A Main Specifications Gearbox type: Dual-stage planetary gearbox Total reduction ratio: 36:1 Motor interface: NEMA 17 Output method: Upper ring-gear output Main output bearing: 35 × 47 × 7 mm Recommended material: PETG or another strong, dimensionally stable material Intended use: Robot arms and low-speed rotary mechanisms Backlash: Very low perceptible backlash during manual testing Quantified backlash: Not yet measured using calibrated equipment Required Hardware M3 × 20 mm hex socket screws: 6 M3 heat-set inserts, 5 mm height: 24 M3 × 8 mm countersunk hex screws: 6 35 × 47 × 7 mm bearing: 1 M3 × 12 mm countersunk hex screws: 6 M2.5 × 7 mm countersunk hex screws: 6 NEMA 17 stepper motor: 1 Hex-drive screws are recommended for all connections. Important Printing Instructions Use a Brim on All Parts Except the Sun Gears and Planet Gears A brim is strongly recommended for all printed parts except the sun gears and planet gears . This includes: Housing parts Ring gears Output components Bearing retainers Motor-mounting parts Covers and other structural components The brim helps provide: Reliable bed adhesion A stable and flat bottom surface Accurate alignment between stacked housing parts Proper bearing and heat-set insert seating Reduced corner lifting and warping The flatness of the housing, ring gears, and output components directly affects the alignment of both planetary stages. Even a small amount of warping may cause uneven rotational resistance, bearing misalignment, or periodic binding. A brim is not recommended for the sun gears and planet gears because removing it may damage the lower tooth edges or alter the critical tooth geometry. Remove all brims carefully without damaging the bottom reference surfaces. Use the Manufacturer-Recommended Bed Temperature Always use the normal bed temperature recommended for the selected filament. Do not unnecessarily increase the bed temperature to improve adhesion. Excessive bed temperature may cause elephant-foot deformation, which can: Enlarge the lower edges Distort screw-clearance holes Affect bearing and insert locations Prevent stacked parts from seating flat Change the alignment of the planetary stages The first layer must adhere securely without being excessively compressed or spread outward. Use a Strong Material A mechanically strong and dimensionally stable material is strongly recommended. PETG was used during development, but another properly calibrated high-strength material may also be suitable. The selected material should provide: Strong layer adhesion Resistance to cracking Reliable bearing retention Reliable heat-set insert retention Adequate wear resistance Low long-term deformation under bolt pressure and mechanical load Different materials may produce different dimensions, tooth clearances, friction, and running-in behavior. Test the fit carefully before completing the full assembly. Correcting Tight Tolerances When the printed clearances are slightly too tight, first check: Flow ratio First-layer compression Bed temperature Nozzle temperature XY compensation Hole compensation Actual printer dimensional accuracy If excessive material flow or thermal spreading appears to be the cause, printing at a slightly lower nozzle temperature may improve the fit. Reduce the temperature only in small increments. Do not lower it so far that layer adhesion or mechanical strength is reduced. Never Scale or Modify the Model Do not scale the model or change its geometry to correct a fitting problem. Scaling or reshaping the components changes critical mechanical relationships, including: Gear-tooth thickness Gear pitch geometry Planetary center distances Ring-gear engagement Bearing seats Shaft alignment Motor mounting positions Fastener spacing Output concentricity Even a small dimensional change may prevent the two planetary stages from meshing correctly. Do not modify: Gear profiles Gear center distances Bearing locations Shaft interfaces Alignment surfaces Overall component proportions Printing errors should be corrected through printer calibration, flow adjustment, temperature adjustment, first-layer calibration, and appropriate hole compensation—not by changing the model. Assembly Instructions and Precautions Tighten every six-screw pattern gradually in a diagonal sequence. Do not fully tighten one screw before installing and partially tightening the others. Uneven tightening may distort the housing or shift the planetary stages out of alignment. Use moderate hand pressure. Excessive tightening may: Deform the printed housing Distort the bearing seat Misalign the planetary stages Damage or rotate the heat-set inserts Increase rotational resistance Distort the output ring gear If an M3 clearance hole prints too small, carefully open only that clearance hole using a 3.0 mm drill bit so that the screw passes through freely. Do not drill: Heat-set insert holes Bearing seats Sun-gear or planet-gear bores Motor-shaft interfaces Precision alignment surfaces The 3.0 mm drill should only be used on holes intended to provide free passage for an M3 screw. Press the 35 × 47 × 7 mm bearing into the housing evenly through its outer ring. Do not hammer the bearing into place, and do not transmit the insertion force through the inner ring or rolling elements. Before applying an external load: Rotate the gearbox by hand in both directions. Check for hard stops or periodic binding. Operate the motor slowly without load. Run the gearbox in both directions. Inspect the teeth and remove loose wear debris. Confirm that the bearing and housing remain properly seated. Increase the load gradually only after smooth operation is confirmed. Stop operation immediately if you observe: Severe binding Tooth skipping Sharp periodic impacts Concentrated heating Large plastic fragments Cracked gear teeth Bearing movement Shaft slipping Rapidly increasing backlash Development Background This gearbox was developed using a printer that I have repaired, modified, and studied for a long time. A newer machine could have produced prototypes faster, but learning the limitations of an imperfect printer taught me how printed parts actually change between CAD, printing, press fitting, assembly, wear, and real operation. I repeatedly printed and measured parts to understand: How internal holes shrink How external surfaces spread How temperature changes the final dimensions How press fitting deforms printed components Which interfaces must remain completely rigid Which microscopic tooth irregularities may safely wear away How initial running changes the final operating clearance The final design represents the complete process: Printing → Measurement → Dimensional correction → Assembly → Running-in → Final operating clearance This is not simply a generic planetary gear set placed inside a housing. The shaft alignment, bearing support, output structure, six-point fastening, gear clearances, and running-in behavior were developed together through repeated physical testing. The precision of this gearbox did not come from a perfect machine. It came from understanding the machine’s limitations and designing around them.

Atmos Mk 1.2 The Atmos Mk 1.2 is a compact 3D-printable model rocket designed for use with Estes E16-6 and E16-8 motors . It features a dedicated electronics bay that can fit a Raspberry Pi Pico/Pico 2 , GY-BME280 pressure sensor , and a 3.7V LiPo battery , allowing makers to add custom flight computers, altitude logging, and other experimental electronics. Designed with accessibility and customization in mind, the Atmos Mk 1.2 can be printed using a wide range of common 3D printing materials. Whether printed in PLA for easy prototyping, PETG for added durability, or other materials for specialized builds, the design can be adapted to suit different launch goals. The Atmos Mk 1.2 is a platform for makers, students, and rocketry enthusiasts who want to explore 3D printing, electronics, and experimental flight systems in a compact and reusable rocket design. Flight Notes Stability margin: Approximately 1.7 calibers . Estimated altitude: Typically reaches 800–1,000 ft (240–305 m) , depending on launch conditions. Flight history: Successfully tested over 3 flights (with a 4th planned) with E16-8 estes rocket motors, demonstrating reliable performance and durable construction, you could use f motors but i wouldn't go below 15N of force engines to ensure safe liftoff. Recommendations: do not attempt to remove the motor directly after flight wait for the plastic to cool read assembly note carefully to prevent hardware issues higher temp materials ensure more durability but i have printed out of both pla and petg for this project and pla will function and work I assembled a flight computer out of a raspberry pi pico a gy bme barometer and a small quadcopter battery for under ten dollars and this platform was mostly designed to test it i encourage others to do the same but also i plan to drop links to my functioning code later once i have it all ironed out Assembly Notes To assemble the Atmos Mk 1.2, you'll need 3–4 pennies, super glue, a nylon or Kevlar shock cord, a small amount of duct tape, recovery wadding, a small i hook, and your choice of recovery system (streamer or parachute) . If any printed parts fit loosely, adjust the tolerances with a small amount of Scotch tape as needed. Finally, don't forget to add recovery wadding before every launch. MiniMoto Educational Drivetrain V1 (Competition Edition) A compact, fully functional educational drivetrain designed to demonstrate how power travels from the engine to the wheels. This model was designed for the Thangs "Keeping Busy - Toys & Projects" contest as a hands-on teaching tool that lets you see the internal workings of a vehicle drivetrain instead of hiding everything inside a transmission case. The assembly includes a working engine, selectable transmission, driveshaft, open differential, and rear axle. Every major component is removable, making it easy to understand how each system works individually and how they work together as a complete drivetrain. Whether you're learning about gear ratios, differential operation, or simply enjoy mechanical engineering, this model was built to make those concepts easy to visualize. As a bonus, assembling small mechanical models can be a relaxing way to focus your attention and take your mind off the day... unless you're fighting with a stubborn 3D printer. Apology I messed up. In my frantic rush to finish this model before the contest closed, I made the holes on the engine frame too big or too small the axles could slip out of the holes, and the control shaft wouldn't fit. This has since been fixed in a new file labeled "Frame_Fixed", but I had to delete the original model, already uploaded (and downloaded by 5 people) so I could add them. If you see double, this is the right one. I apologize for any confusion this caused and can only hope that you will be understanding of my situation. If you catch any more mistake I made, Please write a comment, I will try my best to fix them. Thank you. Features Working inline engine Selectable transmission with multiple gear ratios Functional open differential Rear axle and wheel assembly Modular design for easy assembly and maintenance Designed for education, demonstration, and display Parts Included Main Frame Front Axle Rear Axles Engine Frame Crankshaft Connecting Rods (x4) Piston Heads (x4) Transmission Control Shaft Transmission Frame Transmission High and Low Gears Transmission Power Shaft Transmission Shift Collar Transmission Transition Gear Ring Gear Spider Gears Wheels (x4) Tires (x4) Hardware Required None. The model is designed to assemble entirely from printed parts. Assembly Notes Most components use snap-fit / press-fit features designed to simplify assembly and reduce the need for hardware. (Glue may be required) Take your time during assembly and test-fit moving parts before fully snapping components together. Depending on your printer's tolerances, light sanding or minor cleanup may improve the fit of gears and shafts. Assembly instructions are at : https://thangs.com/designer/MINIMOTO_LAB/3d-model/MiniMoto%20Educational%20Drivetrain%20V1-Fixed-1571745 Tires and Rims are included but not required. Design Notes This project was designed to be both educational and enjoyable to assemble. Rather than hiding the drivetrain inside a solid body, the frame intentionally leaves the moving parts exposed so the complete path of power can be followed from the engine, through the transmission, into the differential, and finally to the wheels. The goal was not to create a scale vehicle, but to create an interactive model that makes mechanical concepts easy to see, understand, and demonstrate. description: UPDATE: Complete 40K 11th Edition Battlefield Terrain Set — Now with Optional Second Levels Take the Guesswork Out of Building a 40K Battlefield 40K 11th Edition introduced some excellent predetermined battlefield layouts that show players how to arrange the battlefield and where different terrain features should be placed. However, the dimensions of those terrain pieces are not always clearly provided, and determining what terrain to use can be surprisingly confusing. There are countless terrain models available, but figuring out which pieces you actually need, what sizes they should be, and how everything fits together on an 11th Edition battlefield can quickly become a project of its own. This collection was created to simplify that entire process. I carefully studied the battlefield layouts shown in the 40K app, determined the different terrain footprints and sizes needed to recreate them, and designed a complete, coordinated set that allows players to print everything required for a functional battlefield in one place. Instead of downloading unrelated models from multiple creators and hoping they work together, this set provides a clear starting point for new players and a convenient, consistent battlefield system for experienced players. I have also included A1 Mini print profiles, making the set accessible to players using smaller-format printers. UPDATE: Optional Second Levels Now Included I originally left second levels out of the terrain set intentionally. My goal was to keep the battlefield simple, easy to understand, and approachable for newer players who may already be learning a large number of rules. However, I also understand that many players want additional verticality and more options as they expand their battlefield. The collection now includes optional second-level components for anyone who wants to add elevated positions and more visual depth to the terrain. The second levels are completely optional. New players can continue using the original single-level terrain for the simplest possible setup, while more experienced players can add the upper levels wherever they want additional height and variety. This allows the terrain set to grow with you: Start with the simple, single-level battlefield Add second levels when you are ready Mix single-level and multi-level terrain on the same battlefield Customize the amount of verticality to match your preferred style of play The original goal remains unchanged: provide a battlefield that is easy to print, easy to understand, and ready to use without unnecessary complexity. What’s Included The complete collection includes: Battlefield terrain footprints Light terrain features Dense terrain features Optional second-level terrain components Standard objective markers Central and expansion objective markers Deployment zone markers Coordinated pieces designed to work together as one complete battlefield system A1 Mini-compatible print profiles The terrain footprints clearly define each terrain area, while the light and dense terrain pieces provide the physical structures needed to make the battlefield easy to understand and play on. The optional second levels allow players to add elevated positions without requiring everyone to use them. The objective and deployment zone markers make setup faster and reduce the need to repeatedly measure important locations before every game. AB, CD, EF, and GH Dense Terrain The dense terrain pieces were specifically designed and marked to correspond with the AB, CD, EF, and GH terrain categories shown in the battlefield layouts within the 40K app. This makes it much easier to identify which dense terrain piece belongs in each location when setting up a battlefield. Rather than comparing several similar-looking pieces, estimating dimensions, or trying to determine which terrain feature matches each layout position, simply select the appropriately marked AB, CD, EF, or GH model. This labeling system helps make battlefield setup faster, clearer, and more approachable—especially for players building their first complete terrain collection. Designed for Fast, Reliable Printing Every part of this collection was created with practical 3D printing in mind. The main design goals were: Fast print times Low filament use High printing success rates No support material required Simple, reliable geometry Easy battlefield setup Clear and consistent terrain sizes Minimal preparation after printing Optional expansion without unnecessary complexity The models were designed to print without supports and can be used immediately after removing them from the build plate. There should be no difficult support removal, complicated assembly, or extensive cleanup required. Print the pieces, remove them from the plate, and place them directly on the battlefield. The optional second levels can be added when desired, while the original single-level configuration remains available for players who prefer the simplest possible setup. These models are intended to be accessible to newer 3D-printer owners and players who may be building their first complete 40K battlefield. They are functional gaming pieces first—not overly complicated display models that require days of printing, large amounts of filament, or extensive post-processing. Recommended Printing Approach For the clearest gameplay experience, I recommend printing the footprints, light terrain, and dense terrain in different colors . Using separate colors makes it easier to quickly identify which terrain category a piece belongs to and helps reduce confusion when applying terrain rules during play. This is especially helpful for newer players, teaching games, or anyone trying to make battlefield interactions more intuitive at a glance. For example, using one color for footprints, another for light terrain, and another for dense terrain makes it easier to determine which terrain rules apply when models move into, through, around, or onto a terrain feature. The optional second-level pieces can be printed in the same color as the terrain category they belong to, helping them remain visually consistent with the rest of the battlefield. A Complete Starting Point for New Players This set is especially useful for someone who has recently started playing 40K and is asking: What terrain do I need? How large should each terrain area be? Which pieces are light terrain and which are dense terrain? Which dense terrain piece corresponds with AB, CD, EF, or GH? How do I reproduce the battlefield layouts shown in the app? Do I need second levels on my terrain? How many objective markers do I need? Where should deployment zones and objectives be placed? The answer regarding second levels is simple: use them when you want them . They are now included for players who want additional height and variety, but they are not required to begin using the terrain set. The goal is to remove as much uncertainty as possible so you can spend less time researching terrain and more time printing, painting, and playing. Modular and Easy to Customize The pieces can be printed as a complete matching set or mixed with terrain you already own. You can use the terrain entirely at ground level, add second levels to selected ruins, or create a battlefield with a mixture of single-level and multi-level structures. Terrain footprints can also be used with ruins, buildings, rock formations, industrial structures, or other decorative terrain placed within the marked areas. This makes the system useful even as your terrain collection grows. Print the included terrain for a quick, lightweight battlefield, or use the footprints, optional second levels, and markers as the foundation for a more detailed custom table. Additional Helpful Models Along with this terrain set, you may want something for taking quick measurements between models. I highly recommend this adjustable compass-style range finder by The Moose and Bolter: https://makerworld.com/en/models/2730760-kt-range-finder-the-ultimate-adjustable-compass#profileId-3026517 For tracking wounds, I also have several wound trackers listed here on MakerWorld. The model linked below was specifically designed to be lightweight and easy to print, just like this terrain set: https://makerworld.com/en/models/3011980-wound-tracker-engagement-range-gauge-11th-ed#profileId-3382976 Important Note This is an unofficial, community-created terrain and battlefield setup system intended for tabletop wargaming. It is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or produced by Games Workshop. Battlefield requirements, event standards, terrain interpretations, and tournament rulings may vary, so always confirm the requirements of your local gaming group or event organizer. The models are designed as a practical way to recreate and organize the battlefield layouts represented in the 40K app while making the process easier for players and 3D-printing hobbyists. Start with the simple single-level battlefield, add the optional second levels when you are ready, and play without the guesswork.

Axen vive en los canales tranquilos de Zoora, donde el agua casi nunca se mueve. Le gusta quedarse muy quieto en el fondo y observar cómo cambian las corrientes. Un día, después de una lluvia fuerte, el agua se volvió turbia y muchos pensaron que una entrada del camino antiguo había desaparecido bajo el barro. Axen no salió corriendo ni removió el agua. Se quedó quieto, esperando. Poco a poco, el barro bajó al fondo y entonces pudo ver algo que nadie había notado: una abertura de piedra seguía allí, escondida bajo tres pequeñas marcas azules. Así descubrió que la entrada no se había perdido. Solo estaba oculta. Desde entonces, cuando algo parece haber desaparecido en Zoora, muchos recuerdan a Axen y esperan un poco antes de rendirse. Moraleja: A veces, quedarse quieto es la mejor forma de ver las cosas con claridad.

Bluegill are a common species of freshwater gamefish native to the the United States east of the Rocky Mountains, but they have also been introduced to most of the other western states too. They're easy to catch and will bite on worms, artificial baits, corn, and even bread. For these reasons, bluegill are usually the first fish that young anglers in the US catch. Their exact coloration can vary between genders and seasons, but bluegill can typically be identified by their dark green bodies, black “ear” at the corner of the gill, reddish, orange chest, and their blue chins and gills. They are usually at the bottom of the food chain and are preyed on by bass, pike, catfish, herons, and other aquatic predators. To defend themselves they have sharp spines poking out from their dorsal fins that teach the young anglers who catch them to be careful when unhooking them. This model has interlocking scale units that allow the model to “swim”. The two halves are printed separately, aligned with the registration pin that fits into the rectangular slot on the bottom of the head segments, and secured together with glue between the head, tail, and perimeter scales. For this model, the pectoral fins are printed separately to maximize strength and then glued into the slots behind the gills. I used bronze silk PLA for most of the body, but a dark olive green PLA might match the real coloration more closely. The full-color model uses 5 colors and requires 2 AMS units, but I've also provided a 4-color version without the dark green on top that can be printed with 1 AMS. Happy printing (and fishing)!

Merek vive en una zona abierta de Zoora, donde le gusta subirse a pequeñas piedras para vigilar el horizonte. Dice que desde arriba las cosas siempre se entienden mejor. Una mañana encontró una losa antigua con dos pequeñas marcas azules . Recordaba haber oído que algunas señales del camino antiguo tenían tres, así que algo no encajaba. En lugar de tocarla o empezar a cavar, Merek decidió observarla durante horas. Cuando el sol quedó justo encima, la sombra de un borde desapareció y dejó ver la tercera marca , que había estado oculta bajo una fina capa de polvo. Así descubrió que la señal no estaba incompleta. Solo había que mirarla en el momento adecuado. Moraleja: A veces, mirar con calma más de una vez es la mejor forma de entender.

Brook trout are vibrant and beautiful members of the salmon/char family native to the eastern United States and Canada. They hold significant ecological significance and are designated as the state fish of 5 states (Pennsylvania, Virginia, Michigan, New Hampshire, and New York)! Due to their sensitivity to pollution, they are a great indicator species, meaning that waterways and environments able to house them are very healthy. Before introduction of brown trout and rainbow trout. the brook trout were the only trout species targeted by anglers for the first 100 years of the United State's history. For both of these reasons, Brook trout are seen as a symbol of pristine North American wilderness. These fish hold special meaning to me too. As a kid my grandfather would take me to small streams in northern Pennsylvania to catch them. Each time I caught one I was surprised at just how vibrant they were, even if they were only 3-4 inches long. Those experiences really made me love being in nature and fishing, which has inspired all of my articulated fish models. So I'm dedicating this model to my grandfather, Wayne. Keyring versions are also available on plate 2 of each print profile. The model was designed to fit on the A-mini but can be scaled up as large as you want it! As mentioned before, Brook Trout are very colorful fish which means a lot of filament swaps in 3D printing. The base model is painted in 6 colors and requires 2 AMS units. I used black as the base color, but a dark-olive color would more closely match the real thing. To get around these requirements though, I've also provided a print profile with only the basic black, white, and orange coloration. For that print profile the yellow squiggles and red and blue spots are left out and can be painted on in acrylic afterwards. In my opinion, the painted blue and red dots stood out more when painted on rather than printed on. The only downside to acrylics paint is it's water solubility so the color could be washed away or smear if the model gets wet. However you decide to print/paint this model, I hope you enjoy your new fishy friend! Happy printing (and fishing)!

description: Kenku Miniature – Cunning Crowfolk Scout and Master Mimic This miniature is part of the Monster Manual 2024 Collection , a series of iconic creatures faithfully reimagined as dynamic, tabletop-ready sculpts. The Kenku is one of the most recognizable avian humanoids in the Monster Manual 2024, combining the appearance of a clever crow with the posture and equipment of an experienced rogue, scout, or thief. Renowned for their uncanny mimicry, stealth, and resourcefulness, Kenku survive through intelligence rather than brute strength. This miniature faithfully follows the uploaded reference, capturing a wary infiltrator caught in the middle of a burglary or reconnaissance mission. The miniature stands on a Medium (25 mm) round tabletop base in a low stalking pose. The Kenku balances with one foot planted firmly on uneven cobblestones while the opposite foot rests atop a weathered wooden crate, giving the impression that it is silently navigating rooftops, alleyways, or forgotten ruins. The crouched posture lowers its center of gravity and immediately communicates stealth, agility, and constant awareness. Every point of contact remains securely connected to the base for excellent print stability. Its anatomy reflects the lean proportions described in Monster Manual 2024. The body is slender and athletic rather than muscular, built for climbing, running, and quiet movement. Narrow shoulders transition into long arms ending in dexterous clawed hands capable of manipulating tools and weapons with remarkable precision. The digitigrade bird-like legs terminate in powerful talons that grip both the ground and the crate naturally, reinforcing the dynamic balance of the pose. The head is unmistakably raven-like, featuring dense layered feathers that create a textured crown across the skull and neck. A long black beak curves gently downward with realistic proportions rather than exaggerated length. Sharp amber eyes peer cautiously toward unseen danger, conveying intelligence and suspicion rather than aggression. The head tilts slightly forward, reinforcing the feeling that the Kenku is constantly evaluating its surroundings before making its next move. The left arm reaches forward with spread talons as though preparing to steady itself or silently grab a nearby object. The opposite arm remains pulled back, gripping a simple steel dagger in a reverse grip suitable for ambushes or close-quarters combat. The blade is intentionally broad and sturdy enough for reliable printing while retaining a realistic profile. Unlike many fantasy birdfolk, the Kenku possesses no functional wings. Instead, its body is covered in layered black feathers that transition naturally into feathered arms and a short fan-shaped tail. The feathers are sculpted in overlapping layers that produce excellent depth when painted while remaining thick enough for clean printing. The tail extends naturally behind the miniature, providing visual balance without creating unsupported elements. Its clothing reflects the practical lifestyle of an experienced infiltrator. A hooded travel cloak drapes across the shoulders before falling behind the body in thick layered folds. Beneath the cloak, multiple leather straps cross the torso to secure pouches, satchels, and equipment. A weathered belt carries additional supplies including small utility bags, bottles, and tools appropriate for scouting or lockpicking. Layered cloth panels protect the hips while maintaining complete freedom of movement. The wrapped forearms and lower legs reinforce the impression of an adventurer accustomed to dangerous environments. The scenic base follows the uploaded reference closely. Uneven cobblestones form the primary terrain while a sturdy wooden crate elevates one foot, creating vertical variation without distracting from the figure itself. Beside the crate lie a small sack, a discarded cup, and scattered debris, suggesting a back alley, marketplace, or smuggler's hideout. These scenic details remain fully integrated into the base and are designed for straightforward printing. The recommended paint scheme matches the reference miniature. Feathers should be painted deep charcoal black with subtle blue-grey highlights applied through careful drybrushing to reveal individual feather layers. The beak and talons use satin black highlighted with cool greys. Leather equipment ranges from warm browns to dark chestnut with lighter edge highlights, while the cloak combines muted olive, brown, and weathered grey fabrics. Metallic buckles and the dagger receive aged steel finishes with selective silver highlights. The amber eyes provide a bright focal point that immediately draws attention to the miniature's expressive face. Every shadow hides opportunity. Every voice can become its own. The silent watcher has already memorized your final words. ✨ Key Features Faithful Kenku based on the Monster Manual 2024 . Closely matches the uploaded reference miniature. Dynamic stealth pose with one foot resting on a wooden crate. Distinctive raven-like head with layered feather detail. Reverse-grip dagger ready for ambushes. Practical adventuring gear including belts, pouches, bottles, and satchels. Fully feathered body without functional wings, true to the classic Kenku appearance. Scenic cobblestone base with integrated crate and urban clutter. Strong silhouette designed for tabletop visibility. No floating parts, magical effects, smoke, or unsupported scenery. Optimized for resin printing and suitable for carefully tuned FDM printers. 🎨 Great for Painting Prime the miniature black before building the feathers using successive layers of charcoal, dark blue-grey, and subtle light grey drybrushing across the raised feather texture. Paint the beak and talons in satin black with cool grey edge highlights to create natural contrast. The cloak works well in muted olive-brown or weathered grey, shaded with dark brown washes before lighter edge highlights. description: The Court of the Vampire Queen Illya'Dra, Former Matron of House 'Dra All models in this series are set in a .2mm Nozzle Profile. These are long prints . To ensure success: Clean the build plate before you start the print. A clean build plate is essential before starting a long print. Nothing worse than a support coming off the plate ¾ of the way through. The supports are designed to be thin and easy to remove. With that stated, some of the points of connection are on or around small details. They will come away cleanly, just go slow and use the proper tool. Flusher Cutter, Razor, etc. The models are designed and positioned for success, so be patient when removing the supports particularly around the Axe , the Sword , and the Cane . If you have not tried my print profile, just use it. It is a high detail, slowed, increased wall and thinned out support profile designed to work well with these models. I post many .4mm profiles models on makerworld as people tend to like the speed over the detail but for home use I print every model in this .2mm profile. For an example see the .2mm Profile Beholder in my models. It takes longer, but it is worth it. The Beholder shown here is cleaned up and thats it. No primer and no paint. For the Vampire with the sword, there is a point on the base with a very tiny hole that the tip of the sword will slip into. If you do not line it up with the hole in the base, the sword point will actually be a fraction of a mm longer than his legs and make it challenging to glue him to the base. For the most part the bases are interchangable, but slightly different per model. If you see one you like more than the rest, resize it to the correct size and print it again. The bases are quick and use very little filament. So use what you like. The Queen is a much larger size model. I did this because I like it. That doesn't mean you need to love it. Resize any or all of these to fit your needs. They are scaled to work with a 32mm TTRPG of your choice, with the Queen being much large and daunting. The others hover right near there, give or take a few mm. if you run into any issues printing these, let me know! I have printed each of them two times. Once for my personal use and once as a followup test print. That doesn't mean all machines and filament are the same. I printed these using Sunlu HS PLA+ 2.0, which is currently a bit of a meta filament in the FDM miniature community as it prints with clean, high detail and cleans up easily. I have also taken the steps to calibrate that filament on my machine. If you find issues during your print, leave a comment and I wil see what I can do to address the comments and help. Aside from some stringing my filament is very dialed in. The stringing i have intentionally left in the pictures so that you can see what it looks like before being cleaned up and primed or painted or whatever else people do to these things to make them seem impossibly clean. These are thinner models with higher level, smaller details. IMO that leads to higher stringing when using a .2 on HS filament even when dried, dialed in retraction and calibrated. So my pictures of the printed models can and will look better after clean up and paint. I have a terrain build that I created spefically to with this Vampire Encounter, my first larger terrain piece. Here is what it looks like but I still on the fence about releasing it. It takes about 1kg of filament to print the entire thing, it has verticality to it as it is supposed to be a fallen temple that has begun to sink into an ever expanding swamp lands. Many might not like the verticality of it as it gently slopes. I have a couryard and a few other areas that would fill an entire table. But they are unique pieces that probably don't see much play, take a ton of filament even on 4% infill, and take up a great deal of space when not in use. I don't know that I want to go down this road. I will let people see it though to help me decide if it's worth releasing or not. I have several projects like this I created over the last couple years that are original and specific to the story I was running at the time. I just don't know how well they fit into anyone elses worlds. Anyway, happy printing all! ***UPDATE NOTE*** I will be adding some .4mm nozzle profiles for the model that I can. If they are just going to fail on people at .4 I won't put the profile up. There are some thin points that will prove challenging in .4
