A collection of seven compact magnetic sliders, each with its own texture and sensory intensity. I created this set in part for the @Pipin.World BONBON Capsules Design Contest . The variety of textures makes each one a fun little surprise to discover from a gachapon capsule, and printing the full set lets you find the one that suits you best! Seven Textures Classic : Smooth and simple, with only the embossed icon on the slider. Spiky : The most intense option, with pronounced points that are especially satisfying to press and run your fingers across. Geometric : Similar to Spiky, but less intense and more rounded, with a structured repeating pattern that still provides plenty of tactile variation. Industrial : A subtle diamond plate texture with a gentler sensory effect. Knitted : A detailed woven pattern with a comfortable medium level of texture. Dots : A playful medium-intensity texture that's surprisingly nice to rub along the sides. This one is my personal favorite. Fuzzy Skin : A soft, understated texture for anyone who prefers something more subtle. The set is designed to cover a wide range of preferences. Spiky sits at the most intense end, Geometric offers a similar experience in a more rounded form, Dots and Knitted land around the middle, and Industrial and Fuzzy Skin offer a more subtle touch. Classic is there for anyone who prefers a smooth surface. Magnetic Snap Each slider uses four 6x3mm magnets. Three are placed inside the base, while one is enclosed inside the moving piece. The center magnet repels the moving magnet, helping the slider snap toward either end with a satisfying magnetic response. Printing and Assembly Each slider requires: 4 x 6x3mm magnets Superglue Follow the included diagram and these steps carefully to make sure the magnets have the correct polarity: Prepare the magnets. Hold the four magnets as a stack and mark the exposed top face of the first magnet. Separate them without flipping. Slide the marked magnet sideways off the stack. Mark the newly exposed top face, then slide that magnet off the same way. Repeat until all four magnets have been separated. All four marked faces now have the same polarity. Insert the slider magnet at the first pause. Add a small drop of superglue to the magnet hole in the slider, then insert one magnet with the marked face pointing up. The slider prints face-down, so the unmarked face will point toward the build plate. Insert the outer base magnets at the second pause. Add a small drop of superglue to each outer magnet hole, then insert both magnets with their marked faces pointing up. Insert the center base magnet. Add a small drop of superglue to the center hole, then insert the remaining magnet with its marked face pointing down. This opposite orientation makes the center magnet repel the slider while the two outer magnets attract it. Let the glue hold the magnets in place. Make sure every magnet is seated fully inside its hole before continuing the print. Keep an eye on them for the first few layers after the pause, since the nozzle can pull up a magnet that isn't secured properly. Check the slider orientation before assembly. The slider must be vertical when you snap it into the rails. The top is square, so use the shape on the bottom to confirm its direction. Don't try to insert it sideways, rotated 90 degrees from the correct position. Snap the slider into the rails. Press it in carefully while keeping it straight. If it doesn't go in with reasonable pressure, stop and check its orientation instead of forcing it, as this may damage the rails. Troubleshooting Depending on the filament, the rails where the slider snaps into place may deform slightly during assembly. I've found this is more likely with softer materials, including certain spools of matte PLA. If the slider doesn't travel all the way to either end, a section of the rail probably bent inward while the slider was being pressed into place. Carefully inspect the full path and either trim the deformed plastic or gently straighten it by prying it back into position with a craft knife. Remove or adjust only as much material as necessary. The slider may also feel stiff at first even when nothing is visibly blocking it. Once you've confirmed that it can travel fully to both ends, slide it back and forth several times. This will usually straighten out minor deformation and make the movement smoother. For an even smoother feel, you can brush a small amount of lubricant onto the rail surfaces. Only do this after the slider already travels freely to both ends without lubricant. Print one texture or collect all seven and discover your favorite!

Vocabulary Tile: A grid square Tile (as part of a ship): Area above a tile on a ship, marked by a hole on the top for the hitmarker Hitmarker: Small piece used to show tiles already hit on a ship by being put in the hole on top Objective: Fully damage all the enemy ships to win. Ships Patrol Boat A fast but lightly armored and small boat. Stats: Speed: Can move up to 3 tiles at a time Range: Can hit within one tile of gun Special: Can shoot and move within the same turn Destroyer Versatile medium sized ship. Stats: Movement: can move up to 2 tiles at a time Range: within 2 tiles of gun Battleship Large, heavy, slow and powerful floating fortress Stats: Speed: 1 tile per turn Range: 2 tiles from anywhere on ship Special: More Guns! Can shoot from anywhere on ship (more range) Aircraft Carrier Ship with planes Stats: Speed: up to 2 tiles per turn Range: 3 tiles from takeoff area Refuel: Cooldown of 1 turn between shots Start of game Place ships in any position on your half of the board. The first move can be determined by anything. Turns Shooting: Each turn, you can only shoot once from one ship, 2 ships cannot shoot on the same turn. You cannot shoot a tile on a ship twice. Movement: Each turn, you can either move forward or back or turn a ship. You cannot shoot and move on the same turn unless it is the patrol boat. You cannot move into a tile with a ship on it or out of bounds. You do not have to move or shoot from a ship. You can move up to 2 ships per turn. Wide Turning: If in a position where turning will put your ship outside of game, or if you want any ship can do this instead of normal turning: Damaged Ships: Tiles that have been hit are marked by the hitmarkers. If the only tiles in range are already hit, you cannot hit that ship. When a ship has all tiles hit, take that ship off of the board, it is sunk. Other Larger boards: Because this game is played on a open board and not on tiles, it is much more suitable for expansion with larger boards, which could introduce more teams, such as other models in this contest. Rule Changes: Make up your own new rules, like using dice to add a luck aspect or something else! Potential Rule changes: Gameplay modifiers you can choose. Simplified Turning: Only use wide turning for simplified gameplay. Missing: Whenever you shoot, use a dice and if it doesn't roll above a 3 you miss your shot. Traverse Thrust: Instead of turning, a ship can move to the side 1 tile while facing the same direction, which would make the game even more complicated.(I don't know it sounds cool that some ships can do that) Made with items from core playgrid parts.

⚠️ Important Printing Requirements This model features extremely tight tolerances designed to push standard FDM printing to its absolute limit. Before printing, please ensure: Dry Filament: Moisture will cause stringing and micro-blobs that can fuse the internal segments together. Calibrated Flow Rate: Make sure your extrusions are dialed in. Over-extrusion will weld the pieces solid. Clean Print Bed: Wash your build plate with warm water and dish soap to remove oils and ensure solid bed adhesion without shifting during intricate base layers. Overview Most print-in-place fidget balls require a significantly larger outer diameter to accommodate high segment counts. By re-engineering the custom cutting tool from the ground up, I optimized the geometry so you can fit up to 20 interlocking segments inside a compact 40mm ball using a standard 0.4mm nozzle. The result is a pocket-sized, incredibly satisfying tactile fidget toy with smooth rotation and flexibility. Customizer Support Prefer fewer segments or wider tolerances? I’ve made this design customizable! You can select anywhere from 10 to 20 segments to match your preference or printer's tuning level: 10–14 Segments: Easier print tolerances, faster print time, and bold, chunky mechanics. 15–19 Segments: A great middle ground for fine detail and high flexibility. 20 Segments: The ultimate challenge—maximum segment density packed into a 40mm sphere. Key Features Customizable Density: Choose between 10 and 20 interlocking segments in the customizer. Pocket-Sized: Compact 40mm design that fits comfortably in your hand. Re-Engineered Geometry: Built with a custom ground-up cutting tool to maximize clearance, wall strength, and FDM printability. Print-in-Place: No assembly required—just print, gently flex to break initial micro-bonds, and twist. description: Bring a little retro gaming nostalgia to your desk with this six-sided Question Block Clicker Cube. Every face uses a standard Cherry MX style mechanical keyboard switch, giving you six clicky sides in a compact desk toy. This is about as small as six full-size MX switches can realistically be packed together while still remaining comfortable to use. Features Six fully clickable faces Uses six Cherry MX compatible switches No glue required (optional if faces loosen over time) Compact desk toy that's great for fidgeting or stress relief Test printed on the Bambu H2C, H2S, and Snapmaker U1 Recommended switches I used these switches from amazon, but any similar one will work (affiliate links): Kailh Box Jade: https://amzn.to/4pKPuNv Kailh Box Navy: https://amzn.to/4bm78kU Printing Supports are required. I've included two print profiles: PETG Support Interface (Recommended) Best surface finish Extremely clean overhangs Minimal additional print time on dual-nozzle printers On a single-nozzle printer I saw roughly a 20% increase in print time and about 12g of additional purge, which I think is well worth the improvement. Standard PLA Supports Simpler if you're printing with a single material Still produces great results The supported overhangs are hidden beneath the faceplates after assembly, but the PETG interface is far superior in my testing. Assembly Assembly is easiest if you install each switch into its faceplate first, then insert the faceplate and switch together into the cube. The Cherry MX switches only fit in one orientation in the body, so make sure each faceplate is rotated the way you want before snapping it into the body. If your faceplate is sticking out from the body significantly, rotate the switch and reinstall . The design is intended to snap together without glue. Description This project started after the original water tank broke when the water gun fell to the floor. Instead of simply recreating the damaged part, I redesigned the entire reservoir to solve another problem the original product already had: it was awkward to store, unstable when laid down, and could leak while not in use. The new tank works both as a replacement for a broken original reservoir and as a practical upgrade for an intact water gun . Its angular shape forms a stable integrated stand, keeping the toy upright, easy to see and comfortable to grab whenever it is needed. There is no separate holder or additional base—the water reservoir itself performs both functions. Despite the completely different shape, the redesigned tank holds approximately the same amount of water as the original. The wider lower section provides a stable footprint while preserving the grip angle and normal handling of the water gun. Once installed, the toy remains balanced and ready to use without needing to be placed on its side. The tank was designed and tested in PETG for better impact resistance, sealing and long-term durability. The provided print profile uses reinforced walls and a slightly increased object flow ratio to improve strength and sealing. The finished reservoir was tested filled with water to verify the connection and watertight performance. A transparent PETG version also makes it easy to see the remaining water level, while opaque colors can create a more tactical or customized appearance. Because similar water guns may be sold under different names or with small manufacturing variations, a fast Fit Test is included. Print this small part first to confirm that the mounting interface fits your toy before spending time and material on the complete tank. A STEP file of the tested connection interface is also provided for makers who want to design their own custom reservoir, larger tank or compatible accessory. This 3D printable water gun tank is designed for outdoor toys, garden play, summer activities and practical toy repair. It combines a replacement water reservoir, upright storage stand and functional upgrade in a single printable part, giving a damaged or inconvenient water pistol a stronger and more useful second life.

model_name: BambuPlot Free Pen Plotter G-code Generator
description: Turn your Bambu Lab 3D printer into a pen plotter completely free, no subscriptions, no accounts, no uploads. Everything runs locally in your browser. The included test file uses the boat drawing shown in the preview image a detailed line-art illustration that works great as a first plot to verify your setup. When using the tool please consider using the included print profile test model. This helps me out and helps supporting this project with since i could not upload the Bambuplot file directly on Makerworld. ⚠ Read this first this is a tinkerer's project This tool is made for people who enjoy experimenting, troubleshooting, and figuring things out. It is not a plug-and-play product. It will probably not work perfectly on the first try , and that is completely normal. Getting a pen plotter working on a 3D printer requires patience: dialing in the Z height, finding the right pen, getting the paper flat, tuning the feed rates, and sometimes just accepting that the first few attempts are learning runs. I do not cover any damages to your printer, pen holder, bed, or any other part of your setup. Using this tool is entirely at your own risk. Sending custom G-code to a 3D printer always carries a risk of unexpected movement, crashes, or damage if settings are wrong. Always supervise the printer, always do a dry run first with the Z height raised so the pen cannot touch anything, and never leave it running unattended especially not on a first test. If you are not comfortable with that, this project is probably not for you yet but if you enjoy the process of making something work from scratch, welcome aboard. What is BambuPlot? BambuPlot is a single HTML file you download and open in your browser. It lets you design drawings and convert them into G-code that your Bambu Lab printer can execute with a pen instead of a nozzle. No internet connection is required after download — it runs 100% on your computer. Supported printers all current Bambu Lab models: Printer Bed size Notes A1 mini 180 × 180 mm A1 256 × 256 mm ✅ Tested P1P 256 × 256 mm P1S 256 × 256 mm P2S 256 × 256 mm X1 carbon 256 × 256 mm X2D 256 × 256 mm ✅ Tested A2L 330 × 320 mm H2D 325 × 320 mm H2S 340 × 320 mm A custom bed size option is also available for any other setup. What you can draw: Text three modes: single-stroke plotter font (looks like real handwriting), your own custom handwriting (draw each letter yourself, up to 5 versions per letter for variety so repeating letters never look identical), or filled outline using any of 13 fonts Shapes square, circle, triangle, star, line, with optional hatch fill Freehand draw directly on the bed preview with your mouse or stylus Images drop any photo or logo, adjust the threshold and line density, and convert it to plotted lines 3MF import drop a Bambu Lab .3mf file and BambuPlot extracts the 3D geometry and renders the top-down footprint as plottable paths, in either vector outline or hatch-fill mode What you need A Bambu Lab printer or anything else that takes gcode A pen holder that mounts on your toolhead (search MakerWorld or Printables for your specific model many different designs exist.) (I used this one: https://makerworld.com/models/2886015?appSharePlatform=copy ) A ballpoint pen that fits your holder Paper to draw on, attached to the bed (see bed preparation below) A way to get pure gcode on your printer (USB stick/microsd) Bed preparation protecting your print surface This is important. The pen tip will press directly down onto whatever is on your bed. Printing on bare paper placed directly on a softer printing bed can cause damage, especially with a stiff pen or too much Z pressure. My recommendation: place an old flat PEI sheet (Like mine from my old ender 3 v2), a thin sheet of plastic such as a folder cover or binder sheet, or any similarly flat, smooth piece of thin plastic underneath the paper. This gives the paper a firm, even surface to rest on and takes any wear from the pen instead of your actual print bed. An old or scratched PEI sheet you no longer use for printing is perfect for this. Attaching the paper: I use small magnets placed along the edges to hold the paper flat and in position they are quick to place, leave no residue, and hold very reliably. Other options that work fine include masking tape or binder clips on the edges. Whatever you use, make sure the paper is completely flat with no bubbles or lifted corners, as any unevenness will cause the pen pressure to vary across the drawing. How to download and open BambuPlot Go to : https://joep648.github.io/BambuPlot/bambuplot-v1.0.1.html to use it online. or Download the bambuplot.html file from: https://github.com/Joep648/BambuPlot/tree/main Open it with any modern browser (Firefox recommended for best performance Chrome and Edge work fine too, but Firefox handles large designs more smoothly) That is it no installation, no internet needed after that Step-by-step: from design to plot Step 1 Select your printer In the top bar, choose your printer model from the dropdown. The bed preview updates to the correct size. This ensures your G-code coordinates match your actual print surface. Step 2 Add content to the bed Use the tabs on the left panel: Text tab type your text, choose a style (single-stroke is best for plotting), adjust letter spacing and line spacing, then click Add text to bed Shapes tab pick a shape and click Add shape to bed . Enable Filled to get hatch-fill lines inside the shape Image tab click the drop zone or drag an image in. Adjust the threshold slider until the preview looks like clean black lines on white, then click Convert & add to bed . High-contrast line art like the included boat image gives the best results 3MF tab drag a .3mf file onto the drop zone. Choose Vector outline for a clean single-stroke contour of the model, or Top-down silhouette for a hatch-filled footprint Freehand in the Shapes tab, click Draw directly on bed and sketch with your mouse Step 3 Position and size your content Once an item appears on the bed preview: Drag the body of the item to move it Drag a corner handle to scale it the line density automatically recalculates to stay consistent at the new size Drag the white circle above the item to rotate it Use the Layers tab to show/hide, duplicate, or delete items Step 4 Configure pen settings Go to the Pen tab and set: Setting What it does Suggested starting value Z draw How far down the pen tip presses 0.5 mm Z lift How high the pen lifts between strokes 8 mm Draw feed Speed while drawing 1500 mm/min Travel feed Speed while moving between strokes 6000 mm/min Z move feed Speed of Z moves 600 mm/min Pen settle time Dwell after each Z move to prevent stray marks 120 ms These values are starting points every pen holder and pen combination is different. Adjust Z draw until the pen just barely touches the paper with light pressure. Step 5 Generate and download the G-code Click Generate G-code in the right panel. The code appears in the preview (large designs only show the first few thousand lines the full file is always in the download). Click the ⭳ button to download the .gcode file. Step 6 Send to the printer and plot My personal workflow: Home the printer manually via the touchscreen or Bambu Studio After homing, clip the pen holder onto the toolhead with the pen inserted Place your protective plastic sheet on the bed, lay the paper on top, and secure it with magnets, tape, or clips Start the file with in bambuplot Home all axes (G28) at start option turned off Always do a dry run first: temporarily raise the Z draw value by 5–10 mm so the pen stays off the paper, and watch the full motion to confirm the design lands in the right place before doing a real plot Alternative workflow using the dwell option: The Dwell after homing checkbox in the Pen tab inserts a G4 S30 command (a timed pause) after the G28 home command, giving you time to clip the pen on before plotting starts. This feature is experimental and untested I have not personally used it this way. Bambu printers do not support the standard M0 unconditional pause command, so a timed dwell is used as a workaround. If you try it, set the duration long enough to comfortably attach the pen holder (60 seconds or more). Tips for best results Use the right paper smooth, slightly heavier paper works best. Thin paper can wrinkle from pen pressure Ballpoint pens are the most reliable. Felt-tips can bleed on paper and dry out if the pen sits in one spot for too long Start with a short test plot a small shape first to calibrate your Z height before committing to a full design Line density matters lower density (higher number on the slider) = fewer lines = faster plot and less ink bleed. Higher density looks more solid but takes much longer to plot The settle time setting (default 120 ms) adds a brief pause after every pen up/down move. This is the main fix for random stray lines on the paper if you see faint marks between strokes, increase it to 150–250 ms Mirror X or Y if your plot comes out flipped Saving your settings In the Pen tab, click Save profile + handwriting to file to save all your pen settings, printer choice, and your custom drawn handwriting alphabet to a single .json file. Load it again any time even on a different device with the load button. Questions, problems, and ideas for future versions If something does not work, you have a question about the setup, or you just want to share your results feel free to leave a comment on this MakerWorld page or send me a message directly through MakerWorld. I am happy to help where I can, though keep in mind this is a hobby project and responses may not always be instant. If you have ideas for features you would like to see in a future version, I would love to hear them. BambuPlot is actively being worked on and new features get added regularly. Things on the radar include better SVG import, more letter styles, and improved multi-layer support. If there is something specific you need for your use case, suggest it in the comments the best ideas from the community are what shape where this goes next. BambuPlot is a fan-made tool and is not affiliated with Bambu Lab. Pen holder designs are not included search MakerWorld or Printables for a mount that fits your specific printer model. Always run a dry pass before plotting on good paper. Use at your own risk.

UPDATED DESIGN - 7/15/2026 Any comments before 7/15/26 are regarding the original version, not the updated version. The original version is no longer available for download. If you are using the old version, the parts will not fit on the old version tumbler. You will need to download the updated version and print. Updates made: Shorter lid. This was updated to speed up print time and to help prevent the lid from getting stuck. This is a friction fit design. The lid should not be loose. I usually twist and pull the lid off. Shorter, thicker drip. This update makes the drip much easier to print at normal speeds and stronger. If you are having issues with any drips snapping when trying to lift them up and glue on the tumbler, please increase wall loops. I do not personally have this issue, but I helped someone who did have this issue and adding wall loops helped. Handle pushes further in and does not require glue. The old version had a shallow hole for the handle and it required glue. Larger tolerance gap for 12oz standard cans and 12oz slim cans. Although the old design worked, the tolerance gap did not allow much room for shrinkage from different filaments, especially matte pla. This updated version also fits 12oz slim Alani cans much better than the original version. Printing Notes: The drip (separate parts print) is not meant to come on and off of the tumbler. It is meant to be glued on. I do not personally glue the top part. I lift up the drips (that are able to be lifted) and glue those in place. I have no issues with the drip staying in place when I do this. The handle is a tight fit, but it does go in. If your filament is too wetor not properly calibrated, you will have to trim the edge of the handle to help it go in easier. I had this issue with a brand new filament, dried it, and had no issues after. If you choose to glue the handle, I highly recommned test fitting the handle before gluing it. Once the handle goes in the first time, it is much easier to get in the second time. The lid is a friction fit. Just like the handle, if your filamement is not dried or calibrated properly, you may have to trim the ring on the lid to help it fit better. There are 2 handle options and 2 lid options. The 2nd options have a larger tolerance gap if you are having trouble with the standard option being too tight. If you cannot get the lid on or the handle in, you need to calibrate your filament and research the best settings for your printer. This design has been extensively tested and it works properly. The lid is a friction fit, but the ring is short enough to prevent it from getting stuck inside the tumbler. Minimal supports needed. I do not recommend supports on the handle. It has only made a mess for me. Support critical regions only for the lid. There is a tight gap on the inside of the lid and supports inside are not necessary and will only make removal difficult. This has been tested with PLA. I use Bambu Lab Basic filament for this design. This has not been tested with PETG. Matte filament can make the fit tighter. You can change the color of the cup if you do not want to print it with the stripes.

description: Always there when you need it. Never in the way when you don't. Like other filament clip giants before me, I decided to throw my hat into the ring. Meet The Wingman . Every spool deserves one. The Wingman securely parks your filament when it's not in use, then quietly stays out of the way while you print. No snags. No rubbing. No surprises. Just a simple clip that's there when you need it and invisible when you don't. (On a side note, if you need something to cut PTFE tubes that's precise, safe, and seriously satisfying, you won't want to miss out on my Bowden Puck Pro !) Why Yet Another Filament Clip? Because I kept trying the "good" ones and finding little things that annoyed me. Some snagged filament. Some didn't stay attached very well. Some required threading way more filament than seemed necessary. Some were so aggressively optimized to save filament that they forgot they actually needed to print successfully. None of these were deal breakers, but together they convinced me to make my own. So I did. Why The Wingman? Curves in all the right places Some clips have sharp edges, straight walls, or little ridges that can catch filament as it moves around the spool. The Wingman was designed with smooth, rounded surfaces wherever filament might encounter it, because nobody wants a multi-hour print to fail because of a 1-cent piece of plastic. Secure enough to forget about Some clips rely on a single spool hole. Others barely fit. The Wingman uses two mounting points and confidently snaps into place with a satisfying click, staying exactly where you put it. Quick filament parking Some clips are designed to capture a long length of filament before they're satisfied. Why? The Wingman only needs a very short section of filament for a secure hold, making loading and unloading quick and painless. Optimized for actual printing Some designs appear to be competing in a least amount of filament contest. Unfortunately, saving 0.05 grams doesn't help much if the part fails halfway through printing. The Wingman was designed to print reliably first. Once that was achieved, material was trimmed away until only what was needed remained. Features Works with the AMS Lite (with or without top mount), AMS HT, AMS, and AMS 2 Pro Secure dual-pin design snaps firmly into place No pliers, tools, or colorful language required Designed to remain attached during printing and drying Specifically optimized for Bambu spools Gently angled filament path for a secure hold and easy insertion Integrated guide line helps with filament insertion while adding a subtle finishing touch Only 0.56g per clip Important Notes Bambu Studio may report open edges. This warning can safely be ignored and does not affect printing or functionality. Print with a filament intended for functional parts. PLA Matte and other brittle materials may not survive repeated use. To remove a clip, simply push the pegs back through the spool holes using any small object. Depending on filament shrinkage, the filament opening may initially fit tightly. If needed, run a short piece of filament through the opening a few times before use. This is most noticeable with abrasive filaments such as PLA Glow. If using a filament dryer, print The Wingman using a material capable of handling the temperatures you intend to use. Instructions Print as many Wingmen as your spools deserve, keeping the supplied orientation unchanged for best results. Align the pegs with the spool holes and push until they snap securely into place. Feel strangely satisfied. Let the guide line do the aiming, then push the filament into place. Consider adding a second Wingman to the same spool. Future You will appreciate it. The best Wingman knows when to stay out of the way. *** Update! *** I updated this models page to include a new wider dumpster (upon request) and a specific Chute size for A1 & A1 Mini and the new A2L printers. There is a height difference this made the Chute a little longer for the A2L and slightly shorter for the A1 & A1 Mini. I made a wider dumpster so if you chose to use the original longer Chute (which looks more realistic IMO) it will not hit the walls of the dumpster. The wider dumpster is bigger too so you can hold more poo. Or you can use it to store stuff. What ever your desire. I am trying to please the masses :-) https://makerworld.com/en/models/3073625-poo-chute-dumpster-for-all-a-series So funny story. I love printing things. Therefore I have a lot of plastic waste from poop to supports etc…. A while ago my husband says “your going to need a dumpster for all that plastic”. Then my neighbor noticed the several bags of plastic “poop” I have and said the exact thing. And only when my nephew comes over and says the same thing once again I thought to myself, I need to make a little dumpster to catch all the poop my printer makes. I pictured the Home Alone 2 movie where the house Kevin rigs up has a chute outside the window going into a dumpster. So that's where the idea for project came from. There are tons of “poop” bins and baskets for the other printers but I wanted to make one for my new Bambu Lab A2L printer. She's a beast. Very detailed and prints well. I love it. It does shake the house though being a large sized bed slinger. I have been printing on silent mode to calm it down in most cases. This took me a week to create. A little longer than usual but I needed to get the tolerances perfecta. My main goal was to make it easy and reliable to print. That was the challenge. I tried several ways to get the chute to print as one piece but it never worked out. So clip or bracket that connects to the printer is separate and has to be glued to the chute. I did make a connection socket so the two fit together perfectly so all is needed is a drop of cyanoacrylate glue (Super Glue) or something similar on each edge of the connection opening and hold it in place for the appropriate time (depending on your glue). I have printed 19 sets of the chute and bracket and glued them together successfully with no problem. Supports were absolutely necessary to accomplish my goal. I tried to keep the settings simple but tweaked the settings like the top and bottom Z distance, speed etc… to get dumpster and chute to come out clean. Just be sure to keep my settings. You can add to them if you please but it wont be necessary as you can tell by my photos. I have had several people that don't have a printer me to print them one just because they wanted the cute little bin. I have even been changing the sizes per their requests. The dumpster itself is scalable and you can make a smaller or larger one depending on your needs. I am sure it will have many uses. This is the A2L model version. I created this first due to the need for a way to control the filament purge waste or “Poop” . Upon request I made a clip portion that fits the A1 and A1 Mini printers. All the A1 series Poop Chute parts are now on the same page. You can find them here: https://makerworld.com/en/models/3073625-poo-chute-dumpster-for-all-a-series Thank you ahead of time and please enjoy. Have a nice day.

model_name: True Spring Filament Clip ⧸ Tangle Free Storage
description: A filament clip that solves the three most common problems of traditional filament clips. Plastic Fatigue Most filament clips rely on a printed flex geometry to generate clamping force. Repeated use and elevated drying temperatures gradually reduce the clamping force as the plastic permanently deforms. True Spring Solution The clamping force is generated by a real steel compression spring. The printed parts only guide the movement. No Plastic Fatigue. Constant tension. Filament Stress Many filament clips bend the filament sharply by securing it through spool holes or around the spool rim. Brittle materials may break after long term storage. True Spring Solution The filament is secured close to the spool core with a large bending radius, minimizing unnecessary stress while keeping the filament securely retained. Tangle Risk Some clips secure the filament directly to the wound filament. This can increase the risk of accidental tangles when the spool is handled carelessly. True Spring Solution The filament is retained independently of the wound filament. Nothing is attached to the filament winding itself. Hardware The clip uses two inexpensive compression springs. You can either use a compatible spring from the BOM or simply try the spring from an old ballpoint pen. Many common pen springs fit perfectly. No screws. No glue. No tools. Everything simply snaps together. Printer Tolerance Test Every printer and every filament behaves slightly differently. Since this model relies on precisely fitting moving parts, I strongly recommend printing the Printer Tolerance Test first. The test consists of one plunger and six labeled test sockets with clearances of 0.05 mm , 0.10 mm , 0.15 mm , 0.20 mm , 0.25 mm and 0.30 mm . The correct fit should move smoothly with minimal friction while having as little play as possible. Don't feel like running the calibration? Simply print Print Plate 1 (0.15 mm clearance) . It provides a good fit for most printers and materials. Temperature Testing Successfully tested after 24 hours of continuous filament drying: PETG - 45 °C ASA - 65 °C ASA - 80 °C PC - 85 °C For comparison, I tested a popular Flexi Filament Clip under identical print settings, using the same material and identical drying conditions. After 24 hours at the respective drying temperatures, the flex geometry had permanently deformed and the remaining clamping force was no longer sufficient for reliable reuse. If you have ever dried filament while using this type of clip, you probably know exactly what I mean. Recommended Materials PETG works perfectly for everyday use. For frequent filament drying or elevated temperatures I recommend ASA or PC . Assembly Printed parts and two compression springs. Insert the filament clamps. Insert the springs. Insert the Double Plunger and press firmly. Finished, enjoy.

model_name: Poo Chute & Dumpster For All A Series
description: *** Update *** Upon request, I have made it so you are now able to print this Poop Chute and Dumpster for the A1 and A1 Mini printers. I added a new Clip to the existing Chute. You now just need to select the correct plate that matches your printer and you on your way. I also added a wider version of the dumpster so it pushes out the dumpster walls so they do not hit the extruder head assembly. You can choose which ever you like best. If you pick the appropriate chute and clip the extruder should be clear. There is the original chute which is longer but I got a few comments stating that the chute will hit the dumpster, which it would if you placed the dumpster walls under the chute, I would suggest not to do this. It would be like placing your cup of coffee under the extruder assembly or print bar, you wouldn't do that right? So funny story. I love printing things. Therefore I have a lot of plastic waste from poop to supports etc…. A while ago my husband says “your going to need a dumpster for all that plastic”. Then my neighbor noticed the several bags of plastic “poop” I have and said the exact thing. And only when my nephew comes over and says the same thing once again I thought to myself, I need to make a little dumpster to catch all the poop my printer makes. I pictured the Home Alone 2 movie where the house Kevin rigs up has a chute outside the window going into a dumpster. So that's where the idea for project came from. There are tons of “poop” bins and baskets for the other printers but I wanted to make one for my new Bambu Lab A2L printer. She's a beast. Very detailed and prints well. I love it. It does shake the house though being a large sized bed slinger. I have been printing on silent mode to calm it down in most cases. This took me a week to create. A little longer than usual but I needed to get the tolerances perfect. My main goal was to make it reliable and easy to print. That was the challenge. I tried several ways to get the chute to print as one piece but it never worked out. So clip or bracket that connects to the printer is separate and has to be glued to the chute. I did make a connection socket so the two fit together perfectly so all is needed is a drop of cyanoacrylate glue (Super Glue) or something similar on each edge of the connection opening and hold it in place for the appropriate time (depending on your glue). I have printed 19 sets of the chute and bracket and glued them together successfully with no problem. Supports were absolutely necessary to accomplish my goal. I tried to keep the settings simple but tweaked the settings like the top and bottom Z distance, speed etc… to get dumpster and chute to come out clean. Just be sure to keep my settings. You can add to them if you please but it wont be necessary as you can tell by my photos. I have had several people that don't have a printer me to print them one just because they wanted the cute little bin. I have even been changing the sizes per their requests. The dumpster itself is scalable and you can make a smaller or larger one depending on your needs. I am sure it will have many uses. Thank you ahead of time and please enjoy. Have a nice day.

description: Successful detection. Every time. No compromises. This model is part of my ongoing BIQU Build Plate Accessories collection. Each model is conceived, printed, and endurance-tested on my own machines, refined through dozens of iterations to match the printer’s true mechanical behavior. Precision isn't assumed here, it’s verified layer by layer. Explore the full collection: BIQU Build Plate Accessories Follow me if you like my work, that kind of appreciation really dries my filament. Likes and boosts feed the Maker World algorithm and keep the new models coming v2 (Dev) Notes During my testing with the newer BIQU FrostBite build plates without the honeycomb handle, I made some interesting observations about the X2D's ArUco detection. The marker was reliably detected between 5 mm and 14 mm in size. Positioning along the Y axis had virtually no influence, as long as the marker remained between the printer door and the printable area. Along the X axis, the center of the marker could be placed anywhere between approximately 35 mm and 135 mm from the left edge of the build plate. These findings differ from my early experiments when the X2D was first released. Back then, the marker seemed to require very precise positioning. Based on my current testing, the detection system appears to be significantly more tolerant than it used to be. Testing on the Glacier plates with the honeycomb handle revealed something different. The honeycomb pattern can interfere with reliable detection, especially when using smaller markers. Based on these findings, I redesigned the marker for v2 (dev). Inspired by the “Cyberdeck” concept, this is a “lapdock” that turns a Modern Samsung phone into a portable laptop using the Samsung DeX mode. description: One print. Twelve failure checks. Every card tells you what to inspect, what the answer means, and the three settings to change next. Now fits the A1 mini. Most calibration prints tell you that something is wrong. Print Doctor tells you what it means and what to do next — the diagnosis is printed right on the part, so you never have to go looking it up. What's new in v2 It fits your printer now. v1 was 204 × 180 mm, which meant A1 mini owners could not print it at all. v2 ships in three layouts: one full 239 × 179 mm sheet for 256 × 256 plates, plus Sheet A and Sheet B at 139 × 158 mm each, which fit a 180 × 180 plate with room to spare. Twelve tests, not ten. Three new cards: Overhang angle — four fins leaning at a labelled 30°, 45°, 55° and 65° off vertical. Find the first one whose underside breaks up: that is your printer's real overhang limit, and the number you should put in your support threshold. Clearance & fit — three print-in-place rings around capped posts at 0.15, 0.25 and 0.35 mm radial clearance. Try to spin each one. The tightest ring that still turns is the clearance you can trust in your own designs. Dimensions — a 18.00 mm square tube and a Ø14.00 mm round tube, both with a two-line wall. Measure the outside, the inside and the wall thickness with calipers to separate a flow error from an XY-compensation error. It adapts to your nozzle. Every gap, rib, wall and slot is derived from your nozzle diameter, so the tests still discriminate on a 0.6 mm or 0.2 mm nozzle instead of being tuned only for 0.4 mm. Better as a keepsake. Every card carries its number and a 4.5 mm hole, so once you snap the sheet apart the twelve cards go straight onto a binder ring and live next to the printer as a flip-through reference deck. The breakaway tabs are thinner than v1's and snap cleanly instead of tearing. Sharper geometry. The Z-seam cup is now genuinely round. In v1 it was a 48-sided polygon, and those facet lines could be mistaken for the seam artifacts the card is supposed to reveal. The cat-shaped Print Doctor nameplate, the mushroom cooling test and the elephant-foot paw all survive the rebuild. The twelve tests # Card What you do What it tells you 01 Under-extrusion Look for gaps in the single-line frame and three ribs Flow, clog, or temperature too low 02 Over-extrusion Find the smallest labelled slot still open How much excess flow is closing your gaps 03 Pressure advance Look at the ten hard corners Bulging after turns, thinning before them 04 Stringing Count the strands between four spires Retraction, temperature, wet filament 05 Weak bridging Feel the underside of the 10, 18 and 26 mm spans Longest span your cooling can hold 06 Overhang angle Find the first fin that breaks up Your real overhang limit in degrees 07 Poor cooling Look at the droop on three mushroom caps Whether the layer below is setting in time 08 Z-seam quality Look down the seam line of a smooth cup Zits, gaps, inconsistent layer starts 09 Elephant foot Look at the base flare of the paw First-layer squish and Z offset 10 Layer adhesion Bend the 0.80, 1.20 and 1.60 mm blades Whether layers split or the plastic yields 11 Clearance & fit Spin the three rings The tightest clearance you can design to 12 Dimensions Measure with calipers Flow error vs XY-compensation error The paw on card 09 prints directly on the build plate through a window in the card, so the first layer is never hidden by a card floor underneath it. Which file do I print? Your printer Print this Bambu A1 / P1S / P1P / X1C, Prusa MK4, Ender 3 (220+) print_doctor_v2_full.stl — one sheet, all 12 cards Bambu A1 mini, or any 180 × 180 plate print_doctor_v2_mini_A_cards_1-6.stl then ..._mini_B_cards_7-12.stl How to use it Slice with the profile you actually want to diagnose — not a specially tuned calibration profile. The point is to test what you print with every day. Supports off . The unsupported features are the test. Brim off if you can. A brim hides elephant foot. Print flat, exactly as supplied. Work through the cards. Each raised LOOK / FEEL / COUNT / BEND / SPIN / MEASURE line tells you what to do with that specimen. Use the three printed adjustments as your shortlist. Change one setting at a time and reprint just the card you are chasing. Snap the sheet apart, put the twelve cards on a binder ring, keep them by the printer. The printed suggestions are starting points, not laws. Material condition, hardware wear, motion settings and slicer behaviour can all produce similar-looking symptoms. Recommended print settings Material: PLA for the first diagnostic print Nozzle: 0.4 mm (the model is parametric if you run something else) Layer height: 0.20 mm — this matters, the print-in-place rings on card 11 are designed around a 0.2 mm air gap Walls: 2 Infill: 15 % Supports: Off Brim: Off where possible Orientation: Flat, as supplied Model dimensions File Footprint Max height Full sheet 239.0 × 178.7 mm 21.4 mm Mini Sheet A 138.9 × 158.2 mm 21.4 mm Mini Sheet B 138.9 × 158.2 mm 19.2 mm One connected, manifold print in every case, with optional breakaway cards. The three rings on card 11 print loose by design — that is the test. Parametric The OpenSCAD source is included and is set up for the MakerWorld Parametric Model Maker. Adjustable: sheet layout, nozzle diameter, layer height, label style (raised or flush inlay), part split for multi-colour, breakaway tab thickness, and the binder-ring hole.

description: Purge Pipes - Modular Purge Chute System Purge Pipes is a modular, twist-lock pipe system designed to route purge waste exactly where you want it. Whether you're directing waste into a bin, around obstacles, or building a more complex routing system, Purge Pipes makes it easy to create a clean, customizable setup. Compatible with: Bambu Lab X1 Series Bambu Lab P1 Series Bambu Lab X2 Series Bambu Lab P2 Series Bambu Lab H2 Series Features Modular twist-lock connection system Secure, tool-free assembly Expandable with additional pipe sections and fittings Reverse-twist components available for easier installation Designed specifically for routing printer purge waste Print Material Recommendations Purge Pipes can be printed in PLA for most applications. However, if you frequently print with a heated chamber , or regularly print materials such as PETG, ABS, ASA, or other high-temperature filaments , printing Purge Pipes in PETG or ABS is recommended for improved heat resistance and long-term durability. Installation The purge chute mounts to the printer using two BT3×10 screws (preferred). These provide a secure attachment point for the entire Purge Pipes system. Reverse-Twist Parts Standard sections lock together with a simple twist. For installations that include a Y fitting , one branch should use a reverse-twist connector. Why? If both the purge chute and the Y fitting are already fixed in place, a standard connector cannot be rotated into both ends simultaneously. A reverse-twist section solves this by allowing the final connection to lock without needing either end to move. This makes assembly much easier and keeps the entire system fully modular. Build Your Own System Mix and match straight sections, elbows, Y fittings, reverse-twist sections, and future accessories to create a purge routing system that fits your workspace. Whether you're simply extending the chute into a nearby container or building a more elaborate routing network, Purge Pipes is designed to grow with your setup. Happy printing! model_name: Light and Fast Dual AMS Mount for H/X/P Series
description: I wanted a mount that didn't take too long to print or require too much material so I designed a mount that utilizes the weight of the AMS itself to help the mount clamp against the machine and keep the structure light. Unfortunately, the machines are not exactly the overall dimensions that Bambu cites. To accommodate this, the structure is broken into pieces that can be connected at various lengths to accommodate various printer sizes. This also makes them compatible with various models of Bambu machines. I also managed to fit all the parts in a single X/P series bed. H2C/H2S/H2D P2S X1C /X1E P1S/P1P AMS 2 AMS (3 Cavity) AMS (5 Cavity) Verified X X X X X Compatible X X Incompatible Note for High Temp Users: High temp printing with chamber heating will heat the printer glass beyond the glass transition temperature of PLA. This will cause warping of the structure. Please print the mount from a high temp plastic if you plan on printing chamber heated materials. If you only print PLA, this should not be an issue. Here is how the structure works: AMS weight hanging over the edge of the machine pushes down, forcing supports to pivot around the edge of the machine. Supports are retained by central tension member, which drives force into the side of the machine. Forces driving into side of machine increase friction between support and machine, improving grip. Small nubs on the central support posts retain both AMS units against each other, and prevent them from moving when the printer shakes. Size the frames so they are snug to the machine. If the notches only allow a slightly loose or slightly tight fit, choose the tight one. Once the weight of the AMS is loaded on top, any bowing in the structure will flatten out. The assembly utilizes toothed connections which are finely tuned to slide together and retain themselves with the layer lines of the print. If parts are too tight, they can likely be tapped together with a hammer without issue, just dont expect to get them back apart. If too loose, you can scale just the tensioning rods (the thin rectangular parts) to 101% to get a tighter fit. This gif shows the assembly process:

Core features of the mount The AMS HT mount conveniently sits on the side, flush with the top of the printer, allowing installation of an AMS Pro 2 or other Risers on top of the printer without interference. You can choose between installing the mount directly to the printer frame, or if you are using an AMS Flipper, to the Flipper handle, using the provided compatible bracket. AMS HT mount allowing full view of the side window with minimal obstruction Some highlights of the model: Strong triangular brackets, balancing strength and material use to mount the AMS HT to the side of the X2D/P2S printer frame Full view of the side window below the AMS HT with minimal obstruction Side bracket provides extra strength and vibration dampening from the printer for the front side of the mount Easy to print flat on the bed with no supports needed for the frame and only minimal supports required for the interfacing slots for precision Easy assembly by slotting the four (4) parts of the mount together using standard hardware of M3 screws and square nuts for a strong hold Can either be used: Directly with the printer using the Standalone main bracket or using the AMS Flipper compatible main bracket which slots around the AMS Flipper handle The mount allows access to the l inear rail belt tensioning ports for maintenance The model print profile has been fine tuned for strength, optimizing extrusion settings to maximize strength and limit support interface swaps and harnessing the power of the X2D dual nozzle system. The print profile is optimized to be printed using the X2D using PETG for the frame, with PLA as support interface support layer for crisp results and easy support removal. Note: As the printer frame is shared between the X2D and the P2S, if printing using the P2S, you will have a few nozzle swaps for the interface layers, but they are minimized to just a few, so it shouldn't affect print time dramatically. NOTE: Please be careful with resetting settings, they have been carefully set to have repeatable successful prints and hold to the print bed. Optional Add-on : Designed to be compatible with my X2D Filament Track Switch mount by having a cutout reserved for the mount and utilizing triangles for chord organization. Optional Add-on: Cable organizer using the triangle brackets. Upon request by another user, I designed another add-on to make the cable organization of the 6-pin cable even neater using a figure-8 cable organizer loop that snap-fits into one of the triangle brackets and can be mounted either vertically or horizontally depending on your preference. Hardware required for assembly and installation You will need a few types of M3 Socket Head Screws and thin M3 square nuts: 7x Socket Head Screw M3x30mm (DIN 912) - Bambu Lab store part AA042 x2 3x Socket Head Screw M3x30mm for the mount assembly 4x Socket Head Screw M3x30mm for the installation to the X2D/P2S printer frame 2x Socket Head Screw M3x20mm (DIN 912) - Bambu Lab store part AA040 x1 5x Socket Head Screw M3x10mm (DIN 912) - Bambu Lab store part AA159 x1 10x thin M3 square nuts (DIN 562, ≤2mm height) Optional: If you plan to install the Cable organizer you will also need 4x size 8x3mm round magnets (Bambu Lab store part CA008 x1) for the mount in the frame (and another 4x for the organizer itself ) Assembly The assembly is fairly simple and requires just a few standard hardware M3 screws and square nuts, providing a strong hold. You can follow the below step by step instructions, or follow the annotated images for location of screws, nuts and (optional) magnets. As the mount sits right next to the printer frame, for durability the model should be printed using PETG - so dry your filament prior to use! - you want to avoid stringing, warping or lifting off the bed. Print the four (4) parts - To help avoid any warping, you may want to reduce the Aux Fan speed to avoid spot cooling, which can contribute to lifting of large prints, or consider installing an Aux Fan deflector . Print the Main Bracket Pick either the Standalone Main Bracket if you want to install the mount directly to the printer frame or pick the AMS Flipper compatible Main Bracket if you are using the Flipper to mount the bracket to the Flipper Handle Print the Side Bracket for strong support of the mount and provide dampening to limit vibrations from the printer Print the Top Front Mount Bracket that holds the AMS HT and interfaces with the back and side brackets Print the Top Back Mount Bracket that holds the AMS HT and interfaces with the front and main brackets Print optional add-ons as desired: (Optional): Print the Filament Track Switch add-on to mount the Filament Track Switch to the frame over the AMS Flipper Handle and into the AMS HT side mount frame (Optional): Print the Cable Organizer add-on for extra neat organization of the 6-pin cable connecting to the AMS HT Annotated location of mounting hardware: Step by Step instructions: Connect the Top Front and Back brackets through their connecting interface Install two (2) thin M3 square nuts into the inside slots on both left and right side of the top arms Screw two (2 ) socket head screws M3x10mm length from the outside through each of the two arms to connect to the nuts to lock the front and back brackets together Slot the assembled Top Bracket into the Main Bracket through the four trapezoid interface arms note this is a precise interface with 0.15mm tolerances, so check that your printer printed the interfacing arms without any blobs or give them a light sand on the edges as needed Make sure the interface arms are aligned straight and push down using the back of your palm until the top and main brackets are flush - if things are tight and get stuck, a light sideways wiggle can help to loosen things Slot the Side Bracket into the Main Bracket through the two trapezoid interface arms using the same technique Install thin square nuts M3 in all remaining slots, sliding them to their embedded depths: One (1) - Inside of the Top Back bracket One (1) - Upper side of the Top Front bracket Two (2) - Inside of the Side bracket Two (2) - Sunk into the two slots on the back of the Main bracket - use a thin long screwdriver or pliers to push them into place Screw one (1) M3x10mm socket head screw from the bottom of the side bracket through the front bracket , watching until the screw surfaces through the square nut and locks the two parts together Screw two (2) M3x20mm socket head screws from the top of the Main Bracket through the interface arms, meeting the sunk square nuts Screw three (3) M3x30mm socket head screws from the back of the Main Bracket into the remaining holes connecting the Main and Top bracket with one (1) and the Main and Side bracket with two (2) screws (Optional) Install four (4) size 8x3mm round magnets into the holes on the back of the Main Bracket if you plan on installing the optional Cable Organizer. Installation Directly to the printer Remove the four (4) screws from the left backside of the X2D/P2S printer frame Remove the external spool holder mount if it is currently installed at the top and move it tothe bottom of the printer Attach two (2) M3x30mm socket head screws to the top of the mount and two to the bottom of the mounting holes aligning them with the four holes from which you removed the screws Using AMS Flipper Lift the left side (from the back) AMS Flipper Handle up and clip the mount into the handle - this should sit evenly almost flush on both sides -the mount will minimally protrude prior to tightening of the screws to create a counter clamping force to the AMS Flipper Handle to ensure a strong tight fit, but it will still allow the Flipper Handle to sit flush against the printer frame once aligned correctly as pictured below. Lower the Handle onto the printer and align the top and bottom evenly. A small gap before tightening the screws is ok but it should only be 1-2mm and be even between the top and bottom of the handle. If mount was correctly clicked into the handle and the handle sits even as shown above, screw the four (4) M3x30mm socket head screws onto the printer frame. I recommend starting with one of the bottom screws, but without fully tightening it, and then moving to the top and then finishing the rest of the screws and tightening things into place. Check that the flush fit hasn't shifted in case you tightened one screw before alignment was locked into place. The AMS HT mount and the top and bottom of the AMS Flipper handle should sit basically flush with the printer if the AMS HT side mount was clicked into place together correctly once everything is tightened as shown below: If things don't sit flush correctly, repeat Step 1-3, check the fit and try again until the mount is properly set in the center of the handle, resulting in a flush fit. If this is your initial installation of the AMS Flipper, follow the rest of the AMS Flipper installation instructions to finish installation of your AMS Flipper. Install optional add-ons Optional: Install the Filament Track Switch mount . Utilize the triangle cutout in the frame or use the cable organizer to store and tuck away the cords of the AMS HT: If you installed the External Spool holder on the bottom of the printer frame, you could route the power chord of the AMS HT through the triangle frame and down and using a cable tie (ideally a good quality Velcro one) attach the chord to the external spool holder for a clean installation. Optional: Install the Cable Organizer for AMS HT side-mount to organize the 6-pin cable using a neat figure-8 loop Done, enjoy easy access to your AMS HT on your X2D/P2S printer. Print Settings Supports: yes, with top interface layer enabled for smooth finish on supported portions Only the interface arms and the cutout for the linear rail adjustment screws require supports Brim: no Layer Height: 0.20mm Infill: 25 % cubic for strength Walls: 2 Print orientation: Flat on the bed Material: Parts: Dry PETG for strength and temperature resistance due to the close proximity to the printer. Loaded into Primary (left) nozzle Support Interface: PLA or specific support material to make removal easy (PLA won't bond strongly with PETG, so removal is easy, but the bond is strong enough for print support and using just interface layer reduces nozzle swaps). Loaded into Aux (right) nozzle if printed on X2D

model_name: Flashforge Creator 5 Pro Top Cover Hinges - Mod
description: DISCLAIMERS This is a fairly invasive modification. It requires drilling eight 3 mm holes into the acrylic top cover and replacing two of the factory screws on the side of the machine with longer ones. If you are not comfortable making these modifications, I recommend not attempting this. I do not take responsibility for any damage that occurs during the installation or use of this model. If I encounter any issues myself or someone reports any, I will try to release an updated version with a fix or, if that is not possible, I will remove the model to prevent further problems. Please watch the video to see the installation process and the finished result. Somebody will most likely come up with a more elegant or more secure solution in the future. I simply wanted to give this idea a try. I do not recommend printing these parts in PLA or PETG. In the video I used PLA only because I was prototyping. I later replaced every part with PA612-CF. A rigid, temperature-resistant filament is highly recommended. You will need several M3 screws in different lengths. The design is fairly forgiving in some areas, so multiple lengths can work. Below I have listed the sizes I used, along with alternative recommendations based on my testing. I also recommend keeping the parts in their supplied/uploaded print orientation for printing. They were arranged specifically to maximize strength by avoiding weak layer line orientations. All of the strength settings have been tested my be. I do not recommend reducing the amount of walls, top/bottom layers or infill percentage. Increasing is fine. Different infill pattern should also be fine. The model consists of: A - 2 hinge assemblies (2 parts each) B - 2 backplates C - 2 side reinforcements D - 1 middle reinforcement Only minimal supports are required. The holes are intentionally designed with very tight tolerances. In most cases you will need to use the screws themselves to thread the holes slightly during assembly. This is intentional to eliminate unnecessary play. If your printer struggles with dimensional accuracy, you can carefully open the holes up using a 3 mm drill bit. Step 1 Assemble the hinges. Refer to the photos for the correct orientation. The two hinge halves fit together tightly. Each hinge requires: 1 × M3x40 mm screw 1 × M3 nut The screw direction does not matter as long as it passes completely through the hinge and is secured with the nut. Step 2 Remove the factory screws from the toolhead communication assembly. Insert the assembled hinges by pushing the locating pins into the holes where the factory screws were removed. Make sure the pins are fully seated. You may need to twist or wiggle the hinge slightly while pushing it into place. If the pins are excessively tight, lightly sand or shave them until they fit. Secure each hinge with a screw, but do not fully tighten them yet. On my printer, an M3x40 mm screw was almost a perfect fit if you want it to sit flush from the inside (see the video, XXXX timestamp). I personally used M3x45 mm screws and secured them with a nut on the inside. Step 3 Place the top cover back on the printer and make sure it sits straight, flush, and pushed as far toward the hinges as possible. Flip the hinges upward so they sit flush against the cover. Install the mirrored side reinforcements onto the hinges. Each reinforcement only fits on one side. With the reinforcements installed, you can rotate the hinges slightly left or right to fine-tune their position. If the hinges move too freely, lightly tighten the screws from Step 2. The goal is for the side reinforcements to sit perfectly flush against the walls and corners of the top cover. Repeat on the opposite side. Once you are satisfied with the alignment, use the eight mounting holes in the hinges to mark the drilling locations on the acrylic cover. Take your time during this step. This is the point of no return. Up until now, every modification has been completely reversible. After marking, use the square backplate (B, Pictured below) to confirm markings are aligned properly. Huge thanks to @UncleJessy for testing and this tip! Step 4 Remove the top cover and place it on your work surface. Using a 3 mm drill bit, drill all eight marked holes. Make sure your drill is sharp and drill very slowly to avoid cracking the cover. After drilling, remove all burrs and debris. Step 5 Install the screws into the backplates. Top holes: M3x20 mm Bottom holes: M3x10 mm for flush fit. Longer screws will work but reduce the opening angle. The 12 mm screws will protrude slightly and slightly reduce the maximum opening angle of the lid. If you want the cover to open a little farther, use M3x10 mm screws instead. Longer screws can also be used if you prefer a smaller opening angle. There is some room for personal preference here. Insert the screws through the acrylic from the inside until the backplate sits completely flush against the inside wall of the cover. Repeat for the opposite side. Step 6 Remove the hinge assemblies from the printer (see Step 2). Slide the hinges onto the screws protruding from the backplates. Because of the tight tolerances, you may need to rotate each screw gradually with a screwdriver instead of simply pushing the hinge into place. Step 7 Secure the lower four screws (two per hinge) with nuts. Install both side reinforcements, then place the middle reinforcement across the top. Secure the remaining four screws with nuts and tighten everything firmly. Step 8 Flip the hinges outward and reinstall the entire assembly onto the printer. Guide the two locating pins back into the holes from Step 2. Having a second person helping makes this step much easier. Once both pins are fully seated, close the cover and reinstall the side screws from Step 2. Tighten everything completely. Installation is now complete. A few things to keep in mind When closing the cover, you may occasionally need to wiggle it slightly so the two locating pins slide back into the frame correctly. If everything was aligned properly during Step 3, the cover should sit just as flush as it did before the modification. Do not slam the cover open or closed. Do not place objects on the open cover in the opened state. I have no idea how durable the acrylic will be over time. It is not particularly thick, and additional weight or force could cause it to crack. I also do not recommend leaving the cover open on the hinges for extended periods. Open it only when needed. Think carefully before deciding whether this modification is right for you. Finally, I cannot guarantee that every current or future Creator 5 will be manufactured identically. Small design changes may occur without notice, so fitment could vary between machines. description: The cutting wall is 1.2 mm at the tip, exactly 3 extrusion lines on a 0.4 mm nozzle, which guarantees a solid wall with no gaps. The bars run across the short side, which is the right direction to hold the shape. Use a 5 to 8 mm brim, since the contact area with the plate is small and the piece is long. PLA works well and gives a rigid cut. For heavy or professional use, PETG holds up better against flexing and humidity over time. Ele foi projetado especificamente para argila, que é densa e exige bem mais da peça que uma massa de cozinha. Por isso a estrutura é reforçada na base e travada por três barras internas, para o formato não abrir nem entortar na hora de pressionar. A ponta de corte é fina e afiada, então a borda sai limpa na cerâmica. O melhor é que o tamanho é totalmente ajustável antes de imprimir, então dá para gerar a mesma peça em outras medidas conforme o seu projeto pede. Imprima em PLA para o dia a dia ou em PETG se for usar muito e quiser durabilidade extra. Acompanha a recomendação de brim na mesa para garantir que uma peça longa assim grude bem na primeira camada.

model_name: BC250 Case MKUU+ (FSP, Apevia, Metalfish PSU)
description: This is a remixed model originally created by the very talented morph91 . Original model link: https://makerworld.com/en/models/2749412-bc-250-gaming-pc-case-mk-ultra-uno . I'm naming this model the MK Ultra Uno Plus : ) Case Highlights: Can be printed in only 3 plates with less than 600g of filament Tool-less design (no screws required) Fits the FSP500-30AS, Apevia ITX flex, and Metalfish flex PSUs Customizable front plates Ability to fit 40 & 50 mm fans on rear Internal clips to attach both halves of case together securely & internal psu lock to securely hold psu in place without external latch Heatsink mod (stick on heatsinks) to help improve thermals Important Considerations: There are two different versions of the fan shroud. One is the exact same as the original, the other is a modified version that allows active airflow to flow to stick on heatsinks that I personally made for my build. You can reference the assembly instructions for photos. Please make sure you only print the plate relevant for your build! Both the apevia and metalfish variants of the back case contain one less internal clip/latch due to space constraints. So these variants may be slightly less rigid when the two case halves are put together The internal psu lock was created specfically for the FSP500-30AS variant. It might fit the apevia variant, but will most likely not fit the metalfish variant. If someone prints either version, I'm more than happy to create a working psu lock for these versions. I just need accurate measurements and someone to test any prototypes. If you're interested then leave a comment/DM me : ) If anyone ends up printing the apevia or metalfish variants, please let me know if anything needs to be adjusted (besides the internal psu lock)! I used morph91 's measurements for the metalfish variant and also lolheyaj 's measurements for the apevia variant, since I do not personally own either of those psus. Also, as a temporary solution for the internal psu lock issue - you could probably use glue to keep the psu secure in the case as a temporary measure. If you have a different flex psu, and can take some accurate measurements for me - I am more than willing to create new versions to suit your psu (as long as dimensions fit the case)! : ) Expected Thermals: Thermals may vary slightly, given differences in thermal paste and depending whether you use the stick on heatsinks like I did. Also depending on 24CU vs 40CU, fan curves, overclock, undervolts, etc. For reference here's my configuration: GPU: 40CU 2000MHz @940mV (+16CU and +500 MHz from stock) CPU: 3800MHz @1060mV (+300MHz from stock) And here are some max temps from a couple games @1080p: My Part List: BC250 PSU (fsp500-30as, apevia itx flex, or metalfish flex) https://a.co/d/0gOMs9rW black petg https://a.co/d/04eTZ6sm for the two brown pla's from this bundle for my fake wood texture front panels makerworld.com/en/models/2527214-bc-250-scooper fin scooper to straighten fins https://a.co/d/0hZ28ifs for 12mm latching button (you may need a wire stripper, wire crimper, and dupont connectors if you copy me 1:1) https://a.co/d/0jdT5jNV arctic p12 pro pst https://a.co/d/0iLAR7Ty arctic mx-4 thermal paste (optional) https://a.co/d/063cMg66 noctua NF-A4x20 (optional) https://a.co/d/00RnzoEo stick on heatsinks, I bought 2 of these kits and used 3 out of the 4 heatsinks (optional) This looks to be a cheaper alternative: https://a.co/d/038s6cPO - it would be the same size as what I used, but as one large piece instead. Based on reviews, it looks like a thermal pad of some sort is already preapplied. If you end up buying this one, let me know how it fits! (optional) https://a.co/d/066uYDJ8 rubber anti vibration screws used to mount noctua 40mm fan Print Instructions: Print the main case components in PETG, and dry filament for 8 hours before printing (reduces stringing). Make sure to print only one of the fan shroud plates. For more information read the important considerations at the top. If you want to make your front panel have the fake wood texture like mine, then use this as a modifier: https://makerworld.com/en/models/1492898-wood-grain-modifier-add-wood-grain-to-any-models?from=search#profileId-1560821 . You can print the front panels in PLA. I recommend using a 0.2mm nozzle if you're doing the wood texture like I did. If you are downloading the model to modify or use with a different slicer (and not bambu studio), then make sure to paint a straight line seam on the bottom part of back half of the case. This helps reduce VFAs: Assembly Instructions: Take off the IO shield and the small bracket next to cmos battery Use the fin scooper to straighten the fins underneath where the fan shroud is gonna go. After straightening the fins, use an air duster to make sure any debris is blown off. Also if you haven't already, repaste the chip! Attach fan (recommend arctic p12 pro pst) with pins to fan shroud. Then attach fan shroud to pcb. Make sure the two small latches are pushed as far up as possible (in pic below you can see the one latch is in the corner of the pcb). Optionally here, if you have the stick on heatsinks (120x40x20mm), you can stick them right next to the fan slit. Doing this mod helped my ingame temps by 3-7C. VERY IMPORTANT NOTE: If you do not have/don't plan to use stick on heatsinks print the plate with the original fan shroud instead! Put PSU into back half of case: Add psu lock on left side (currently only known compatible for fsp500-30as): Mount any 40mm fans now (both screws or rubber mounts work): Slide bc250 on alu backplate onto the back half of case. Plug in exhaust fan to the Y splitter of main fan. Plug in the 8 pin power cable: (optional) Place any lower custom front panels on now before you install your 12mm button (This step is for FSP500-30AS psu, idk what pins to short for apevia/metalfish psus but you can probably find out on reddit) Plug in latching button to PS_ON and GND. I crimped the wires into two male dupont connectors and put them in a 2pin housing. I slightly have to bend the metal pins to fit into the psu which creates enough friction where the pins don't fall out. There's probably a better solution for this… Attach front half of case, and slide until both halves attach together. Enjoy!

model_name: P2S X2D - BIQU All Plates ArUco Marker ⧸ Magnetic
description: Successful detection. Every time. No compromises. This version is designed exclusively for the Bambu Lab P2S and X2D. This model is part of my ongoing BIQU Build Plate Accessories collection. Each model is conceived, printed, and endurance-tested on my own machines, refined through dozens of iterations to match the printer’s true mechanical behavior. Precision isn't assumed here, it’s verified layer by layer. Explore the full collection: BIQU Build Plate Accessories Follow me if you like my work, that kind of appreciation really dries my filament. Likes and boosts feed the Maker World algorithm and keep the new models coming Tested Compatibility, Fitting And Detection Checked Blue BIQU CryoGrip Pro Glacier Build Plate for Bambu X2D/X1/P1/P2/A1 (256mm*256mm) Matte Orange BIQU CryoGrip Pro FrostBite Build Plate for Bambu X2D/X1/P1/P2/A1 (256mm*256mm) Should Work But Unable To Check Myself Because I Don't Have the Build Plates Blue BIQU CryoGrip Pro FrostBite Build Plate for Bambu X2D/X1/P1/P2/A1 (256mm*256mm) Purple, Green, Pink, Yellow and Blue BIQU CryoGrip Pro Build Plate for Bambu Lab X1C/P1S/A1 (256mm*256mm) BIQU SSS Super Spring Steel Build Plate for Bambu A1/P1/X1 (257mm*257mm) BIQU Designer Series Dual-textured Build Plate for Bambu X2D/X1/P1/A1 (256mm*256mm) BIQU Double-sided (PEI/PEO/PET) Build Plate for Bambu X2D/X1C/P1S/P1P/A1 (257mm*257mm) Remarkably Forgiving During my testing with the newer BIQU FrostBite build plates without the honeycomb handle, I made some interesting observations about the X2D's ArUco detection. The marker was reliably detected between 5 mm and 14 mm in size. Positioning along the Y axis had virtually no influence, as long as the marker remained between the printer door and the printable area. Along the X axis, the center of the marker could be placed anywhere between approximately 35 mm and 135 mm from the left edge of the build plate. These findings differ from my early experiments when the X2D was first released. Back then, the marker seemed to require very precise positioning. Based on my current testing, the detection system appears to be significantly more tolerant than it used to be. Just slap the marker in the general direction of the original code and you are fine. The Model The BIQU build plates are excellent, but there is one frustrating drawback. Some ship without an ArUco marker, others include the wrong code, and some come with stickers that simply do not work reliably. This model puts an end to that. Developed specifically for the BIQU build plates, with or without the honeycomb handle, on the Bambu Lab P2S and X2D, this magnetic marker provides precise alignment and reliable build plate recognition every time. The marker is held securely in place by seven 5 × 1 mm magnets (see BOM). The design has been tested in both PETG and ASA. PETG is an excellent long term choice, while ASA is the ultimate install it once and forget about it solution. Transparency Notice Some of the BIQU build plates used for testing were provided by BIQU free of charge. No payment was received, and BIQU had no influence over the design, testing, measurements, or the content of this model page. All opinions and test results are entirely my own.
