description: First-Layer-Flussraten-Kalibrierungstest Finde mit einem schnellen und materialsparenden Test die optimale Flussrate für die erste Schicht deines Filaments und Druckprofils. Diese Kalibrierungsplatte enthält 16 einzelne Testflächen, die jeweils mit einer unterschiedlichen Flussrate für die erste Schicht von 0,85 bis 1,15 gedruckt werden. Nach dem Druck kannst du die Oberflächen direkt miteinander vergleichen und den Wert auswählen, der die gleichmäßigste und vollständig geschlossene erste Schicht erzeugt. Warum dieser Test sinnvoll ist Eine falsch eingestellte Flussrate der ersten Schicht kann zu folgenden Problemen führen: sichtbare Lücken zwischen den Drucklinien schwache Haftung der ersten Schicht raue oder überfüllte Oberflächen erhöhte Rillen durch zu viel Material ungleichmäßige Unterseiten Mit diesem Test kannst du mehrere Werte in nur einem Druck vergleichen, anstatt jeden Wert einzeln testen zu müssen. Enthaltene Flussraten Obere Reihe: 1,08 · 1,10 · 1,12 · 1,15 Zweite Reihe: 1,00 · 1,02 · 1,04 · 1,06 Dritte Reihe: 0,92 · 0,94 · 0,96 · 0,98 Untere Reihe: 0,85 · 0,87 · 0,89 · 0,90 Nutze das beigefügte Referenzbild, um den jeweiligen Wert der einzelnen Testfläche eindeutig zuzuordnen. So wertest du den Test aus Drucke die enthaltene 3MF-Datei, ohne die individuellen Objekteinstellungen zu verändern. Löse die Testflächen vorsichtig vom Druckbett. Vergleiche die Oberflächen aller Testflächen. Halte die einzelnen Teststücke gegen eine helle Lichtquelle. Wähle den Wert, bei dem die Drucklinien vollständig miteinander verbunden sind und die Oberfläche gleichzeitig glatt und gleichmäßig aussieht. Flussrate zu niedrig sichtbare Lücken zwischen den Linien Licht scheint deutlich durch schwache oder leicht trennbare Oberfläche Flussrate zu hoch raue oder wellige Oberfläche erhöhte Rillen zu viel Material zwischen den Linien Optimales Ergebnis Drucklinien sind vollständig miteinander verbunden glatte und gleichmäßige Oberfläche keine deutlichen Lücken oder übermäßigen Rillen Übernimm den ermittelten Wert anschließend als Flussrate der ersten Schicht in dasselbe Filament- und Druckprofil, das du für den Test verwendet hast. Wichtiger Hinweis Dies ist ein Test für die Flussrate der ersten Schicht und kein Z-Offset- oder Druckbett-Nivellierungstest. Für zuverlässige Ergebnisse solltest du dieselben Einstellungen verwenden wie bei deinen späteren Drucken: Filament Düse Druckplatte Temperatur Filamentprofil Druckerprofil Effiziente Kalibrierung 16 Werte in einem Druck etwa 23 Minuten Druckzeit etwa 6,02 g Filament keine Stützstrukturen erforderlich keine Montage erforderlich Druckzeit und Materialverbrauch können je nach Drucker, Filament und verwendeten Einstellungen leicht abweichen. Wenn dir dieser Kalibrierungstest geholfen hat, freue ich mich sehr über eine Bewertung, einen Make oder einen Boost.

description: FULL EXPLANATION HERE: https://www.reddit.com/r/FDMminiatures/comments/1v0rerw/introducing_the_curling_tower_a_simple_solution/ This is a “Curling Tower” - A Model designed to combat “Curling”, especially when printing Miniatures. What happened here? When 3D Printing Miniatures with an FDM Printer, we run into some unique issues. One of which is the fact that even though it takes a long time to finish the print, the time spent on each individual layer is fairly short. Ideally, by the time the current layer starts printing, the previous one should have cooled down as much as possible. Now, if you're printing something large this isn't a problem - By the time the nozzle circles back to the starting point of the next layer, the previous one will have solidified. But, as you can probably guess, this isn't always the case for miniatures. It usually doesn't affect the entire model - Most of them are still large enough that the Layers will have enough time to cool down. Where it becomes an issue is with "isolated" parts of the model - Parts that are either only partially connected to the Model, or only become fully connected throughout the print. Examples of partially connected isolated parts are but are not limited to Swords raised towards the sky, Staffs and other weapons. Examples of isolated parts that only become fully connected throughout the print, are usually legs or similar body-parts. But what exactly is Curling, and why is it such an issue? When printing these isolated parts, the time spent on each layer is very short - So short that by the time, say Layer 100 starts, Layer 99 hasn't fully solidified yet. The heat of the Nozzle as well as the new layer of filament being placed on top of the previous Layer will re-soften the material further, causing the layer to be slightly lifted upwards. If this happened only once, it wouldn't be a major issue - The lift per layer is relatively small. But if it happens over multiple layers it becomes a problem. Eventually the filament will be curled enough for the Nozzle to slam into it, at which point it will most likely break of that part and ruin the print. With print times reaching the double digits, this is - as you can imagine - moderately upsetting. So how do we fix it? There are four common solutions to curling: Since Curling is caused by filament not cooling quickly enough, the easiest way is to simply increase the speed of the cooling fans. However, since most HQ Profiles already have these maxed out, this is unlikely to help most people. However: If they are already maxed out, but you still run into the issue - Make sure that they are actually clean. The fans on my A1 were stuffed with dust, which significantly lowered the cooling effect. If it's been a while since you last cleaned the fans, or never cleaned them at all, now might be a good start. If the fans are clean and already running at 100% speed, we might need to give them a little help by lowering our printing temperature. Filament leaving the nozzle at 220° will take longer to cool down than filament leaving the nozzle at 200°. The problem here is that you can only go so low before you start creating new issues, namely Nozzle Clogs. If you are already operating in the 195-200 range, you don't have much room left. If the problem is caused because the surface of the model is too small, we could simply increase the size of the Model. By upscaling it until the "vulnerable" part of the model has enough surface area for it to be printed with regular infill as opposed Solid Infill, the likelyhood of it warping becomes substantially smaller. Of course, this solution substantially increases print time and if you're printing Wargaming Proxies where scale matters, it's not suited for you at all. Printing multiple models. Following the same logic as Solution #3, instead of going for Model Size, we aim to increase the total print volume. By introducing at least a second Model to our print and print by layer, we can give each layer a cooling-buffer. As the printer finishes the Layer on Model A, Model B will have more time to cool down and vice versa. This solution also drasticially increases print-time, and comes with the downside of not only introducing additional risks in case the print fails somewhere, but also the simple fact that not everyone wants or needs multiple models. While all those four solutions work, I wasn't satisfied with any of them. The first two are limited by Hardware which, in some cases, simply isn't enough. The other two force you to print something other than what you actually wanted to print. So, I wanted to use a compromise. The Curling Tower - It's just a simple, hollow, square tower with thin walls. The idea here is simple - You print it alongside your actual model, with some distance between the two. Once the Printer has finished a layer for the Model, it will move to the Tower, giving the Filament on the Model enough time to cool down. Now, you might be thinking - That's just Solution #4 again, printing with more than one model at the same time. And you're right - But there is a catch. Because the Curling Tower is much more basic than any miniature, there isn't a whole lot that can go wrong with it. It's "safer" to print alongside your actual print, because there can't be any failed supports, harsh overhangs or even curling. And, because it's such a simple design - it will add significantly less time to the total print duration than a second, actual miniature would. But the real difference and big advantage, is that the Tower is adjustable. Remember when I said that Curling mostly affects the isolated parts of the model? In this case, it's the leg of the Skeleton - You don't need to print the entire Tower. You can just match the height of the tower to the point where the isolated part re-connects with the model and is out of the "Danger Zone" This means that you will have all the benefits of the "Cooling Buffer" that Solution #4 gives you, at a fraction of the increase in print time and material waste. To give you some numbers: Skelly without Tower or 2nd Model to serve as a Cooling Buffer: 3h45m Skelly with a 2nd Skelly as a Cooling Buffer: 6h56m Skelly with a Curling Tower equal to the Model Height: 4h54m 4h54 Skelly with a Curling Tower adjusted to the "Danger Zone": 4h14m That's an increase of only 13% when compared to the 86% increase you'd get when printing with a 2nd model. Now, is this something that you should use for all of your prints? No, of course not - Although in theory, it should also very slightly improve Overhangs for the same reason it fixes Curling - By giving them more time to cool before the next layer is added on top. But this is primarily meant as a tool for models that have a lot of isolated parts, or if you are struggling with Curling and none of the other solutions work out for you. So next time you're running into Curling even though your fans are already maxed out - Give this one a try.

description: This modified top-mount AMS 2 Pro flipper moves the AMS 55mm further forward, allowing it to raise fully when the H2D is positioned close to a wall. It was designed for setups such as mine where there is not much clearance behind the printer (about 85mm in my case from the wall to the back of the printer), where the original flipper would cause the AMS lid to hit the wall before it could be raised enough. You will need the Original H2 AMS Flipper long arms for this: https://makerworld.com/en/models/1815860-h2-simple-ams-flipper The brackets are a direct replacement for the two small AMS 2 Pro mounting brackets from the print above, so there is no need to reprint the larger arms that attach to the back of the printer. The modification also includes a front handle to make lifting the AMS easier. The handle is secured from below using one of the original AMS transport screws 3x16mm, so no additional hardware is required. Assemble by sliding the folding arm upper bracket onto the dovetail joint of the handle, you can use a bit of filament to secure it, but as it fits from the bottom it won't come off anyway so not really needed, just for extra peace of mind. The arm uses gopro style pronged fitment, just slide this on and push through the securing pin, it should sit flush so give it a firm press, this is tapered at the end so should secure well. The folding support arm holds the flipper securely in the raised position once lifted. Also as the AMS does not tilt all the way back with this mod, the printer can continue printing while it is raised because the filament spools remain securely seated on the rollers. There is a stopper on the long arm so it won't flip forward so be aware and don't force it to fold out front, it fold back neatly out the way, there is a bit of friction at first, but over time it should loosen so the foot/arm will fall into place when you flip the AMS. The Arm will work with the glass in place or not, so you can use this when you need access to the top while printing such as when using TPU to feed directly in from the top without having to remove the AMS unit. Hope you like this mod, if you can leave some comments and feedback I would appreciate it!

This is a Remix of Bambu Labs PTFE guide that was released alongside the Filament track switch. After months of usage, I started to notice some of the design flaws and things that I did not like. I downloaded the step files Bambu Lab provided in their original listing and proceeded to make my changes. The changes I made are: Reduced the PTFE guide's overall footprint to simplify it, reduce the use of filament and make it more widely compatible with AMS stacking solutions. Widened the sides of the guide to make room for the use of piece of 25mm x 10mm double sided tape (I used the Gorilla Invisible Hold Mounting Tape). Slightly increased the thickness of the guide to increase strength and rigidity, and ensure correct alignment with the AMS, AMS 2 Pro, AMS HT. Strengthened the tabs that hold the tube by increasing its thickness by .25mm. While this seems very minimal, it is very effective at preventing the tube from dropping down over time. An unexpected benefit from my changes is that you can place the guide exactly where the PTFE tube wants to be. Installations instruction: Cut a 10mm by 25mm piece of double sided tape and place them on the tabs that face the AMS, AMS 2 PRO, and AMS HT. Place the tube into the base. Remove the plastic/paper lining from the tape. Remove the PTFE tube from the AMS. Slide the PTFE tube into the guide tube. Slide the PTFE tube into the AMS. Use the PTFE tube to help you install the guide and ensure proper alignment. Aim for having the AMS and AMS 2 PRO release button to be right in the center of the guide. For the AMS HT, ensure air vent is in center of the guide. Please refer to the photos provided which are for an AMS 2 PRO and AMS HT. I do not have an AMS 1 so I am unable to provide a photo for that. If you have one, I would greatly appreciate you posting a photo in the comments and let me know if I can use your photo in my listing. I will ensure to give you credit for your contribution. Press the base firmly against the AMS, AMS 2 PRO, and AMS HT. I have tested this and have had no issues. As long as you use a good quality tape, you should not have any issues. I used the Gorilla Invisible Hold Mounting Tape because it is strong, sticky, and can be easily removed without leaving staining or debris. Please share any feedback and let me know if you run into any issues to make changes.

model_name: Gridfinity Filament Swatch Holder with Tags
description: Keep your filament swatch library sorted, visible and always within reach. This is a Gridfinity-compatible swatch holder designed around the 24×24 mm Bambu-style filament swatch . Each slot holds one swatch upright, so you can flip through your collection like a card index instead of digging through a drawer. Drop it into any Gridfinity baseplate and it locks into your existing bench setup. Included in this project are six ready-to-print sizes plus a set of customizable divider tags — the part that makes this one different from the usual swatch trays. What's included Plate Model Gridfinity footprint 01 Swatch Holder 4×2 168 × 84 mm 03 Swatch Holder 3×3 126 × 126 mm 04 Swatch Holder 2×5 84 × 210 mm 05 Swatch Holder 2×1 84 × 42 mm 06 Swatch Holder 2×2 84 × 84 mm 07 Swatch Holder 2×3 84 × 126 mm 02 Tag set (PLA / PETG / Multicolor / Out of Stock) — Start with a 2×2 if you just want to try it, or go straight to the 4×2 / 2×5 if you already have a big filament collection. The tags — the real difference Most swatch holders give you slots and nothing else. Once you pass ~30 swatches, slots alone stop being enough: you can't tell where PLA ends and PETG begins, and you have no way to flag a colour you've run out of. The included tags slot into the same rails as the swatches and act as dividers and labels . Four are included ready to print: PLA PETG Multicolor Out of Stock The text is a raised emboss, so a simple filament change at the top layer gives you a two-colour tag with no AMS and no multi-material setup — yellow on black, red on black, whatever reads best on your bench. With an AMS it's a single-click multicolour print. And because the text is just a body on the model, you can swap it for anything you want : ABS, ASA, TPU, PETG-CF, Silk, Matte, "Ordered", "Sample", brand names, project names, or your own shop labels. Print a handful and re-organise the tray whenever your stock changes. Print profile No supports needed on any part. Everything prints flat on the bed. Setting Recommended Material PLA or PETG Layer height 0.2 mm Nozzle 0.4 mm Walls 3 Top / bottom layers 4 / 3 Infill 15 % gyroid Supports None Brim Not needed on a textured PEI plate Notes from my own prints: The slot walls are thin by design so the swatches slide in with a light friction fit. Don't scale the model — a few percent is enough to make the swatches either fall out or refuse to go in. If your swatches feel too tight, a 0.02–0.04 mm bump in X-Y contour compensation (negative) usually fixes it without reprinting at a different size. The bodies print fine at 0.28 mm draft layers if you want speed, but the tag lettering looks much cleaner at 0.2 mm or 0.16 mm. For the tags: insert a filament change / colour change at the first layer of the raised text (around 0.8–1.0 mm from the top of the tag) to get the two-tone look shown in the photos. Which swatches does it fit? Designed for the 24 × 24 mm Bambu Lab-style filament swatch . Any of the popular printable swatch models in that format will fit — for example Customizable Bambu Style Filament Swatch Sample . Print one swatch per filament, label it with the brand and colour, and file it in the tray. Over time you end up with a physical colour library that beats any screenshot when you're deciding what to print next. Credits Base cups generated with the Parametric Model Maker — Gridfinity Basic Cup . Swatch format based on the Customizable Bambu Style Filament Swatch Sample . Gridfinity system by Zack Freedman. Tags designed by me. If this helped tidy up your bench, a like or a boost goes a long way. And if you print a custom tag set, post it as a Make — I'd like to see what labels people come up with. I created this project out of pure frustration. I was very dissatisfied with the performance of the original wheels on my robotic lawnmower – I tested both the standard version and the one supposedly designed for "heavy terrain." The result was always the same: the robot constantly dug in, stalled, and damaged the lawn. I decided to design my own solution. For several weeks now, my robot has been running on these wheels, and the problem has completely disappeared. The machine finally drives without any problems, doesn't dig into the ground, and maneuvers smoothly throughout the garden. Key design features: Optimized spike design: The shape, length, and spacing of the spikes have been designed to prevent the robot from digging in. The design provides excellent traction while allowing the machine to turn smoothly without tearing up the turf. Rearview of the original weight: This is a very important detail – the inside of the wheel has been modeled to easily accommodate the original weight. This allows the robot to maintain a proper center of gravity and ground pressure. Dedicated cover: A flat cover encloses the inside of the wheel, protecting the weight and hub from the accumulation of dirt, mud, and grass clippings. Mounts to the wheel bolt, and a removal key is included. Removal key: A simple but extremely useful T-shaped key is included. It fits perfectly into the slots in the cover, allowing for easy and safe removal when cleaning or servicing is needed. Printing instructions: Material: I highly recommend PETG. The wheels are used outdoors and are exposed to moisture, impact, and sunlight. PETG provides the necessary flexibility and durability that regular PLA might struggle with over time. Airflow Capsule Kompakter Silikat-Behälter für Filamentrollen, Dryboxen und luftdichte Lagerlösungen. Kurzbeschreibung Die Airflow Capsule ist ein wiederverwendbarer Behälter für 2–5 mm Silikatkugeln zur Feuchtekontrolle bei der Filamentlagerung. Die Bauform ist so ausgelegt, dass die Capsule in den Kern vieler Filamentrollen passt und damit vorhandenen Leerraum nutzt , statt zusätzlichen Platz in Beutel, Box oder Lagerbehälter zu belegen. Durch die offene Geometrie mit seitlichen Schrägstrukturen, perforierter Innenstruktur und zusätzlichen Bodenöffnungen kann die Luftfeuchtigkeit im geschlossenen Lagerraum wirksam an das Trockenmittel gelangen. Gleichzeitig bleiben die Silikatkugeln sicher im Behälter. Vorteile Für 2–5 mm Silikatkugeln geeignet 1 mm Sieböffnungen halten die Kugeln sicher zurück Kompakte Bauform für den Einsatz in vielen Filamentrollenkernen Kein zusätzlicher Platzbedarf in vielen Lager-Setups Wiederverwendbar und leicht nachfüllbar Drehverschluss mit Gewinde für sicheres Öffnen und Schließen Saubere Alternative zu losen Silikatbeuteln oder losem Granulat Geeignet für Dryboxen, luftdichte Beutel und Lagerboxen Warum die Airflow Capsule sinnvoll ist Filamente reagieren je nach Material mehr oder weniger stark auf Luftfeuchtigkeit. Eine trockene Lagerumgebung hilft dabei, Feuchteaufnahme zu reduzieren und die Materialeigenschaften länger stabil zu halten. Die Airflow Capsule unterstützt das, indem sie das Trockenmittel dort platziert, wo es praktisch und platzsparend eingesetzt werden kann: direkt im Kern der Filamentrolle . Das Produkt ist nicht einfach nur ein geschlossener Behälter mit Löchern. Die Geometrie ist darauf ausgelegt, einen guten Feuchteausgleich zwischen Umgebungsluft und Silikat zu ermöglichen. Deckel und Verschluss Die Airflow Capsule wird über einen Drehverschluss mit Gewinde geschlossen. Der Deckel wird aufgesetzt und durch Drehen sicher verriegelt. Dadurch sitzt er fest auf dem Behälter und kann sich im normalen Einsatz nicht unbeabsichtigt lösen. Vorteile des Gewinde-Drehverschlusses: sicherer Halt im geschlossenen Zustand einfaches Öffnen zum Nachfüllen oder Wechseln des Silikats saubere und wiederverwendbare Lösung ohne loses Einstecken besser kontrollierbares Schließen als bei reinen Steckverbindungen Der Verschluss ist damit auf praktische Wiederverwendung ausgelegt: sicher im Betrieb, aber jederzeit wieder lösbar . Physikalisches Prinzip Silica Gel arbeitet über Adsorption . Wassermoleküle werden an der großen inneren Oberfläche des Trockenmittels gebunden. Entscheidend ist deshalb nicht nur die Menge des Silikats, sondern auch, wie gut die Luftfeuchtigkeit das Material erreichen kann. In einer geschlossenen Box oder einem Beutel gibt es in der Regel keinen starken Luftstrom. Die Feuchteverteilung erfolgt daher vor allem durch: Diffusion geringe natürliche Mikro-Konvektion langsamen Feuchteausgleich im gesamten eingeschlossenen Volumen Genau hier ist eine offene Behälterstruktur sinnvoll. Die seitlichen Schrägöffnungen, die durchlässige Innenstruktur und die zusätzlichen Öffnungen im Boden vergrößern die Kontaktfläche zwischen Umgebungsluft und Trockenmittel. Das beschleunigt nicht im Sinne eines Ventilators den Luftstrom, aber es erleichtert den Feuchteausgleich , weil die Luftfeuchtigkeit von mehreren Seiten an das Silikat gelangen kann. Warum die schräge Struktur sinnvoll ist Die schräg angeordneten Öffnungen erzeugen in einem stehenden Luftvolumen keinen gerichteten Windkanal . Das wäre physikalisch übertrieben. Sie haben trotzdem einen realen Nutzen: mehr freiliegende Austauschfläche weniger abgeschirmte Bereiche bessere Erreichbarkeit des Trockenmittels von mehreren Seiten stabile Außenstruktur trotz offener Bauweise guter Kompromiss aus Luftzugang und mechanischer Stabilität Die Wirkung entsteht also nicht durch „Luft wird aktiv hineingezogen“, sondern durch eine offene, günstig zugängliche Geometrie , die Diffusion und Feuchteausgleich unterstützt. Technische Daten Außendurchmesser: 54 mm Höhe: 36,8 mm Außenwand: 2 mm Innenwand: 2 mm Lochdurchmesser Sieb Deckel: 1,5 mm Lochdurchmesser Boden/Gehäuse: 1,3 mm Lochabstand Seitenbereich: 2,844 mm Lochabstand Boden: 3 mm Geeignete Füllung: 2–5 mm Silikatkugeln Verschlussart: Drehverschluss mit Gewinde Eignung für Silikatkugeln 2–5 mm Die 1,5-mm-Öffnungen sind deutlich kleiner als die verwendeten Silikatkugeln mit 2–5 mm Durchmesser. Dadurch bleiben die Kugeln sicher im Behälter, während Luftfeuchtigkeit weiterhin an das Trockenmittel gelangen kann. Das macht die Capsule geeignet für: Silikatkugeln wiederverwendbare Trockenmittelgranulate in passender Körnung Filamentlagerung in geschlossenen Systemen Geschätzte Füllmenge Je nach tatsächlicher Innengeometrie liegt die realistische Füllmenge bei ungefähr: ca. 30–40 g Silikatkugeln Diese Angabe ist als praxisnahe Bandbreite zu verstehen, da Boden, Deckel, Gewinde und Innenkontur die exakte nutzbare Füllmenge beeinflussen. Was diese Menge bringt Silica Gel kann je nach Typ und Umgebungsbedingungen typischerweise etwa 20–35 % seines Eigengewichts an Wasser aufnehmen. Bei einer Füllmenge von ca. 30–40 g Silikat ergibt sich damit eine praxisnahe Wasseraufnahme von ungefähr: ca. 6–10 g Wasser im typischen Einsatzbereich Für einen geschlossenen Lagerraum einer einzelnen Filamentrolle ist das relevant, weil nicht nur die eingeschlossene Luftfeuchtigkeit abgefangen wird, sondern auch Feuchte, die beim Öffnen eingetragen wird oder langsam in das System eindringt. Abschätzung zur Wirkdauer und Feuchtereduktion Die folgenden Angaben sind keine garantierten Messwerte, sondern technisch und praxisnah abgeschätzte Richtwerte unter typischen Einsatzbedingungen. Sie gelten für einen gut geschlossenen Lagerbehälter, eine Füllmenge von ca. 30–40 g Silikat und den Fall, dass der Behälter nicht ständig geöffnet wird. Unter diesen Annahmen ist typischerweise zu erwarten: eine spürbare Reduktion der Luftfeuchtigkeit innerhalb einiger Stunden ein deutlicher Effekt nach etwa 12–24 Stunden eine Stabilisierung des Lagerklimas meist nach ca. 1–3 Tagen Die voraussichtliche Wirkdauer einer Füllung liegt je nach Einsatzbedingungen grob im Bereich von: mehreren Wochen bei normalem Gebrauch bis zu einigen Monaten in einem sehr dichten System mit seltenem Öffnen ca. 2–4 Monate in einem sehr dichten, kleinen Lagerraum unter günstigen Bedingungen teils auch länger, es hängt auch mit der Restfeuchte im Filament oder Undichtigkeiten ab. Diese Werte dienen ausschließlich der Orientierung. Die tatsächliche Wirkung hängt unter anderem ab von der Dichtheit des Behälters, der Umgebungsluftfeuchtigkeit, der Häufigkeit des Öffnens, dem Feuchtezustand des Filaments sowie von Menge, Qualität und Zustand des verwendeten Silikats. description: Top right side spool holder with PFTE tube connection for P1S/P2S/X2D. My setup consists of a single P1S with an AMS2 pro. I was tired of how, when I was drying filament in my AMS I couldn't easily print. (I know there is a side mount and I could change some PFTE tubes on the back, and maybe also add a PFTE tube splitter - but that is not easy fix…) I found some top side mounts, which worked fine for me. However, I noticed that the sudden movements of the tool head could cause a big pull in the filament, which could cause it to unroll a bit. The sudden pulls are also not ideal when printing in TPU. So I designed a version where you can connect a PFTE tube from the tool head to the spool holder. This eliminates any sudden pulls in the filament (I know it might give more resistance in the PFTE tube when printing in TPU). It has worked flawless when I want to print in PLA and PETG when my AMS is busy drying other filament. See attached video. Instructions Cut a piece of PFTE tube at 35 cm (or more conveniently, the width of the opening in the top after removing the glass plate). 2. Add one end of the PFTE tube to the holder from underneath. 3. Push the PFTE tube through the holder until it is flush with the surface 4. Attach the holder to the right side by pushing it down from the left side. It should be place roughly in the middle. 6. Push the holder down for a more secure fit 7. Take off the front of the tool head and take out the existing PFTE tube 8. Insert the PFTE tube from the holder 9. Put the front cover of the tool head back ín place 10. Put on a roll of filament on the holder and Insert it into the PFTE tube . Push the filament all the way though the PFTE tube until it can't go any further . On your printer or from the software, load the filament from the external spool and you are now ready to print :-)

model_name: Bambu X/P series XL Removeable Purge Bucket
description: This is an enlarged and improved version of my popular removeable purge box for the K2 series This is an easily removeable purge box with a side mounted handle. Designed for use in tight spaces, and to avoid the issue with purge chute clogs. Standoffs on the box keep it clear of fans and airflow in the back, while the large handle and mounting notch make removal and replacement a breeze. The box is angled to catch wayward filament poops before they disappear forever. This new model is over twice the capacity compared to the original (1750cm^3 vs 750cm^3), without requiring more depth behind the printer or interfering with vents or cables. I have been using this box for months and have only emptied it once, so it has plenty of capacity for large projects. Compared to the original model the handle is larger and the standoffs print cleaner. I also improved the geometry of the handle for smoother support interface. Highly recommend printing in PETG or something stronger/more heat resistant. Supports are needed for the box catch and handle, but no supports are needed on any of the bracket designs. To install, simply unscrew the self-tapping screws on either side of the purge chute, then screw in the bracket using those same screws. The box simply sits on the notch in the bracket, allowing for easy removal to the side or top. The box design is reversable if you want to pull from the other side, just mirror the model in your slicer. Included in this release is a new bracket for Bambu P and X series printers. Tested with an X2D, but to my understanding all of these printers use the same purge chute screw layout. The bracket design allows clearance for the external filtration box on the X2D. The box and bracket were originally designed for the K2 series. The original bracket should work for both the K2 and K2 pro. There is an additional bracket model for the K2 plus. The beauty of this box design is that it is platform-agnostic! If you have another printer (flashforge, elegoo, etc.) you would like to use this box design with, let me know! I would be happy to design a bracket to hang this box on! I'll just need some dimensions for the chute and screws. Need a smaller, faster to print box? Check out the original model here! https://makerworld.com/en/models/2007164-bambu-x-s-series-removable-purge-box

I invite you to test your printing skills and show me the smallest working version you can create! Model link in this post: https://makerworld.com/community/post/1832304 Have fun! Assembly Demonstration Maker’s Note I’m a hobby modeler, and I'm trying to enter MakerWorld contests with designs that push me beyond my limits. This is my biggest project so far, and it took many weekends of modeling, printing, testing, breaking parts, and going back to the drawing board. (I have an ever increasing pile of failed prototypes) My long-term goal is to create a free, easy-to-print and easy-to-assemble parametric generator that lets anyone generate a set of toy fingers fitted to their own hand. I do have a slight tendency toward maximalism, so I’m not ready to publish the fully customizable version until I’ve confirmed that it works reliably across a wide range of finger sizes, but in the meantime, I wanted to see how people react to the idea and whether it is worth putting the extra work into the generator. Please try the current version with an open mind, and feel free to leave constructive feedback. I’ll do my best to incorporate the feedback into the customizable version. Background I first came across this type of finger extension in this Adam Savage video. It immediately looked like something that would be incredibly fun to build and wear… Then I looked at the price tag :D (after spending so much time on this, I fully understand the pricing. Gary's fingers are truly a work of art both aesthetically and mechanically) That sent me down the rabbit hole of researching how I could make my own. While looking through existing projects and mechanisms, I found the work of Dragonator , whose notes were invaluable during the development process. A big shoutout to him. Seeing his amazing model, I’m sure he is one of the few who understand both the pain of designing a mechanism like this and the joy of finally putting it on for the first time and feeling the fingers move with your hand. Design Considerations I’ll demonstrate the main design decisions with pictures below, but these were the areas I focused on most: Cylindrical, adaptive geometry The mechanism is built around mostly cylindrical finger sections. This makes a final design I find aesthetic. I believe most similar finger have an adaptable base section that goes around the fingers, and the rest of the mechanism is interchangeable. I wanted the whole finger to be driven by parameters. Low-profile control shaft movement One thing I struggled a lot with is how to keep the controller shaft as low to the body as possible both at the two end states, and during the movement. With a few tradeoffs, I think I well achieved both. Easy assembly This was the thing I feared the most. In the commercial version, there is obviously no assembly required, it is put together beautifully with additional hardware. I tried different ways of connecting parts, and after multiple failures came up with a snap-in design, which I'm truly proud of. Clean seam lines I wanted the finger to have a clean, cylindrical look when it's straight. However cylinders generally have problems with seam lines. I intentionally placed a straight groove at the bottom of the parts, so you wont need to paint seam lines yourself, you can just hit print and know the lines will look acceptable. The support tradeoff This is the price I decided to pay. Many things in my design are supported, and while many I could have eliminated, I decided the one-time price of removing the supports is well covered by the gains I got in aesthetics and assembly. How the Mechanism Works The finger sections are linked together so that movement from your real finger is transferred through the control shafts to the extended segments. This is not a difficult project, but it is still somewhat complex. I ask everyone to first watch the mechanism animation on the bottom, go have a high level understanding of what we are building. BASIC CUSTOMIZATION MIDDLE_LENGTH The desired length of the middle phalanx. DISTAL_LENGTH The desired length of the distal phalanx. (for thumbs as well) INNER_PART_WIDTH The width of the components inside the mechanism. (gears, shafts) ADVANCED CUSTOMIZATION WALL_THICKNESS The thickness of all walls, including the hinge wall around pins, where applicable. PIN_DIAMETER The diameter of connector pins. PIN_OPENING_NARROW_WIDTH_MULTIPLIER The width of the pin hole openings' narrow part as a percentage of the PIN_DIAMETER. The wider it is, the easier to press in the pin, but also the less resistance to keep it in the hole. CLEARANCE The distance between parts. (e.g. if the gear is 5mm wide, and the clearance is 0.4mm, then the gear-space will be 5.4mm wide) HOLE_CLEARANCE How much bigger should the pin-holes be than the pins. (e.g. if the pin's diameter is 2mm, and the clearance is 0.2mm, then the pin-hole has a diameter of 2.2mm) SUPPORT_CLEARANCE The distance between the support and the part it supports. If it is too small, the support will fuse with the part, and not break off easily, if it is too large, the support will not help the part, and the part will sag. It is wise to set the support clearance in relation to the layer height. Since by default I'll use .2mm layers, that is the default of this) RENDERING RENDER_MODE Different views of the model. complete: shows you the finger as it is supposed to be assembled print: arranges the parts ready for printing others: individual parts can be rendered in isolation SHOW_SUPPORT If enabled, the supports are added to the model, if disabled, then not. If you have trouble printing the supports accurately, feel free to disable this, and autogenerate supports by the slicer. XRAY Chops off half of the parts, so you can better see the inner mechanisms. Maker’s Note I’m a hobby modeler, and I'm trying to enter MakerWorld contests with designs that push me beyond my limits. This is my biggest project so far, and it took many weekends of modeling, printing, testing, breaking parts, and going back to the drawing board. (I have an ever increasing pile of failed prototypes) My long-term goal was to create a free, easy-to-print and easy-to-assemble parametric generator that lets anyone generate a set of toy fingers fitted to their own hand, and as promised, here it is! (perhaps you have found this model through my first prototype ) Background I first came across this type of finger extension in this Adam Savage video. It immediately looked like something that would be incredibly fun to build and wear… Then I looked at the price tag :D (after spending so much time on this, I fully understand the pricing. Gary's fingers are truly a work of art both aesthetically and mechanically) That sent me down the rabbit hole of researching how I could make my own. While looking through existing projects and mechanisms, I found the work of Dragonator , whose notes were invaluable during the development process. A big shoutout to him. Seeing his amazing model, I’m sure he is one of the few who understand both the pain of designing a mechanism like this and the joy of finally putting it on for the first time and feeling the fingers move with your hand. I have already shared my prototype on MakerWorld, and now sharing the fully parametric version. Design Considerations Thin Frame I've got some constructive feedback on the first attempt's cylindrical design. In this version, I kept the mechanism profile as low as possible, to allow you to create decorative skins around it to your liking. (Let me know in the comments if you want cutters or examples, but most parts are simple rectangles) Easy to Replace Parts The parts are designed to be easy to replace and change. (e.g. different fingertip designs) Parametric Dimensions In order to best fit all finger sizes and preferences, I allow users to change a wide range of parameters through MakerWorld's Parametric Model Maker. Not only the finger sleeve, but the whole model is driven through parameters, including the gears. Low Profile Shaft One thing I struggled a lot with is how to keep the controller shaft as low to the body as possible both at the two end states, and during the movement. With a few tradeoffs, I think I well achieved both. Easy Assembly While I believe my snap-in mechanism was elegant and simple, it still took time and preparation to use filament hinges. In this version, I simplified assembly even further, so all hinges are already printed into the model. You just print and assemble. Designed Support I built support into the model itself. (depending on your printer accuracy, they might fuse. in this case you have the ability to individually remove the problematic support pieces and replace them with auto generated support) How the Mechanism Works The finger sections are linked together so that movement from your real finger is transferred through the control shafts to the extended segments. The animation below shows the movement more clearly than I could explain it in text. FAQ Q: Your model is so amazing, can I give you multiple boosts? A: Yes, you can. Thanks. Final Note If you happened to have a failed print, please don't be mad. If it makes you feel a little better, I burnt through this many failed prototypes, to be able to create a good generator for you :)

description: Description A modular cyberpunk / sci-fi gauntlet armor kit designed to turn a simple glove into a futuristic wearable cosplay prop. The model includes separate armor plates for the fingers, thumb, knuckles, back of the hand and wrist area. The pieces are printed separately and then glued onto a real glove. I used a fleece glove, but the parts can be attached to many types of fabric gloves depending on surface, flexibility and glue compatibility. I also included a raw full-glove reference file with all parts placed together, so you can see where each element is intended to go before assembly. This file is mainly for placement reference; for printing, use the separated armor parts / print profile. Sizing / Scaling This gauntlet was designed for my hand size: 20 cm from the wrist crease to the tip of the middle finger . To resize it for your hand, measure the same distance on your own hand and use this formula: Scale (%) = Your hand length / 20 cm × 100 Examples: 18 cm hand → 18 / 20 × 100 = 90% 19 cm hand → 19 / 20 × 100 = 95% 21 cm hand → 21 / 20 × 100 = 105% 22 cm hand → 22 / 20 × 100 = 110% Apply the same scale to all armor parts so the proportions stay consistent. Hand width, finger thickness and glove stretch can vary, so I recommend printing one or two finger plates first and testing the placement before printing the full set. Assembly Print the separate armor plates. Place the parts on the glove and check the full layout before gluing. Start with the larger hand and wrist pieces, then continue with the fingers and thumb. Glue the parts onto the glove one by one. I used hot glue for assembly. Be careful: hot glue can pass through thin fabric and burn your hand. I recommend wearing a second glove underneath the glove you are working on while positioning and pressing the parts. Test each part placement before gluing permanently. Printing Notes The included print profile has support settings tuned for easy removal. The model does use supports, but in my test print they came off cleanly and without much effort. Approximate material use from my print: Total material: around 120 g Supports: around 40 g The model was created as a wearable prop, so the armor plates are separated to make assembly easier and to allow the glove to remain flexible. description: Want a replica of a US WW1 grenade? This is the original "pineapple" grenade from WW1 that was the predecessor to the Mk2 grenade we all know from WW2. This grenade has a spoon handle that flies off when you pull the pin, just like the real thing would. Background: Introduced in 1917, the US Mk1 Grenade was the first fragmentation hand grenade developed by the United States for use in World War I. It was notoriously complicated to operate in the field, often requiring the user to manually ignite the fuse before throwing. Due to soldiers struggling to arm it under pressure, the Mk 1 grenade was quickly recalled and replaced by the improved Mk 2 grenade fuze in 1918 (which this model depicts). Spring options (for flying handle) Metal Spring (recommended) – if you have a metal spring, even a pen spring will usually work, then print the metal spring profile. It is designed to work with the Bambu Store's 0.5x7x12mm spring (linked lower on the page). If you use a pen spring, you can usually cut it in half and get two springs. Plastic Spring – if you don't have a metal spring, but still want the handle to fly off, then print the plastic spring profile. If the spring eventually wears out, just print a new one and pop it in. Don't leave the spring under tension when not using it as it will wear out much faster. Avoid Matte and Silk filament for the spring itself, Basic and Metal work better. No Flying Handle - if you don't want the handle to fly off and just want a grenade model, simply print either version and don't put in a spring. Bambu filaments used Basic Bronze Dark gray filaments are also period appropriate Silk+ Silver Assembly takes seconds Metal Spring Version 1. Insert the peg into the topper while its upside down. 2. Then insert the metal spring in the same way. 3. Then screw the grenade topper onto the body of the grenade. Doing so upside down is easiest. (this depicts a Mk2 grenade with the yellow stripe, but this Mk1 screws together in the same way) Plastic Spring Version 1. Insert the printed spring into the topper. Make sure the peg pops out, rotate it if it doesn't until it does. 2. Then simply screw the topper onto the grenade while upside down. (this depicts a Mk2 grenade with the yellow stripe, but this Mk1 screws together in the same way)

Geralt’s steel sword from The Witcher game series, designed for slaying humans. The silver sword consists of a total of 14 3D-printed parts. Like the other swords from my production, this sword is assembled using an M5 threaded rod that runs through the entire length of the sword. Everything is fully concealed and not visible anywhere. Thanks to the use of the threaded rod, the sword is very sturdy, suitable even for fencing, and will not break. All parts of the sword are connected by an M5 threaded rod with a length of 1000mm , which runs through the center of all components. M5 lock nuts are installed at both ends of the threaded rod. One M5 nut is located in the Blade_4 part, and the other in the Pommel part. Start screwing the threaded rod into the Blade_1 part until the end of the rod is 974 mm from the bottom of the Blade_1 part . Then slide the remaining parts onto the threaded rod according to the assembly drawing. The nut in the Blade_1 and Pommel parts are embedded during printing. To insert the nut, a pause is created in the print profile, allowing the nut to be placed into the 3D print. Blade_1 and Pommel are printed on a separate build plate in order to minimize potential losses in case the nut insertion into the 3D print is unsuccessful. For the first time on this sword, an improved anti-rotation system has been used to prevent the blade sections from twisting relative to each other. The alignment pins are now integrated directly into the printed parts, so there is no need to print and insert them separately. Enjoy the print, and I hope you like Geralt the Witcher’s silver sword. CYBERPUNK OUTCAST FLINTLOCK MUSKET (DART BLASTER) "In a dark cyberpunk future, everything and everyone belongs to the corporations. Only the outcasts have never been owned. Corporations can lock your implants, freeze your bank account, and disable your smart rifle. But they cannot disable steel, black powder, and flint. Free people are forced to fight with the weapons of the past. A flintlock requires no firmware, no subscription, and answers to no one but its wielder." Inspired by this concept, the CYBERPUNK OUTCAST FLINTLOCK MUSKET is a fully 3D-printable elastic-powered toy dart blaster that combines the appearance of a cyberpunk firearm with the operation of a traditional flintlock musket. Rather than simply resembling a flintlock, it recreates the complete firing sequence with a functional cock, frizzen, powder pan, trigger, sear, and half-cock safety. The blaster is muzzle-loaded. Insert the dart into the barrel, seat it with the ramrod, cock the lock, aim, and fire. The entire loading and firing sequence is designed to resemble the operation of a historical flintlock while using a completely different internal propulsion system. The model features a compact folding design. Both the stock and the front assembly lock securely in their folded and deployed positions, allowing the blaster to be stored or transported in a much smaller package while remaining ready for use within seconds. Designed primarily for PETG printing, the model is almost entirely 3D printed. No metal springs, screws, glue, filament retaining pins, or other additional hardware are required. The only non-printed components are the elastic bands used for propulsion and mechanism operation. In addition to the original HEX 13 mm dart version, the project also includes a separate conversion profile for standard 0.5-inch foam darts. Features Fully functional flintlock-style firing mechanism Functional half-cock safety Muzzle-loaded operation with ramrod Folding stock with adjustable length of pull Folding front assembly for compact storage 99% PETG 3D printed No metal springs, screws, glue, or additional hardware. The only non-printed components are the elastic materials; the carriage guide rails also require lubrication during assembly. Includes a conversion profile for standard 0.5-inch foam darts Compatible with Bambu Lab P1 and A1 build volumes, as well as similar-sized printers (not compatible with the A1 Mini) Ammunition & Performance The primary configuration is designed to fire lightweight HEX 13 mm PETG or TPU printed darts weighing approximately 1–2 g. Typical performance: Muzzle velocity: approximately 40 ft/s (12 m/s) Effective range: approximately 3–10 m Shot dispersion at 3 m may reach approximately 0.25 m A separate conversion profile is included for users who prefer standard 0.5-inch foam darts. This project is intended primarily as an engineering and mechanical showcase that faithfully recreates the operation of a flintlock mechanism using almost entirely 3D-printed components. I got just the thing for you — some shiny, brand-new military-grade chrome. Just make sure to upgrade your ICE and keep those damn netrunners off your back, hermano. So, what's it gonna be... time to become a legend, no?» 1. Concept Few pieces of sci-fi equipment are as iconic as the cybernetic mantis blade. This project is inspired by that legendary concept while deliberately avoiding a direct reproduction of any specific design. Instead of replicating an existing prop, the focus was placed on engineering, functionality, and manufacturability. Every component was designed from the ground up to create a fully mechanical model that is both visually convincing and practical to build. The result is a 100% 3D-printable, fully functional mechanism that requires no additional hardware — no screws, springs, magnets, pins, or glue. Every moving part is printed and assembled into a working extendable blade mechanism. Rather than being just a static display piece, this model was created as an engineering project that demonstrates what can be achieved using modern desktop 3D printing while capturing the unmistakable aesthetic of the cyberpunk genre. 3. Description Overview The model consists of a forearm bracer, decorative hydraulic cylinders, a three-link extension mechanism, an extendable claw blade, and a manual drive handle. The complete project consists of 78 printed parts, plus two dedicated assembly wrenches used during construction. The wrenches are assembly tool only and are not part of the finished model. Despite the term "blade" being used, the model does not incorporate an actual sharpened blade. All exposed edges are intentionally blunt, with a minimum chamfer of 1.5 mm, making the finished model suitable as a cosplay prop or display piece rather than a cutting tool. To operate the mechanism, place the bracer around your forearm and secure the two halves using the integrated locking clips. Pull the drive handle downward to deploy the linkage and extend the blade. Pull the handle upward to fully retract the blade and fold the mechanism back into its compact position. The mechanism is fully mechanical and operates reliably in any orientation, whether held horizontally, vertically, or upside down. With the exception of several screws and the internal gears used in the blade extension mechanism, the design is fully symmetrical and can be assembled for either the left or the right arm. Dimensions Deployed: 800 × 196 × 124 mm Folded: 350 × 130 × 124 mm The articulated linkage extends to an overall length of 600 mm, measured from the first folding pivot to the end of the claw blade. 4. Every assembly step is explained in detail, making the build process straightforward despite the model's sophisticated mechanical design.

description: Want a life-size replica of the Laser Guided APKWS Rocket used by the US, Ukraine, NATO, and many other militaries? This is around ~6ft / ~2m long and can be assembled in seconds just by screwing the printed parts together, no glue is required. It comes with moving fold-out fins for extra realism. You can also print optional wall mounts to place it on the wall. It is designed to use as little filament as possible while still being strong and sturdy. Note: this new model is completely interchangable with my other Hydra rocket models (the screw-together version, not the peg assembly version). So you can print any parts from this model and combine it with other hydra rockets you've printed. Bambu filaments used Warhead at the top Basic Yellow Silk+ Titan Gray Overture Silk Copper ( Amazon link ) Polymaker Army Green ( Amazon link ) Rocket Body Basic Light Gray A white filament would work as well Silk+ Red Silk+ Silver (for the mid-body fins) Polymaker Metallic Silver ( Amazon link ) Basic Silver would work great too Engine Metal Iridium Gold Silk+ Gold would work too Assembly is super easy The parts simply screw together, so if you make a mistake you can just unscrew and re-screw in seconds, no problems. Make sure you don't over tighten – they are quite strong, but all plastic screws can eventually break under enough pressure – you should be able to screw them until they feel snug. 1. Screw the main body together, which includes 4 longer white/gray segments, one shorter red segment, and one short white/gray segment. 2. Then take each of the silver fins and connect all 4 to a base by sliding them together. It may take a little bit of forcer, pushing down on a table can help. 3. Now the assembled fins and clip them into the tall gray section. They should snap in easily if you line it up right. If you can't get the fins to snap in, try a different (probably lower) angle. 4. Next begin screwing on the other parts one by one to the far right end (the end with the red strip). 5. Then, assemble the warhead portion at the tip with the pegs provided like you see below and screw it onto the top of the rocket. 6. Lastly, begin connecting the rocket motor by connecting the top threaded piece to the bottom piece with the two long pegs provided. 7. Then the final step is to attach the fins to the rocket motor – the will snap into place with little force. Note that they must be facing clockwise , not counter clockwise. If you insert them counter clockwise you will find that they don't fold all the way.

description: "Why does that pirate have a ship's wheel attached to his belt?" "Arrr... it's driving me nuts!" Now you can finally tell one of the oldest pirate jokes... while being the punchline. description: Spartan/Trojan War Hound Dog Helmet – Fully Articulated Bring the glory of the ancient world to your furry companion! This isn’t just a costume piece; it’s a high-detail, 3D-printable tribute to the legendary warriors of Troy and Sparta, specifically designed to fit the unique anatomy of a dog. Whether it’s for a photoshoot, a convention, or just to show the neighborhood who the real "Alpha" is, this helmet is the ultimate accessory for your four-legged warrior. 🏛️ History of the Model The design is inspired by the Corinthian-style helmets used by ancient Greek hoplites and later stylized in Trojan lore. Historically, these helmets were symbols of strength, protection, and status. I wanted to translate that intimidating, majestic silhouette into something comfortable and wearable for pets. The intricate swirls and Celtic-inspired patterns on the cheek guards add a "mythical" flair, bridging the gap between historical accuracy and high-fantasy cosplay. ⚙️ Functional Design & Assembly This model is unique because it features fully functional articulated cheek guards (flaps) . The Hinge System: Unlike static models, this helmet uses custom-designed hinges. You will need to print the included hinge pins separately. Assembly: Once printed, align the cheek guards with the main helmet body and slide the 3D-printed pins through the knuckles. This allows the flaps to swing outward, making it much easier to put on and take off your dog while ensuring a comfortable fit against their jawline. Durability: The crest is reinforced to handle the "zoomies," but it remains lightweight enough for medium to large breeds to wear comfortably. 📏 Sizing and Fitting Your Warrior Because every "Good Boy" is a different size, scaling is critical. Measurement: To get the perfect fit, I highly recommend using my Cosplay Calipers Measuring Tool . Measure the width of your dog's head between the ears and the length from the brow to the back of the skull. Scaling & Orientation: If you need to scale this up for a Great Dane or down for a Terrier, or if you need to slice it to fit a smaller print bed, check out my comprehensive guide: How to Size, Scale, Cut, Pin, and Orient Armor in Bambu Studio . 🛠️ Printing Tips Filament: Looks incredible in Silk Silver PLA or "Antique Gold." tags: halo|halo energy sword|elite|elite energy sword|arbiter|master chief|halo cosplay|energy sword
description: Ever wanted a life-sized Halo energy sword? Me too! I was surprised that I couldn't find a print for this, so I made one myself. Coming in at just over a metre long, this is a faithful replica of the iconic Halo weapon. It looks great printed in either translucent blue or clear PETG, with light channels down the middle of each blade and compartments on both blades for electronics (batteries - sized for 18650 cells, control boards etc). Everything is designed to key together to allow for easy printing and assembly. This print takes up 5 full plates on my P2S and took a few days to print, with around 1.5kg of blade material. Each plate is as packed as it can reasonably be. It can of course be printed on smaller printers like the A1 and can be scaled down appropriately to suit this. Key assembly steps: Print and attach hilt sections together. I printed these in a grey PLA+, then stuck them together with CA glue. The fit is tight and may need a bit of force. There is a channel down the inside of the hilt to route wires for lights or switches. Optional - sand, prime, paint hilt. I painted with a base of black acrylic and then steel / silver acrylic on top, then sanded paint down in places to give a weathered look. Print blade base parts and attach to hilt. The fit between the hilt and blade base is a bit looser than any of the other joins, as this gives a bit more tolerance for any accumulated accuracy errors throughout the print. The intended attachment method is to use an M8 nut / insert / T-nuts heat-set into the handle, and an M8*40mm bolt through the blade into this nut / insert. You could however just use a suitable epoxy to bond the two parts well. Either way, this should be a secure connection once properly glued / torqued down. Attach blade pieces to blade base, finishing up with the optional reinforcing bar (secured using M3 heat inserts and M3*10mm bolts into the blade sections). You could use a suitable glue to attach these together, though the keyed fit is pretty tight. Optional finishing steps. I used a UV-set clear resin to fill the join lines between sections and make things look a bit more continuous. This certainly isn't a magic fix as it is obviously still printed in pieces, but it does help! You can then install electronics if desired. I found LED rope or LED-strips worked well (ideally with high density RGB COBs. If they're too far apart you get a less diffuse effect). Want a replica of the frag grenade from game PUBG (Player Unknown Battleground)? This grenade even has a spring-loaded handle that flies off when you pull the pin. The PUBG frag grenade is similar to the real-life M67 grenade, however, there are some distinct differences in its rounded shape and differences with the fuze that this model reflects. Spring options (for flying handle) Metal Spring (recommended) – if you have a metal spring, even a pen spring will usually work, then print the metal spring profile. Bambu Store's 0.5x7x12mm spring is what this model is designed to work with. Pen springs work as well though, many different types have been tested and work fine. You can often cut pen springs in half and get two grenade springs since this model only needs a 12mm long spring and pen springs tend to be about 24mm. Plastic Spring – if you don't have a metal spring, but still want the handle to fly off, then print the plastic spring profile. If the spring eventually wears out, just print a new one and pop it in. Don't leave the spring under tension when not using it as it will wear out much faster. Avoid Matte and Silk filament for the spring itself, Basic and Metal work better. No Flying Handle - if you don't want the handle to fly off and just want a grenade model, simply print either version and don't put in a spring. Bambu filaments used Silk+ Silver Matte Yellow Polymaker Army Green ( Amazon link ) Matte Dark Green works too Metal Spring Version Assembly 1. Use the two pegs to connect the two halves of the grenade together. 2. Flip the silver top upside down and insert the peg. Make sure the peg is sticking out of the top, if not rotate 90 degrees. 3. Insert your spring into the silver top next, just like you did with the peg. 4. Screw the silver top onto the grenade – keeping the silver top upside down makes this easier (so spring doesn't fall out while screwing it on). That's it – now you can attach the spoon handle, put in the pin, and use it – enjoy! Plastic Spring Version Assembly 1. Use the two pegs to connect the two halves of the grenade together. 2. Flip the silver top upside down and insert the spring. Make sure the spring's peg is sticking out of the top, if not rotate 90 degrees. 3. Screw the silver top onto the grenade – keeping the silver top upside down makes this easier (so spring doesn't fall out while screwing it on). That's it – now you can attach the spoon handle, put in the pin, and use it – enjoy!

description: Model for Thor's Hammer from Thor: Love and Thunder. Hammer head splits into different pieces like in the movie and are held together using magnets. Print orientation in the .3mf matches the orientations I used when I printed it, but you might need to test printing in different orientations if the fit between two of the hammer head pieces isn't lining up well. The magnets used are 10x2mm and are superglued into the holes. You'll need around 210 magnets. Depending on the infill percentage and what you intend to do with the hammer (display vs carry around), you might need to adjust the strength of the magnets. I used 20% infill for a display build and the hammer stays together, but the pieces can come apart come apart when yanked. 20% infill gives the hammer a nice weight to it, but 10-15% might be better for balancing with the magnet strength. I printed all the pieces on an Ender v2 with a smooth plate. I used Cura to slice it so it just had straight supports. I used a generic coffee brown PLA for the handle and generic silk silver PLA for the hammer head pieces. The Bambu filaments selected below should match the generic ones I used. I tested some of the prints on my Bambu P2S and they printed fine. I used tree supports on the starting textured plate to test the prints. I would recommend a smooth plate since most of the head pieces print on one of the hammer faces so smooth will look better. I transferred all the settings I used in Cura into the .3mf, but did slow down the print settings for the P2S with silk. Leather strap was found at craft store and cut to fit the hole in the hammer hilt.

Hey everyone! A life size model of the iconic WW1 shotgun, the Winchester model 1897. This does not fire or technically cycle, but it does have a simple moveable pump action mechanism. Each plate has been separated to individual parts, such as the receiver, barrels, foregrip, stock, etc. Of course some of the larger parts (like the stock and heatshield) had to be split and have dowels that are printed with them. These dowels aren't meant to hold the model together alone, they more act as guides to make sure everything is straight, so make sure to use glue as well!!!!! :) In order for the foregrip to slide on the mag tube, you may need to do a bit of sanding post printing, but it shouldn't be too bad. I apologize for the inconvenience, getting tolerances right with these kind of things can be difficult! Assembly is easy as pie. Start by gluing the 2 tubes halves together. After this insert the longer tube (barrel) into the top hole of the receiver, then insert the bottom one as well. Make sure the flared end of the second tube is AWAY from the receiver (this is what the heat shield will later rest on/touch). Add the assembled stock to the other end (make sure to join the two stock sides in the correct orientation). Afte this simply slide on the assembled heat shield and the foregrip to the bottom tube! If you have any questions feel free to ask. Assembly shouldn't be too hard :), I will likely post assembly pics soon as I am going to print another. If this model does well, I will also add a bayonet for it!

description: Want a replica of the stackable grenade made for the US Marines and Special Forces? This grenade can be stacked to combine multiple grenades, just like the real thing. It features a realistic replica fuze that is spring-loaded with a spoon handle that flies off when you pull the pin. What is it a replica of? The Scalable Offensive Hand Grenade is a modular military munition designed to produce blast overpressure instead of utilizing traditional metal fragmentation. This weapon system allows for the configuration of multiple explosive segments to adjust the blast yield based on specific mission requirements. Developed for use in confined spaces like bunkers or trenches, it is intended to provide a controlled concussive effect while reducing the risk of collateral damage to friendly forces during close-quarters operations. This grenade has been used by special forces teams in Ukraine as well as the US Marine Corps under the designation Mk21 Mod 0 Scalable Offensive Hand Grenade (SOHG). Connecting grenades together You can string together as many grenades as you want. Simply use the screw fitting attachment (shown in orange below) to screw multiple grenades together. Karambit Lore A fast and simple two-color karambit model featuring a bold Lore-inspired design in gold and black . The model is printed in two separate halves , which are glued together with superglue after printing. Two built-in alignment connectors help position both halves correctly and ensure a clean and precise assembly. Extra attention has been given to the strength of the blade and finger ring. The thickness and weight have also been carefully adjusted to give the karambit a satisfying and substantial feel when held, spun or used for simple tricks. model_name: Zote the Mighty Mask - Hollow Knight
description: This one is for Squidward who relentlessly pushed for me to make the model, and then was so grateful when I got started! I hope you enjoy it! I designed this mask a bit different from my others and I am happy with the outcome. Essentially, I incorporated the mesh eyes directly into the mask so they don't need to be added or printed separately. If you would prefer to print it all in one color (to save time and money), you should be able to easily paint the mesh portion black with some black acrylic paint. I also experimented with how the horns are printed and attached to the head to make them more integrated into the design and also to avoid needing supports on them. My first version was a bit to tight to fit on my head, but it fit on everyone else's in my home. In this version I tweaked the hole size for the head and flattened the bottom of the print a bit to improve printability and eliminate some of the supports. I believe this should fit any head pretty easily now. One under appreciated part of my work is figuring out how to get a model absolutely maximize the space of a p1s sized printer. In this case of this print, lots of adjustments were made to get it just right. For this hobby (designing and 3d printing models) I certainly go through phases. After filling up all the wall space in a room with Hollow Knight masks, I prioritized new areas. This was a nice break from my current phase which has been pond fountains, I think I have one more of those left in me before switching again. I am experimenting with designing a toy for kids during long car rides, I am excited about it and hope to share it soon!

description: A fully 3d printed Single-shot Cap-powered BB pistol! Fully 3d printed springs. Has 10 bodies to print, can fit on an a1 build plate at minimum. To use, get a standard 8-shot ring cap, then cut off an individual cap using a utility knife, being careful with fingers. Break the barrel (shown in images) by pressing the barrel release latch (shown in images as well) on the left hand side of the pistol body, then lift the barrel, tilting it upwards from the end near the hammer. Load the singular cap into the recess at the end of the barrel, making sure it sits snug. To lock the barrel, manually push the barrel release latch now protruding from the right hand side back into its original position. this can be fiddly ads the hole is quite precise. This is a muzzle loader-so from the muzzle, cut out a small square of tissue. Place it on the muzzle and get a standard 6mm BB. place the BB on top of the tissue wad and using a blunt skewer, ram the BB and the wad into the barrel until you feel it stop (do not ram too hard as the cap holder will snap). Then you are ready to fire! To reset the trigger, pull the hammer back manually and hold it, then let go of the trigger and it should spring back into place. You can pull it gently to help with this. *DISCLAIMER* I am not at fault for misuse of this toy causing damage to living beings and surroundings. model_name: Mandalorian Grav Charge With Lightup Mod (Breach)
description: This is my version of the Grav Charge and holder from the show The Mandalorian. I designed it looking at pictures from the show to be as accurate as I could but also be a light up prop. To that end I designed it around these little magnet operated light up warning lights: https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0CMTJQRYX . The lights have a reed sensor in them that when the magnet is on the back they don't do anything but when you remove the magnet they light up. And the pattern is similar to the actual grav charge, close enough without needing expensive electronics or wiring anything. The back of the holder has some indents of 15mm magnets. Glue some magnets to the back and that will be strong enough to keep the light off. When you pull the grav charge off the holder the reed switch turns the unit on and the lights start to flash then after about 10 seconds go to the circular pattern. I added magnets on the bottom of the grav charges themselves also so you can still stick it to something like in the show but without affecting the light. Place it back on the holder and it turns back off. I went with these lights because they also turn themselves off after a couple minutes so they won't kill the battery if you leave them out. Print Details I printed the body and holder in Bambu ABS - Silver. The body has scarf seam turned on in its object settings which leaves less of a seam on the outside but does sometime affect the color slightly in that spot. If you are going to paint them leave scarf seam on, if you are going to leave them as is you may want to turn that off so the color is more consistent but the seam will be more noticeable. The cover is Bambu PETG Translucent Clear that I then used a red Sharpie oil based paint pen on because I couldn't find a good clear red filament. The combination ended up looking really good so that's what I would recommend or even possibly just a red marker. For printing the cover I have the speeds set to 20mm/s and a custom Bambu Transparent PETG setting that turns off cooling. It's the only way to get a mostly clear lens but you can of course use standard settings, the lens just might not be as clear and the LEDs won't be as distinguishable. Or you can buy a after market clear lens sized for about 28mm. I tried to optimize the print so no supports are required and the 2 x 4 magnets on the bottom should be press fit although I'd add a dab of glue behind them. The holder for the light also is press fit but you can also glue that in to be more secure. Since the lights turn themselves off the batteries should last for years so personally I glued them in.

model_name: Instant Ronin Double Tanto - Magnetic Knives
description: Instant Ronin Double Tanto - Magnetic Knives Channel your inner samurai with the Instant Ronin - Double Tanto (Magnetic Edition) ! This isn't just a pair of sleek 3D-printable props—it's a fully mechanical, dual-sword ecosystem. By utilising a precise arrangement of 5-off 6mm x 3mm magnets per sword, these Tantos completely ditch traditional metal springs for solid-state physics. But here is the real kicker: One sword acts as the activator for the other. Mating the companion sword into the other triggers the magnetic mechanisms, releasing the internal locks and allowing for an instant, seamless locking - and the reverse when withdrawing. Absolutely zero glue required. Every magnet pocket has been engineered for a perfect, satisfying, push-fit. Print two, link them up, and prepare to lose hours of your life to the ultimate fidget experience. Features Triple-Action Magnetic Mechanics: Uses opposing and attracting magnetic fields to safely lock the blades closed, assist the deployment, and lock them open. 5-Magnet Precision Layout: Optimised specifically for standard, high-strength 6mm x 3mm cylinder magnets (5-off per sword). 100% Glue-Free Assembly: Meticulously tuned tolerances mean every magnet snaps tightly into place. Save the superglue for fixing the things you break with the Tanto. Zero Mechanical Springs: No metal springs to find, bend, fatigue, or lose tension over time—magnetism doesn't wear out! Dual-Tanto Blade Profile: A sleek, aggressive geometric aesthetic that looks as sharp as the mechanism feels. Maximum Fidget Factor Magnet Assembly Guide ⚠️ Crucial Tip: Because these are a push-fit, double-check your magnet orientation before you press them home. Getting a backward magnet out of a tight 3D-printed pocket is a special kind of pain you don't want to experience. Use a spare magnet as a reference tool! Follow this exact sequence to ensure the polarity works flawlessly, see my sectioned CAD image and assembly pictures to help with the below: The Master Slider Magnet [1]: Push a magnet into the bottom pocket of the Blade Slider . This can face any direction you like. Once it’s in, this magnet is the "Master" that dictates the rest of the build. The Extended Lock [2]: Press a magnet into the lower forward pocket of the Handle . This magnet must REPEL Magnet #1. (This repelling force is the secret sauce that lifts the slider up into the notch to lock the blade open!) The Retracted Lock [3]: Press a magnet into the bottom rear pocket of the Handle . This magnet must ATTRACT Magnet #1, snapping the blade securely closed so they doesn't slide apart when closed. The Kinetic "Spring" Caps [4]: Press one magnet into each of the two Circular Caps at the top hilt. Both of these magnets must REPEL each other, creating that crisp, snappy detent.

After a longer wait than I hoped, the supported version of my unexpectedly popular flamberge print is ready!! This was the first ever success that I had with taking a large video game sword and making a good, 3D printed version of it. I identified some problems with the original design and I have added some very minor details to the model and added a channel for a 4ft/1.22m long, 5/16"/.794cm diameter fiberglass rod through about 3/4 of the length of the prop sword. The sword is 5.6ft/1.71m long when fully assembled. In the U.S. I have found that the easiest access to rods like this is by purchasing driveway markers from a hardware store like Home Depot or Lowe's. To assemble, start with the end of the hilt, add your rod, and start stacking the pieces from there. If a piece doesn't slide easily over the rod and overlapping section of the piece below it, there's a good chance that it needs to be rotated 180 degrees. IMPORTANT FOR ASSEMBLY: Please do NOT print this version if you can't find a supporting rod - the rod doesn't leave space for meaningful printed structure (keying blades only) and the blade will snap with ease if assembled without support. Also note that the last 1.6ft/.5m of length are unsupported in the interest of balance and weight reduction - this means that hitting something with more than gentle force will likely snap the end of the blade. That said, I think that with appropriate caution this version should work well to take to conventions/festivals. My build was done with SUNLU PETG. I would recommend PETG or a material with high impact toughness, especially if you want to take it out and about at an event!
